LESTER STAFFOR D McELWA IN is the 106th Grand Master of the
Gra nd Lodge of California and the 52nd Attorney to serve in that office. His
large six foot two inch frame, typical of his Scotch-Iris h and English ancestry,
is dedicated to the advanceme nt of our high Masonic principles. H e will be
remembered for his dynamic and innova tive leadership, which reflected determination, initiative, strength and wisdom.
His ability to view all facets of a problem and quickly find the best solution is indica tive of his legal training. This attribute has been of great value
to the Fraternity ; for men knowledgeable in the field of jurispruden ce consider him to be an outstandin g lawyer .
"LES," as he is affectionat ely known, while the chief executive officer of
Gra nd Lodge, made important decisions relative to its operation which will
affect the Grand Lodge for years to come; and while he did so with a firm
hand, he always maintained a considerate attitude toward every one concerned.
His sincerity and conscientio us attention to every detail of his office, together with his love of family and the emotional sensitivity concerning those
with whom he has close personal ties, are familiar to all who know him.
A friendl y personality and smile graced all of his visitations; and whatever the size of the gathering, large or small, all present always enjoyed the
warmth of his fellowship.
A native son, born January 1, 1910 in San Mateo, the son of George W.
McElwain a nd Ethel Dickson McElwain, Les spent the first seventeen years
of his life in San Mateo a nd Burlingame. He was one of the first eagle scouts
in San ::\fateo County and all three of his sons are eagle scouts. He attended
Stanford University , where the leadership qualities of his personality first
became evident. He was prominent in t be University 's athletic program, as
were two of his tall sons. Les graduated from Stanford in 193 1 with a Degree
in Economics, and· in 1934 received his Doctor of Jurisprudence D egree from
the Stanford Law School. He was admitted to the Bar tha t year and commenced t he practice of law with a leading Oakland law firm with which h e
was associated for six years until he resigned to serve his Country.
Like all three of his sons, who have served in the U.S. Navy, L es volunteered for active duty in 1940 a nd was commissioned a Lt. (jg) in the U.S.
Naval Reserve. H e served five years in the United States Navy during World
War II and was released from du ty in 1945 with the rank of Commande r. H e
then established his law office in Oakland, where h e presently specialize.<; in
the trial of civil cases and probate matters.
It was during h is military service that he met and married l\fargrite B.
Ludlow of Worland, Wyoming, and both share a mutual pride in their fine
family of three sons.
Les McElwain throughou t his entire life has given of himself in many
activities of public service. These are too numerous here to mention. Because
of his commu nity service, he recognized early the responsibil ity of all men to
participate in civic affairs. His conviction of every Mason's duty in this regard

State of California commenced its One Hundred Twenty-T hird Annual Communication in the California Masonic Memorial Temple on October 9, A.L.

Morning Session were presented to the Grand Master at the Centennial celebration of Doric Lodge No. 216 and by the Oakland Public Schools Masonic
Club.

The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge was
opened in ample form, following
which the Flag of Our Cou ntry was recei
ved. Grand Sword Bearer Jose F.
deLarios made the following state men t:
"We have pledged allegiance to our flag.
Let us now reflect on the
meaning of wha t we have done, and let
us in the future think of wha t
we are doing each time we pledge allegiance
to our flag.
When we behold our flag, we behold more
than the cloth of red,
white, and blue; more than the symbol of
our land ; more than the symbol
of a government; more than the symbol
of a people. We behold a set
of ideals which leap across all lines of
nationality, race, and creed; a
set of ideals for our own nation and for all
nations of the earth ; a set of
ideals we can teach to others by precept
and -mo st imp orta ntly -by
example; a set of ideals we can teach and
practice only if we ourselves
know them.
When we behold our flag, we behold grea
t deeds of valor in battle,
heroic accomplishments in time of peace,
and awesome sacrifices in both.
When we pay tribute to our flag, we ackn
owledge our debt ; and we
pledge to keep faith with those who gave
their lives and fortunes, while
maintaining their sacred honor, and with
all who have since joined them,
loving freedom and bringing their contribut
ions from other lands. We
pledge our adherence to the principles of
justice, freedom, and opportunity ; and we pledge our own active and
dedicated efforts to fulfill the
promise our herit age holds out to mankind
. We pledge that we will strive
for a decent, safe, peaceful, and healthful
community and nation, that
our people may be strong; for only the
strong can sustain freedom. We
pledge a totally incorruptible governme
nt, the only means by which
democracy can main tain itself. We pledg
e to look for the best in others
in our quest for perfection, that we may recog
nize our own imperfections.
We pledge our personal integrity and cour
age.
Each time we pledge allegiance to our flag,
our hear ts should stir and
soar at the priv ileg e-th e privilege of shar
ing in the high est hopes for
hum anki nd."

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

MEMORIAL SERVICE
DEVOTIO NAL AND NECROLOGY

Maybe some of you have heard me tell how continually I am badgered to do
this or to do that. I imagine that if the right people had been around this
morning, someone would have told me to make sure and pray for sunshine
rather than rain in this beautiful City of San Francisco. The mother of the
prospective bride calls me and says, "Can't you arrange for a beautiful day
for the wedding?" And some of you request the same kind of impossible demands. I simply stand here to remind you that I am in sales and not
management .
Because some of the Grand Lodge Officers tended to be falling asleep, let
me continue to remind you of another delightful experience that I shared with
some of them. How it is that people take a preacher sometimes; sometimes
they really take him. But one of the most delightful experiences that I ever
had as a clergyman was while I was flying to the East Coast. I've always
made it my habit never to divulge my occupation when I am traveling. I really
don't care to talk about religion all of the time, or to hear of how many of
you were Sunday School teachers forty-five years ago, or telling me the name
of the church from which you stay away. Therefore, I move about rather
incognito, and on this particular occasion I was sitting enjoying the flight;
enjoying the pretty stewardesses who walked up and down ; seeing the sights,
looking out the windows as we crossed the country. Finally, the gentleman
seated next to me became curious and he said, "What is your business?" No,
he didn't ask that. He asked, "What is your racket?" And I knew I was
talking with a real human being, and so I responded in like kind and I said,
"I'm a salesman." And so the stories and all the interesting experiences went
between us as we flew along, headed for New York City. And gaining some
confidence in one another he finally turned to me and said, " And what do you
sell?" I said very quietly, "I sell fire escapes." And without batting so much
as an eye he mumbled to himself, "Fire escapes, fire escapes, sure, you've got
to have them on your building or your fire insurance would be prohibitive, in
fact you couldn' t even have it," and he went on, mumbling to himself somewhat puzzled, "Fire escapes!"
Finally he turned to me and he said, " For whom do you work?" I said, "I
work for Lord and Company." With that the conversation continued to move,
when all of a sudden it began to dawn on him that I was pulling his leg.
Recalling all the stories with which he had regaled me, the color began to
rise in his neck and finally it covered his whole face, and for the rest of the
trip he apologized profusely. Finally, be said to me, "You're a clergyman,
aren't you? You're the best blankety-bla nk clergyman I've ever met! " When
we arrived in New York City, we walked down the ramp together. And when
we got ready to depart and to say our "goodbyes," he was so nervous and so
shaken up that he said, "Come on and I'll buy you a drink l"
Brethren, more seriously, may I share with you what to me are four pressing questions which I believe every Master Mason ought to ask. Each question
deserves a reasoned and a thoughtful answer; informed by the tenets of
Masonry and the tenets of whatever faith you profess.

Invocation - Devotional

Most Worshipful Grand Master and M embers of the Grand Lodge:
I c~unt it a high and s?le~ privil~ge to stand in this place as you r Grand
~haplam and to 1~.d you m this devotional service. Throughout the past year
it has been ?1Y pnv1lege to make brief presentations on the occasion of Grand
Lodge ?pemngs and I must admit to you that I felt as though I was a kind of
professio~al talker, or e~en a kind of religious huckster. I assure you, however,
that I en1oyed every minute of these occasions, graciously assigned to me by
the Grand Master.
. I would like to pre~ace O:Y remarks this morning by sharing with you somethmg of. the. deep satisfaction that I derived through the acquaintance and
fellowship with all of these Grand Lodge Officers. To serve with these dedicated and ~oughful men has been a refreshing and a joyous experience. It
wa.s .ref~eshmg because the;: accepted me as a person, not as a professional
~ehgiomst. To be treated this way, I tell you, is a breath of fresh air. It was
Joyous for me beca.use these men shared with me the joy of life and a lot of
good humor. That 1s also a breath of fresh air for any padre or clergyman.
May r. be so personal. as to tell you that I've never grown accustomed to
the sometimes str~nge, s1l~nt, soft-glove treatment that is directed toward
clergymen. From. ti.me to time some delightful experiences come to me as a
clergyman, pernuttmg me to be as truly human as you, my brethren, are
human. J~t ~e other day,~ pretty, new teller at my branch bank looked at
my deposit shp and she qmpped, "What kind of a doctor are you?" I responded. truthfully _and I said, "I am pastor of the church up the block." And
then, Wl~out b~tting an eye she said, "Weill Who would believe it? You
sure don t look like a preacher!" And I tell you that made my day. I squared
r:1Y shoulders as I walked out of the bank. I don't know what preachers look
like, but really I don't ever want to look like a preacher!
You know, some strange attributes are assigned to clergymen these days.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Question number one. Write it down in your mind. In this topsy-turvy
world, brethren, you and I had better know the answer to the question,
"Who am I?"
Am I only a blob of protoplasm as some of my friends tell me, that
sooner or later is headed for the dung heap? Or, as some of my friends tell me,
am I just a fragile reed shaken by the winds of time, soon to be blown away?
Or as others of my friends have tried to persuade me that I am simply a
fortuitous confluence of atoms and molecules soon to disappear into nothing?
Or am I something more than all of this?
I tell you what we are. You are the most important thing in the world.
Every one of you. Everything that has happened in the sweep of history has
happened for us! Some two billion years after planet earth of ours broke off
from the sun and began to cool, upwards from the first pre-primitive protozoa,
man finally stood, and the Supreme Architect breathed into him the breath of
life, and endowed him with mind and spirit and body, and created you in his
image. That's who you are. I say that it seems as if everything that has ever
happened from the very beginning of time happened in order that you might
be seated here today. You were created in his image and that means, brethren,
simply this, you were created with the capacity to love, to care, to hope, to
dream, to forgive and to respond to that Supreme Grand Master. You are the
most important thing in the world, that's who you are! And please don't
let anyone ever persuade you otherwise.
Question number two. Where are you? Do you know in what kind of a
world you live? Do some of your friends try to persuade you as they try to
persuade me that this world in which we live is a very haphazard world? You
and I believe that we live in a precise world, in a world with cause and effect,
in a world where if you love, you'll be loved, and if you hate, you'll get back
hate, where truth is truth wherever you find it no matter who says it or where
it is found. We are hemmed around not only by physical laws but by moral
and spiritual laws insisting that whatever you sow, that you will get back
and reap. If you cheat, you'll be cheated. If you lie, you'll be lied upon. If
you hate, you'll be hated. Ours is a world upon which we can depend, because
you and I invoke always the blessing of the Supreme Architect who made this
world and who called it at the very beginning, "good." You and I ought to be
about the business of supporting our local planet earth. Napoleon thought he
could beat the world. Hitler thought he could do it with his gas chambers.
Stalin thought he could, and the prisons are full of men who have thought
they could thumb a universal nose at the good world that the good God gave
to us.
Question number three. Why are you? What is your purpose? Is my
purpose simply to eat, to sleep, to procreate and then die? Animals live this
way you know. Cats, dogs, cattle. They eat, they sleep, they procreate, and
they die.
Brethren, so far as we know, you are the only creation that has a conscience. You know the difference between right and wrong. What are you

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

9

doing with that disti nction? You are the only creation, so far as we know, that
can consciously create beauty. No other par t of creation can do this and I ask
you this morning, how much beauty have you created? You are the only
creation that can live not purely on the physical level of life, but you and I
can lift ourselves up to service and devotion. How far have you lifted your
life my brother ? Why am I? \Vhy are you? Brethren, I believe that you and I
were called into life and given life in order to enrich it! That's our only
excuse for taking up this precious air and oxygen, occupying a few square
feet of space, building a little real estate and living out our years. We were
placed in this world to enrich it. It doesn't take a religionist to understand
that. We were given the gift of life right out of the blue and asked by the One
who gave it to us to enjoy it. That's the reason I appreciate the privilege of
humor that you share with me. To make life more human, that's it. Listen,
to make life more human, to care, to be compassionate, to be benevolent, to be
loving and merciful; that's what it's all about!
And my last question. When are you? How long are we here? How long do
you expect to live? This is not a morbid question! How long? 'What are the
dimensions? What are the parameters of a human soul? When I have completed this pilgrimage of mine, when I have walked on this earth and I have
finished my journey, the question that I ask you, "Is that all?" The answer,
I tell you in all honesty, is that there are no buildings or temples or houses
in which you can store a human soul. There is no real estate big enough and
grand enough for the spirit that is breathed into each one of us in the image
of the Other Mind. You and I are m<ilre than all that we see, we are more
than all of the real estate we will ever accumulate. Don' t ever forget that.
We are more than all we see with these eyes that someday will not see. We
are more than an that these hands can grasp when someday these hands will
no longer grasp. This is a transient world and it does not satisfy us because
you dream and I dream. You hope and I hope. We do this, my brothers,
because we reach out far beyond where we see, planning for our children,
planning for their childrens' children, investing your life and my life in
concern of our brotherhood, of our fraternity, investing not just for when we
shall be here, but investing into eternity. Where are you, where am I? We
were created, my brothers, with the power for endless life.
Well, this is one philosophy of one brother. I think that it is fit for a king.
I believe that it is fit for all Master Masons. It is fit precisely for you, and
you, and you. Please believe me. And may God love you always. Amen.

N ecrology
At a Devotional Service, when our spirits are lifted to that which is supreme in life, as our Grand Chaplain has done, it is but natural that we
should remember with devotion those who shared with us our ideals expressed
through Freemasonry and who have preceded us into the mysteries of the
beyond.

10

11

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

There is an ancient teaching that the highest form of philanthropy is our
loving remembrance of the dead. They cannot reward us. They cannot repay
us. When we do favors for those who are among the living - the loan of
money perhaps, or the use of a contact, or the extending of good advice or a
helpful hand - there is always the possibility that the recipient might at
some time be in a position to reciprocate the favor. But those who have departed from this world, what can they do for us? Therefore, to love them and
to honor them is the most altruistic deed of beneficence.
However, there is one sense in which they do confer benefit upon us.
Those who have lived an exemplary life, those who have made this world
a better place because of their deeds and thoughts, those who have endeared
themselves to us, and specifically those who have given thrust and impetus to
the purposes of Freemasonry - though they are no longer among the living,
when we remember THEM, we are repaid. We receive inspiration to emulate
their example, to do as they did, to strive always to become better Master
Masons.
It is for this purpose that we remember today the 491 Masters, Past
Masters and Wardens of our Grand Lodge who have closed the earthly chapter
of their lives during the year and whose names are to be inscribed in the
printed record of our Annual Communication.
A necrology, you see, need not be lugubrious. More truly, it is a lustrous
tribute of love and admiration.
When I have concluded, there will be special acknowledgments of distinguished service of Past Master Philip N. Myers, to be given by the Most
Worshipful Past Grand Master, Eugene S. Hopp ; of Alfred W. Odle, VicePresident of the Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes, to be given by Worshipful Ralph Head, and of Edward A. Underwood, my predecessor Chairman

These, and all our brethren whom we recall - we say, they
have died. But
what is it to die? Might they not ask us, " What is Life?"
We would have to reply: "Life is a mystery as deep as ever
death can be."
One truth we know for sure. An unknown poet expressed
it like this :
"For me to have made one soul
The better for my birth,
To have added but one flower
To the garden of the earth,
To have fought one fight for truth
In the daily fight with lies,
To have done one deed of right
In the face of columnies,
To have sown in the souls of men
One thought that will not die,
Shall be - immortality."
Yes, yes, yes - for these reason s our departed brothers
of Grand Lodge
have found immortality.
They do indeed live in our hearts.

EULOGY
PHILIP NORBOURNE MYERS

By Eugene S. Hopp

PHIL N. J\1IYERS
Grand Master Born
January 12 , 1897
Hemet , California

19 58

Died
July 6, 1972
San Francisco, California

Our brother Phil Myers endeared himself to all by his life of brotherhood,
his sympathetic understanding, his humility and his fervent intensity and
dedication in the discharge of his duties, whether fraternal, occupational or
familial.
He was born January 12, 1897 in Hemet, California. When he was twelve
years old, his family moved lo Los Angeles where he attended the public
schools. Here, the great qualities of fortitude, stead-fastness, innate ability
and tenacity of purpose, which remained his distinguishing characteristics
through life, became manifest.
After a little more than two years at Los Angeles High School, financial
circumstances compelled Phil to leave school for gainful employment. And
yet he continued his education at night and by correspondence, specializing in
accounting and management while working hard for the Southern Pacific
Railroad Company. With the entry of the United States into World War I,
Phil Myers volunteered for Army duty and the War ended as he was
graduating from Officers' Training School at Camp Pike, Arkansas.
Phil returned to Los Angeles and the endeavor at which he excelled. He
was employed by the Los Angeles Motor Transit Company and later the
Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe R.R., in Fresno, Los Angeles and Chicago.
So obvious were his leadership qualities, so great his will to do a better
job, that in six short years with that Railroad he rose from accountant to
senior traveling accountant. Even in the depths of the depression his outstanding ability was recognized by the McCloud River Railroad Company,
who asked him to become their Auditor.
Phil Myers' talent, ingenuity and efficiency and his compassionate understanding of people rapidly moved him, in this McCloud short line, from
Auditor, to Assistant Superintendent, to General Manager, to Treasurer, to
Vice-President and finally to President of the line. The 27 5 industrial and
shortline railroads of the United States, in recognition of his humanitarian
achievements, his management ability and his willingness to exert all his
efforts in a good cause elected Phil Myers a director of the American Shortline
Railroad Association, and in 1954, the Vice-President for the Pacific Region.
While residing in McCloud, Phil became a Master Mason on January 23,
1945, in McCloud Lodge No. 430. So great was his capacity for the ritual and
so exemplary his understanding and living it, that, after serving only as
Senior Deacon and Senior Warden, he was elected Master of the Lodge in
1948. The very next year the then Grand Master, Edward Siems, recognizing
the superlative qualities of our brother Phil, appointed him Grand Standard
Bearer of the Grand Lodge.

14

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In his livelihood, Phil's talent was well-known to so many of his collea.,,.ues
that in 1952 he was offered, and accepted, the Presidency of the Trona Railway Company, and as a result moved to Los Angeles.
On January 15, 1927 at Calipatria, California a n event took place in the
life of Phil Myers which brought fulfillment and contentment - he married
the charming widow, Anne Fletcher Thorp. Their three delightful children
brought them much pleasure, comfort and happiness.
Phil Myers served Grand Lodge with distinction on numerous Committees
as well as a Trustee of the Masonic Homes Board. On October 3, 1958 he was
elected Grand _l\faster of Masons in California. His year was truly outstanding
as he urged his brethren to community involvement in Public Schools and
Constitution Observances, as a Masonic duty.
Phil was a member of both York and Scottish Rites, honored with the 33°
in th~ Scottish Rite Bodies of Los Angeles and elected Sovereign in Saint
Gabriel Conclave of the Red Cross of Constantine.
Those of us who had the privilege of working with Phil l\1yers on Committees and on the Homes Board - and for many years he and I rode to the
meetings together - will always treasu re the memory of a man who never
raised ~is voice in anger, who always practiced brotherhood in his judgments;
a.genuine leader of men but with an humility of spirit that produced a magnificent aura that will forever light his memory in our hearts.
Phil Myers very life says to us: " Help us, 0 God, to treat every human
heart as if it were breaking, and to consider the feelings of others as we do
our own. Help us to be gentle, and to control our tempers, that we may truly
learn to love one another."

EULOGY
ALFRED WAYNE ODLE

By Ralph H. Head
Alfred Wayne Odle was born in N ew Jersey on November 3, 1911. He
passed away in Los Angeles on December 2 7, 19 71. Funeral services were
conducted in California Masonic Memorial Temple on December 31 1971.
He is survived by his wife, Lillian, his son, Robert, his father and ~other,
his brother and sister.
This then supplies the information needed for government and vital
statistics records.
What it does not reveal is the story of a remarkable man who in his

lifeti~e, contributed_ unstintingly of himself to his family, to his co~munity
and hlS church, to his profession, to his country, and to Freemasonry.
Before he died in 1690, the devout Quaker leader Georoe Fox addressed
a letter to his friends with the admonition "Do not ' open before' the time."

15

When the letter was opened a fter his death, it was found to contain a message
of hope and confidence and a reaffirmation of his faith .
Most of us would like to impart some las ting words of consolation and
encouragement to our family and friends besides the customary last will and
testament.
:Martin Luther ctict. He wrote "What is death but a night's sleep? As
through sleep all weariness and faintness pass away and in the morning we
rise fresh and strong and joyous, so at the Last Day we shall rise again as if
we had only slept the night and we shall be fresh and strong."
Few men are a George Fox or a Martin Luther, yet in our daily lives we
are constantly giving testimony which shall be examined later like footprints
in the sands of time.
The footprints of Al Odle are a legion. He was completely devoted to his
family. H e gave his time and talent to the community of San Francisco
through the Chamber of Commerce and civic organizations. In his business
and professional life he was a ba nker of renown as Vice President and senior
appraiser of Crocker National Bank. His love for his country was manifest
in his service to the United States Navy as a chief petty officer in World War
II. He was a member of the Presbyterian Church of Burlingame and a man
to whom laymen would invariably call to lead them in prayer.
With his deep conviction in the efficacy of the Fatherhood of God and
the Brotherhood of Man, it is no wonder that early in his life he knocked at
the door of Freemasonry. After being made a Mason in Park Lodge No. 449
on November 24, 1935 , his ability and dedication were recognized in 1944
when he became Worshipful Master while still in Navy uniform. Later he
joined the Burlihgame Scottish Rite Bodies.
In recognition of his integrity and devotion, Al Odle entered Grand Lodge
service as a director, and then President, of the Board of California Masonic
Memorial Temple. In I 969 he was appointed to the Board of Trustees of the
Ma~onic Homes of California and soon thereafter was elected its vice president. It was during the very time he was in Southern California on duty
for Masonic Homes that he passed away.
Some men embed their footprints in clay which the sun dries and preserves
for only a season or two. Y!ost of us leave our footprints in sand, marks
which are swept away by the tide at night. Al Odle left his footprints in
indestructible stone, never to be forgotten by his beneficiaries.
With his footprints, he left, by his deeds and actions, his signature added
symbolically to the words written by the Apostle Paul:
"I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have
kept the faith. Henceforth, there is laid up for me the crown of
righteousness which the Lord, the Righteous Judge, will award me
on that Day, not only to me but also to all who have loved His
appearing."

Ed was a member o f Al Malaikah Temple, Ancient Arabic Order, Nobles
of the Mystic Shrine and also a member and Past Worthy Patron of Holly
Vista Chapter No. 51 7, Order of the Eastern Star.
His interest in our Masonic Youth Organizations inspired him to become
active in the International Order of Rainbow for Girls and he was a member
of the Advisory Board of Hollywood Assembly, where on June 10th of this
year, his granddaughter, Louise, was installed as Worthy Advisor.
When William B. Ogden Lodge No. 816 was formed, it was dedicated to
support of our DeMolay boys. It was typical of Ed that he became one of its
charter members. For his many contributions to and interest in our D el\Iolay
youth, he was awarded the Honorary Legion of Honor, Order of DeMolay.
In the enumeration of these various dates, activities and organizations, we
have been given some insight as to the tremendous physical exertions expended
by Ed on behalf of his fellow man, but they do not completely delineate the
man.
Ed was one of those rare individuals who learnecl early in life that true
happiness can only be achieved by giving of ourselves to others. His warm
smile and friendly affection made others feel at ease in his presence. He had
an abundant sense of humor which he displayed on every possible occasion,
some special brands of which he reserved for the Past Masters of his Lodge.
Ed had a reverence for life and a consuming desire to aid his fellow man.
Some of his happiest moments came after returning from an errand of kindness, when he would offer a silent prayer to God, thanking Him for the opportunity to serve.
Ed had the faculty of being at ease in any company and his countless
friends from all walks of life attest to this virtue. His straight.forwardness,
unequivocation, and plain dealing distinguished him among men and by
precept and example, he inspired his friends and acquaintances. He had an
indefatigable zest for life, a tremendous physical capacity, a youthful spirit,
and above all a reverence for God.
Edward A. Underwood, a devoted husband and father, a man who truly
lived by the Golden Rule, a man who experienced true happiness in service to
others, a man loved, admired and respected by his countless friends,

PROCEED INGS OF THE

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
My brethren, one year ago on October 15, 1971, you greatly honored me
by electing me to the high office of Grand Master of all Free and Accepted
Masons in the States of California and Hawaii. My term in office will conclude this Friday on October 13, 1972; and like all of my predecessors, I
hope that my efforts upon behalf of our great fraternity have been in some
way beneficial to the Craft.
No one can truly appreciate the awesome responsibility which the Grand
Master feels upon assuming this office, unless he has served you, my brethren,
in that capacity. \Vhen you entrusted me with the care and supervision of
the Craft in California and Hawaii, it was a tremendous honor, but one for
which I wish I had been better trained. However, with the implements of
speculative Masonry and the assistance of the great architect of the Universe,
I have endeavored to carry out your wishes to the best of my ability.
This has been an exciting and interesting year for your Grand Master
and one that he will always remember with much pleasure. To be sure, as is
always the case, there have been problems to be solved; but I am happy to
report that with the help of many dedicated and able Masons about our great
jurisdiction, these problems have been solved.
The counsel, full cooperation and support of all of the elective Grand
Lodge Officers have been of great help to me. All of the appointive line of
Grand Lodge Officers have loyally supported the program of the Grand
Master and have done much to spread fraternal good will througho ut our
jurisdiction.
As harmony should prevail in all Masonic Lodges, I am happy to report
that harmony does prevail within the Grand Lodge official structure ; and
that in the very few constitue nt Lodges where some disagreement arose during the past year, the matters involved were amiably resolved by the speaking of good counsel to those concerned.
As of the present, there are slightly less than 230,000 Masons in the 697
Masonic Lodges comprising the jurisdiction of California and Hawaii.
I am pleased to report that again this year we have experienced ecumenical fellowship, for the Knights of Columbus on several occasions have participated with us in our cornerstone ceremonies, often presenting the flag of
the United States to the school when and where the Grand Lodge has laid
the cornerstone.
In June of this year the Grand Master and his wife were invited to attend
the third annual social event, a steak barbecue and picnic, of the Masons
and Knights of Columbus of the Monterey Peninsula area. Due to a previously confirmed commitment elsewhere we were unable to accept this invitation, but were ably represented at this event by Past Grand Master and :Mrs.
Laurence E. Dayton, who reported that the occasion was one of good
fellowship and a splendid opportun ity to bring about better understanding
between our two fraternities.

On February 22, 1972, the anniversary of the birthday of our first
President George Washington, a Master Mason, the Conference of Grand
Masters ~f Masons in North America convened in Washington, D.C.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Grand Lodge of California was represented at this conference by
your Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, William H. Price, the
Grand Secretary, Edward H. Siems, P.G.M., Guy B. Mize, P.G.M., and
Herbert A. Huebner, P.G.M.
Concurrently with the Grand Masters' Conference, the Grand Secretaries
hold their meetings.
Guy Mize was present as a Trustee of the George Washington National
Memorial Association. After many years of service upon the Board of
Trustees of the latter, Most Worshipful Brother Guy determined not to
stand for re-election although strongly urged to do so by those who had
served with him upon this Board. When he declined, he was replaced by
another distinguished California Free Mason, the Most Worshipful Edward
H. Siems, P.G.M. and our Grand Secretary, who was elected to take Most
Worshipful Brother Guy's place upon the Board of Trustees of the George
Washington National Memorial Association.
California was again singularly honored when our Grand Secretary also
was elected as the first Vice President of the Conference of Grand Secretaries in North America; and in accordance with past precedent, we can
proudly look forward in anticipation to his election as the President of the
Conference of Grand Secretaries in North America in February, 1973.
The Masonic Leaders at this Conference represent approximately 4y;i
million Masons in North America and the Conference is an opportunity for
these brethren to share ideas with their counterparts and in general promote
the welfare of the Craft.
Our own Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner, P.G.M., as the retiring
chairman of the Conference of Grand Masters in North America, opened the
1972 Conference in his usual very amiable and efficient manner. He then
turned the gavel of authority over to his successor in office, the Grand
Master of the Grand Lodge of Illinois. California Masons have been greatly
honored by having one of their distinguished leaders selected for this position
of high honor and respect.
Your Grand Master was a member of one of the discussion groups at the
Conference and continues to serve as a member of the permanent Committee of the Conference of Grand Masters of North America to plan the
Masonic celebration of the 200th Anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence in 1776.
Joining with the Californians already mentioned, in various portions of
the conference programs, were Earl Warren, P.G.M. (former California
Governor and former Chief Justice of the United States), Henry Clausen,
P.G.M. (present Sovereign Grand Commander of the Scottish Rite, Southern
Jurisdiction), Robert B. Watts (former Grand Chaplain and former Grand
Orator), and Brother Thomas H. Kuchel (former United States Senator
from California) .
One of the special events was a luncheon hosted by Henry Clausen at the

House of the Temple, which is the magnificent headquarters of the Scottish
Rite, Southern Jurisdiction.
The entire meeting was a very rewarding experience in which your
representatives all ably participated and contributed to the successful conclusion of the Conference. California, because of its great numbers of
Masons, among other reasons, is recognized as one of the leaders of the
Grand Jurisdictions of North America.
CHANGE IN PHRASEOLOGY OF CORNERSTONE CEREMONY

At the last Grand Lodge Communication it was pointed out that the
wording of our cornerstone laying ceremony is somewhat archaic and should
be brought up-to-date; for it is rare, if ever, at the present time that a
cornerstone is laid before any of the superstructure is built. As a matter of
fact, most of the cornerstones laid by your Grand Master and immediate
past Grand Masters have been laid only symbolically after the building involved bad been constructed.
Accordingly, at the last Communication of the Grand Lodge, it was suggested that the Ritual Committee review our present cornerstone ceremony
and the phraseology thereof with the intent of adopting wording for the
same which would be more appropriate to our laying of present day cornerstones after the completion of the superstructure.
I am pleased to report that the Grand Lodge Ritual Committee has considered this problem and continues to work upon the same with the hope
that at the following Grand Lodge Communication, a completely revised
up-to-date modern ceremony for the laying of cornerstones by the Grand
Lodge will be presented for the consideration of those attending the Grand
Lodge Communicati~n next year.
CEREMONY FOR PRESENTATION OF 75-YEAR MASONIC VETERAN PINS

At the 1971 Annual Communication the then Grand Master recommended
that the Ritual Committee compose a ceremony for the presentation of a
veteran's award to those of our brethren who have completed 75 years as a
Master Mason; and I am pleased to report that the Ritual Committee during
the past year diligently worked upon this assignment and has composed such
a ceremony, so that in the future whenever a brother is entitled to receive a
75 -year Masonic veteran's pin, it will be presented to him with an appropriate and proper ceremony written for that purpose.

REVISION OF THE CALIFORNIA MASONIC CODE

The Committee for the revision of the California Masonic Code has
worked long and diligently for the past four years in redrafting and recodifying our Masonic Code. It has been a tremendous job which has been completed by extremely able and dedicated brethren, all of whom have endeavored to compile a one-volume understandable and easily read 2\fasonic
Code. All of the l\Iasons of our jurisdiction owe these brethren, the members
of the Masonic Code Revision Committee, a debt of gratitude for the great
many hours of time and energy they have devoted to this important task.
The new revised Code will be submitted to you for your approval later this
week.

HARD BACK ONE-VOLUME HISTORY OF GRAND LODGE

The Grand Master at the Grand Lodge 19 71 Communication recommended that the Grand Lodge approve the preparation of a single volume
hard back history of the Grand Lodge of California to be available in time
for any Masonic observance of the 200th Anniversary of the signing of the
Declaration of Independence. That Anniversary will occur in 1976. However,
in 1975, the Grand Lodge of California will celebrate its 12Sth Anniversary.
Accordingly, the present Grand Master appointed a Committee to consider
the compilation of such a volume; and this Committee has been discussing
the appropriate type of history for the eventual presentation to Grand Lodge.
I recommend that the incoming Grand Master continue the existence of this
Committee in order that the completed work may be a vailable in 1975 or
1976.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION

The Board of Directors of the California Masonic Foundation has labored
long and diligently during the past year and has accomplished much in its
many varied activities. One of the most important has been its endeavors to
dispose of our !vlasonic Club House at the University of California at Los
Angeles at a fair and reasonable sale price. Efforts in this regard have been
under way for several years, but now it is anticipated that a sale of this
property will lake place within the relatively near future. The report later
in the week of the President of the Foundation will provide details concerning the proposed sale.
AMARANTH GIFT TO MASONIC F OUNDATION

One of the greatest and the most pleasant of the many surprises which
your Grand Master received this year occurred on Monday, March 6th, 1972
in San Francisco at the 15th Annual Communication of the Grand Court,
Order of the Amaranth. On that occasion the Grand Royal Matron upon
behalf of the Amaranth Homes of California, Inc. presented two gifts to me
in my official capacity as Grand l\Iaster. They totaled almost $218,000.00
($11 5,000.00 being in cash and $102,790.81 being evidenced by a promissory
note secured by a first deed of trust). These gifts are to be used by the
California Masonic Foundation to provide scholarships for deserving young
women under twenty-one years of age, who require financial assistance in
obtaining higher education. The funds represented by these gifts have been
deposited to the credit of the Masonic Foundation and have been drawing
interest thereon since March 7, 1972. The provirting of scholarships from the
income of these.gifts now is being consummated.
RITUAL

I am pleased to report that the California Masonic Ritual, which is
supervised by the Grand Lecturer, Right Worshipful H. Douglas L emons,
with the help of the six Assistant Grand Lecturers, continues to be
recognized in all jurisdictions as outstanding in its teachings of l\1asonic
principles. The schools of instruction which have been conducted by the
Assistant Grand Lecturers for the Inspectors of our jurisdiction and the
other schools conducted by the Inspectors for the Officers of the Lodges
continue to stress excellence in the performance of the Ritual; and while all
agree that ritual in itself is not the important element (for it is the tenets or
principles of Free Masonry which are important), it still remains true that
the excellence of our ritual is responsible for impressing upon the mind of
the candidate the great truths of Free Masonry which we strive to implant
in his mind. The outstanding service of our Grand Lodge Ritual Committee
and the Inspectors of our jurisdiction who serve with it can not be measured
monetarily; for the service they render can only be carried out and reflected
by those who are dedicated Masons and who thoroughly believe in the principles of Free Masonry.

COMMITTEEMEN AND INSPECTORS

All committees have functioned well and effectively. Some have been
outstanding. Without attempting to praise one Committee's work more than
another, each year the Committees all seem to accomplish more and better
results as time goes on.
I am very pleased to report that each year contributions by members
of our Lodges to the Homes Endowment Fund continue to grow. This is
good, for it indicates an awareness and concern for our two great Masonic
Homes by members of our Fraternity. It also indicates that an outstanding
effort again has been put forth by all Masons in this Grand Jurisdiction to
attain this fine result.
All of us should have a warm feeling of accomplishment for our own
part in helping to achieve the largest total annual contribution ever made
to the fund, almost a million dollars, or $959,157.90 was contributed by
our members through the various Lodges of our jurisdiction. This sum represents direct out-of-pocket contributions and is exclusive of all other gifts
and bequests which have been received by Will or devise.
The members of our Homes Endowment Board, as well as the Lodge
Officers of our California and Hawaiian Lodges, are due our thanks and
appreciation for their leadership in this regard. We should never forget that
of the Great Lights of Masonry (Faith, Hope and Charity), the greatest of
these is Charity; and that what we do for ourselves dies with us and that
what we do for others lives forever and is immortal.
Complete details outlining this year's activities, efforts and results of
the Homes Endowment Board will be found in its report which will be given
later this week by the committee's Chairman.
Other Committees likewise in their respective fields have accredited
themselves well; and as the reports of the Committees are presented by each
Chairman, I hope that they will have your careful attention, for there has
been much accomplished by the various Committees which should be of
great interest to you.
I am sure that every Grand Lodge Elective Line Officer, as he moves forward from one chair to the next, thinks that he knows about the great
amount of work each one of our Committees does for Grand Lodge and the
Masonic fraternity. However, it was not until the Grand Master's chair
was actually occupied that your present Grand Master fully appreciated
how many truly dedicated Masons we have serving upon our many Grand
Lodge Committees. My heartfelt thanks go out to each of our Committeemen for their support and efforts upon behalf of the Grand Lodge activities
in which they participated.
I would likewise be remiss if I did not thank the Inspectoral Corps for
the many hours they have devoted to the craft during the past year. We in
CaJifornia like to think that the ritual taught in our Masonic Lodges is the
finest exemplification anywhere; and rightly so, for our Inspectors spend

INSURANCE

The Grand Lodge Insurance Committee was requested to take on new
and additional duties this year in assisting the Grand Secretary concerning
the insurance coverage for the protection of the Grand Lodge and other
entities of the constituent Lodges. In that regard the Grand Lodge Insurance
Committee was requested to keep, and for the past year has kept, a log book
or record of all losses involving our insurance coverage. This has been done
with the full cooperation of our insurance brokers who now have been instructed to report each insurance loss in triplicate. One such report form is
sent by the broker to the Grand Master, another to the Grand Secretary,
and the third to the Chairman of the Grand Lodge Insurance Committee.
It is hoped that the ultimate result from keeping this record will be an
eventual decrease in the premiums for our insurance coverage; for now when
it comes time to renew our insurance policies, a record of our previous losses
will be available to Grand Lodge, as well as the insurance company. If we
have had a low loss record during the previous insurance period, we may
justifiably anticipate and request lower premium for the insurance involved.

Our brethren in the States of Pennsylvania, Virginia and South Dakota,
as well as in our State of California in the Sacramento River Delta area, have
suffered great loss this year due to natural disasters. Upon learning of the
disaster in the Rapid City, South Dakota area caused by most unseasonable,

his State.
We did not receive any request for assistance from Grand Lodges in the

suffering loss, were not in need of assistance from our Grand Lodge.

MEM:DERSHIP

As of June 30, 1972 there were 227,214 Masons who were members of
Lodges in our jurisdiction composed of the States of California and Hawaii.
This is a net decrease of 3,369 from the number who were members of
Lodges in our jurisdiction on June 30, 197 1 when our total then numbered
230,583.
There were 3,571 newly raised Master Masons in our jurisdiction between
July 1, 1971 and June 30, 1972, as well as applications for 403 of our
brothers for restoration to membership and 755 for affiliation from other
jurisdictions. Against this sizable increase in new, renewed and affiliated
memberships, there were 5,690 deaths and 1,725 suspensions for non-payment of dues, plus 12 expulsions for charges. It is unfortunate but obvious
that the net loss in our membership is due largely to the grim reaper, which
takes bis toll of all of us in due course. However, as we know that the
pendulum swings to and fro throughout our l\fasonic History, we can
optimistically look forward to another eventual up swing in our total
membership.
QUALIFICATIONS FoR MASONIC MEMBERSHIP

My brethren, our regulations state that among other qualifications an
applicant for the degrees of Masonry must be 21 years of age, come well
recommended and be considered a good man by his associates.
What about the applicant's religion? Should that be considered important? In the past some Masons have suffered religious persecution from
a variety of faiths. For this reason, the man who is to become a Mason must
have a tolerant consideration of the other man's religion. As Masons, we are
concerned only that the applicant have a belief in a Supreme Being. We
should never be concerned about what church, synagogue or mosque the
applicant attends. This is his personal business.
Let us continue to remind ourselves of these facts when applications for
membership are considered in our Lodges.
What I am stressing here is that the merit of the individual applicant
alone should be the sole concern of the Lodge and its members when passing

35

MASONS, NOT MERELY MEMBERS

Much more is required of each Mason than committing to memory a
portion of our degrees. A man, upon becoming a Mason, has new responsibilities in citizenship, in his moral conduct, and in his family considerations.
Above all, we Masons should seek to strengthen the character of the newly
raised brother. To learn more about Masonry should be the goal of each of
us, and the Lodge should make this task an easier one. The Master should
request a brother Mason who is knowledgeable in Masonic subjects to talk
with and teach each newly obligated Master Mason, so that the latter truly
will be a Mason and not just a member of a Masonic Lodge. To this end, I
urge all Masters, as well as all other Officers of every Masonic Lodge, to take
whatever steps are deemed necessary to see that all of the candidates who
seek Masonic membership receive Masonic light in such sufficiency that the
candidates will become M asons, as well as members of a Masonic Lodge.
FAMILY PARTICIPATION IN LODGE A CTIVITIES

Last year and again this year your Grand Lodge opened to the public
certain of its ceremonies, which formerly were tiled ceremonies and for
Master Masons only, so that the family and friends of California Freemasons
could attend these Grand Lodge activities. Your Grand Master believes
that each Lodge should follow a similar practice wherever allowable under
Masonic statutes. It is my firm belief that the constituent Lodge is strengthened as the family of a l\Iason comes to know more about the efforts we
undertake for his self-improvement.
We have many precious jewels of Masonry with which the family of
every Mason should be more conversant.
Our Masonic Homes (one for the elderly at Union City and the other
for children at Covina) are two of these, and in addition there are two
Masonic Temples which have been set aside by the State of California as
memorials to the greatness of Freemasonry. One is located at Columbia in
the Mother Lode Country near Sonora, and the other is the old Los Angeles
Lodge building near the Court House in downtown Los Angeles.
The members of our Lodges and their families are urged to visit whenever possible these precious jewels of Freemasonry, either individually or in
groups. You can be assured that you will be glad you did; and if you take
your family with you, it will result in a very happy Masonic experience.
CONCORDANT GROUPS

Your Grand Master during the past year has endeavored to bring all of
Masonry to a realization that the Masonic family is one great fraternal
organization, even though there may be many component parts thereof ;
and to that end, the Grand Master has endeavored to bring about a spirit
of true fraternity between our constituent Lodges and all concordant bodies.

For the past several years residents have been admitted to our Home for
the elderly at Union City solely on the basis of need. Prior to that time a
proposed resident upon admission was required to be ambulatory and able to
reasonably take care of his personal needs.
In 1968 the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes determined that
certain of our facilities at Union City should be used for borderline and
non-ambulatory cases. This enlarged policy opened up a host of new admissions; and as a result, the population of the elderly there has increased
greatly. It is now the largest of all time. There now are 408 guests at Union
City. While it is commendable as Masonic charity to extend these facili ties
to those Masons and their families in urgent need, the consequent costs of
operation of our Homes has increased at a very rapid pace.
It must be borne in mind that if the costs at our two Homes continue to
escalate as they have in recent years, careful financial review must be given
to the scope of the present programs there. It may be necessary in the future
for our Homes Board again to limit admissions to the Masonic Home at
Union City to those who are not only ambulatory at the time of admission,
but to those who may be expected to remain ambulatory for the reasonable
foreseeable future thereafter.
The report of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees will make you
proud of the work we are doing for our less fortunate brothers, their children,
wives and widows.

(EMERGENT MATTER)

At the Annual Communication in 1970 it was determined that it would
not be necessary for the Deputy Grand Master to serve as a member of the
Masonic Homes Board of Trustees. The reason for this determination was
the heavy work load already assigned to the Deputy Grand Master.
However, during the past two years, experience has shown that it would
have been very beneficial to the incoming Grand Master to have served
upon the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees while serving as the Deputy
Grand Master. At the suggestion of the incoming Deputy Grand Master,
with the concurrence of the incoming Grand Master, it was moved, seconded
and unanimously passed at the last meeting of the Masonic Homes Board
of Trustees that the Deputy Grand Master be made an active additional
member of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees. A copy of the resolution
in that regard will be found in their report.
Those of us whose duties were lightened as a result of the aforementioned
change two years ago, as well as the other present elective progressive Grand
Lodge Line Officers, all believe it to be desirable for the Deputy Grand
Master, as well as the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, to serve as active
members upon the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees.

the Masonic Homes.

March28, 1972
To Masters of Each Hawaiian Lodge:

It has recently come to my attention that some Masonic Brethren living

this resolution.

and ballot ; and (2) no separate mailings or other form of solicitation in an

The total Hawaiian membership as of June 30, 1972 was 3,165. The total
number of ballots cast for or against the proposed Grand Lodge of Hawaii
was 1,565. The latter is 49.2 % of the total Hawaiian membership. Two of
the Hawaiian Lodge:> did not distrib ute ballots to their members, because
the ballot taken the preceding year had been negative, and a third did not
reply to the Grand Master's letter. Of the I ,565 ballots cast 1,110 or 70.9%
were in favor of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii. Four hundred fifty-five (455)
ballots or 29.1 % of the ballots cast were opposed to the formation of a
Grand Lodge.
It is startling to note that 50.8 % of the total Hawaiian membership did
not vote on this matter. It may be concluded that the members represented
by this percentage were not interested in the formation of a Grand Lodge
of Hawaii. When we consider the total membership involved in all of the
Hawaiian Lodges, only 35.07 % expressed a favorable vote for the formation
of the Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
It is also to be noted that as of J une 30, 1972 only 1621 members of
the Hawaiian Lodges lived in the Hawaiian Islands, or about 51.2 % of
the total membership of the Hawaiian Lodges.
Because of the outcome of the ballot and because of my recent discussions
with various members of the Hawaiian Lodges indicate to me, among other
reasons, that there is grave doubt as to whether or not there are sufficient
qualified Masons (Past Masters of Hawaiian Lodges) who will actively support and work in and for a Grand Lodge of Hawaii, I seriously doubt the
wisdom of forming a Grand Lodge of Hawaii a t this time, although that may
be a desired eventual result. However, the Grand Master and all of the
Elective Line of Grand Lodge Officers, who have carefully considered and discussed this subject in detail, together with apparently a better than sixty-four
per cent majority of the total membership of the Hawaiian Lodges, have failed
to indicate a belief that the present is the proper time for the formation of a
Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
If in the future a substantial change in favor of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii
becomes apparent, I am sure that the Grand Lodge of California will be
pleased to consider whether the situation then prevailing will justify encouragement from this Grand Lodge, on the subject in the light of what is considered best for the fraternity.

PATRIOTISM WEEK AND RESPECT FOR OUR FLAG

As the Grand Master's term in office began to unfold and as he traveled
about the State, it became more and more noticeable to him that some o~ t~e
rank and file members of our great State were disrespectful to our Nat10n s
flag; some failed to uncover their hea~s when the flag passed by; others
failed to salute when the Pledge of Allegiance was called for; and some even
desecrated the flag. All of this indicated to your Grand Master that some of
the citizens of our Nation had forgotten their great heritage, which we should
frequently recall.
Recently the Master of one of our Masonic Lodges informed me that
three of the brethren of that Lodge during the opening ceremony failed to
salute the flag of the United States of America and were remonstrated by
him for their action.
I was shocked and amazed that any Masonic brother would act in such a
manner, particularly when our degrees and charges emphasize good citizenship.
Investigation disclosed that the three brothers involved did through carelessness or inadvertence fail to salute the flag when it was being presented;
but each in writing has assured me that it was an oversight which he regretted, and that no disrespect for the flag of the United States was intended.
Because Masonry teaches us to be charitable of a brother's mistakes, I
accepted the statements of the brothers involved at face value, and after admonishing them to be more attentive and respectful to the flag of our Country
in the future, I took no further action; for I believe that each of them will
be more attentive to his duty to respect our flag in the future.
All Masons who are United States citizens at all times must respect the
flag of the United States; and when our flag is presented in a Masonic Lodge
and the Pledge of Allegiance called for , our flag must be properly saluted and
the Pledge stated.
During the month of September each year the Masonic Lodges of California and Hawaii have long called the attention of our brethren to the
United States Constitution, that great document which guarantees life,
liberty, freedom, and the pursuit of happiness to all of o~r ~itizens. Howev~r,
past efforts often failed to kindle the spark of true patriotism and appreciation for our great heritage. For this reason I believe that an additional effort
now is necessary on the part of all Masons in order to call the attention of
all citizens to the very many advantages we have under that great symbol,
the flag of the United States of America.
The apathy of some of our citizens toward the flag and love of Country
causes me great concern and distress. For many months I pondered how your
Grand :Master could in some way effect a change in this regard. After careful consideration and with the wholehearted approval of the entire elective
line of Grand Lodge Officers and the Past Grand Masters, I determined that
we, as Masons, should take some action which would help to turn around the
apparent growing negative attitude toward patriotism which seems to be

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

47

presently existing in our Country. To that end, I promulgated an edict on
June 23, 1972 declaring that the week following September 17, 1972 (the
anniversary of the signing of the Constitution of the United States) should
be known to and by all Masons in California and Hawaii as "Patriotism
Week" and that during that week no Masonic Lodge should have any activity
or program nnless it were a patriotic one. Each Lodge was directed to plan
and carry out a patriotic program, singularly or with other Lodges or organizations.
While I realire that because this edict was not promulgated until three
months before the designated " Patriotism Week" and therefore caused some
inconvenience to the Lodges and Concordant Bodies of our jurisdiction, I
am pleased to report that all Lodges and Concordant Bodies gave overwhelming approval and support to this edict, for all Masons everywhere
stated that we should continue to support patriotism and that this edict was
long overdue.
It is my sincere hope that in time others, in addition to Masons and our
affiliated groups, will pick up the ball and run with it in this regard, so that
eventually the public in general will celebrate Patriotism Week every September, just as the public now celebrates Public Schools' Week every April.
To that end I am pleased to report that this year the Mayor of Bakersfield after learning about our Patriotism Week issued a proclamation from
bis office on September IS, 1972 to those residing in that City as follows:
"I, Donald M. Hart, Mayor of the City of Bakersfield, do hereby
proclaim the week of September 17, 197 2 as
"PATRIOTISM WEEK"
and urge all citizens of this community to join with others throughout the nation in a rededication to the principles of the Constitution
and the Bill of Rights that protect, with no less meaning for all
segments of our society, the inalienable rights of all citizens of the
United States."
Also, other of our civic and State leaders likewise have approved of this
patriotic suggestion.
As we go forward in the years ahead I am sure that many non-Masons
will join with us in celebrating " Patriotism Week" to traditionally honor our
great heritage.
SusPENSION oF MASTER: OCEANSIDE LoooE, No. 381

A short time after taking office last October, I was informed that the
Master of a Masonic Lodge in this jurisdiction was charged by the civil
authorities with a violation of Section 647(a ) of the California Penal Code.
I requested the Inspector of the Masonic District involved to verify that
fact, and upon being informed by the Inspector that said charges had been

48

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

lodged against the Master, I suspended him from the exercise of the powers
and duties of his office and directed that the Senior Warden of the Lodge
succeed to the powers and duties of the Master until such time as the election
and installation of the Lodge's Officers for 1972, or until the civil trial involved had been completed and guilt or innocence determined. Subsequently
the Master pleaded guilty in the civil Court to the criminal charges, and in
due course I directed that Masonic charges be brought against him.
As a result of his suspension on November 22, 1971, I directed that the
then Master of Oceanside Lodge, Number 381, not be accorded the designation of Past Master.
DECISIONS

Numerous questions were propounded during the year calling for a ruling
or interpretation by the Grand !\faster. Most of them could be answered by
reference to the California Masonic Code or recalling a precedent or tradition
which governed. However, there were two matters which required official
decision by the Grand Master.
Decision No. 1 - Sale of Circus Tickets
I was asked by an Assistant Grand Lecturer to rule on whether it is a
violation of Masonic Law if a Shrine Temple, having obtained permission
from Grand Lodge to sponsor a circus, sends books of tickets for admission
to its members requesting them to purchase the tickets. My decision and
answer was "no," providing there is no follow-up in case the tickets are not
used. Sending books of tickets under such circumstances must be limited to
only members of the sponsoring Temple, club or organization. This decision
is not in conflict with Section 333(v) of the California Masonic Code for the
circumstances under consideration differ from those set out in said section.
Further, Section 330(b) of the California Masonic Code apparently authorizes the action mentioned above.
Decision No. 2 - Use of Lodge Refreshment Funds
I was requested by the Chairman of the Grand Lodge Youth Activities
Committee to rule on whether or not a Lodge could use a portion of its refreshment funds to sponsor and assist in the payment for a float by one of
our Masonic Youth Groups in order for them to participate in a Constitution
Month Observance Parade. I ruled that if members of one of our Masonicaly
affiliated Youth Orders were identified with a Constitution Observance Program, such as building a float to participate in a parade for that Observance,
the reasonable use of Lodge refreshment funds for this purpose was proper.
RECOMMENDATION ( 1)
THE CONSTITUTION OF MASONIC LODGES

Last year the Grand Master, Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner,
recommended that the dedication of Masonic halls no longer be a tiled

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

49

ceremony, but one open to the public. This was concurred in by all of
the Grand Lodge elective line Officers, including myself and the Chairman of
the Ri tual Committee. This year we constituted one Masonic Lodge, Tustin,
Number 828, Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California.
As we were preparing for the constituting of Tustin Lodge, it occurred to
me that Masonry would be far better served if this ceremony of the constitution of a Masonic Lodge were opened to the public. The reasons are the same
as stated by Past Grand Master Huebner in his 19 71 Grand Master's
Message for making the T emple Dedication Ceremony an open one, namely :
"The Ceremony is one which illustrates certain principles of Masonry
wi thout revealing any of its secrets. The entire Ceremony is printed .
. . . the image of Masonry would be enhanced by making this Dedication Ceremony open to non-Masons. Also relevant are the facts that
the wives and families of Masons frequently contribute services and
gifts in the erection and furnishing of a Temple, and consequently
hold a personal interest in it. The Order of Eastern Star and the
Youth Organizations frequently hold their meetings in the Temple."
After Grand Lodge is opened, it can be called off for the purpose of constitution, the same as calling off for a cornerstone laying or a temple dedication ceremony, and the public then may be invited into the Lodge Room.
There appears no reason to bar the public from this ceremony, any more
than from the Dedication Ceremony; and an open ceremony will involve
no change in the Ritual. Since no legislation is involved, I therefore, recommend the adoption by Grand Lodge of an open ceremony as a matter of
policy for the Constitution of Masonic Lodges.

RECOMMENDATION (3)

51

TERM IN OFFICE OF INSPECTORS

All committeemen who are appointed by the Grand Master take office
effective with the installation of the Grand Master. At the present time the full
term of office of the Inspectors in our jurisdiction by custom becomes effective
on January first following the Grand Master's installation and terminates on
December 31st thereafter. However, there seems to be no valid reason as to
why the term of office of Inspectors should not coincide with the term of office
of committeemen, or why the term of the appointment of Inspectors should
not run concurrently with the term of office of the Grand Master who appoints
them. Therefore, to be consistent with other appointments by the Grand
Master (including all Assistant Grand Lecturers), I recommend that the term
of office of all Inspectors hereafter appointed by the Grand Master conclude
on the same date as the Grand Master's term in office.

RECOMM ENDATION (5)
SELECTION AND NOTIFICATION OF JUNIOR GRAND \VARDEN

For many years your Grand Master has thought that improvement could
be made in the manner of identifying to Grand Lodge members the brother
who has been suggested for selection as Junior Grand Warden. It is my considered opinion that some manner should be devised so that all Grand Lodge
Officers, appropriate Lodge officers, Inspectors and Committeemen receive this
information at the same time and by the same method.
I am convinced that the members of Grand Lodge desire to retain the
procedure whereby any taint of politics or electioneering in Grand Lodge is
avoided. It is most important that the choice of any Grand Lodge officer
should not be the result of a popularity contest. I am also certain that it is
the desire of an members of Grand Lodge to elect as Junior Grand Warden
the most qualified brother available for this high office.
Therefore, I recommend that the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to carefully consider all phases of this subject, including procedures
of selection and notification, and to report back its recommendations in regard
thereto at the next Annual Grand Lodge Communication.

RECOMMENDATION (8)
125TH ANNIVERSARY CELEBRATION
In 1975 the California Masonic Grand Lodge will celebrate its 125th year
of activity. In 1850 the Grand Lodge of California came into existence and
it is only fitting and proper that 125 years thereafter we should properly
celebrate that event. Accordingly, I recommend that there be appointed a
committee in sufficient time to plan an appropriate celebration by the Grand
Lodge of California, perhaps at its Annual Communication in 1975, or otherwise during that year, in order to properly commemorate the 12Sth anniversary of our Grand Lodge.
RECOMMENDATION (9)
STATE-WIDE JURISDICTION-APPLICANTS FOR THE DEGREES
As a result of present transportation facilities and easy accessability from
one area to another, most of which are intertwined by freeways, it does not
seem longer necessary that the requirement for membership in a Masonic
Lodge be that the applicant reside within the limited areas as defined by
applicable Sections of the California Masonic Code. Therefore, I recommend
that a person otherwise qualified, wherever resident for 12 months within this
Grand Jurisdiction and who has met the requirement of age, may apply for
the degrees of Masonry without regard to the location of the Lodge to which
he is applying.

RECOMMENDATION ( 11)
FUTURE RESOLUTIONS
My attention has been invited to the fact that frequently when resolutions
are submitted for consideration at the Grand Lodge Communication, the
language involved in the resolution as filed with the Grand Secretary's office
is not always in proper language. The Grand Lodge Jurisprudence Committee always is available for assistance in the drafting of resolutions.

year at the time he notifies all Lodges as to the cut-off date for the time

Annual Communication, also, at that same time he notify the Master of each
of the Lodges in our jurisdiction that the aforementioned service by the Grand
Lodge Jurisprudence Committee is available, if any Brother or Brethren
desire to use the same.
RECOMMENDATION ( 12)
GREATER EMERGENCY RELIEF FUNDS
When the disaster of the great floods in South Dakota occurred in June
of this year, my attention was called to the fact that only $1,000.00 had
been provided as the Grand Master's Relief Fund for use of our brethren in
emergency circumstances. It is evident that this amouut might be only a
" drop in the bucket" if an area in California were to suffer a disaster; for
it is readily seen that an earthquake, tidal wave, or other disaster in either
the States of California or Hawaii might well require the distribution of a
far greater amount by the Grand Lodge of California to needy Masons and
their Lodges in this jurisdiction.
Accordingly, I recommend that the Grand Lodge set aside and make
permanently available a sum for such possible disaster relief in not less than
the amount of $10,000.00, which would be subject to distribution by the
then Grand Master in his good judgment for the relief of our brethren in any
such disaster area in our jurisdiction.

THE GRAND MASTER'S "GET INVOLVED PROGRAM"

It has long occurred to me that we :!\fasons, who believe in the better
things of life and for the general welfare of our fellow man, are a part of the
great silent majority, in that many of us fail to make our influence felt by
those with whom we come in contact. In an effort to urge our members, as
individuals, to become more involved in the day to day affairs of their respective communities, early in the year I wrote to every Master, Inspector,
Committeeman.and member of our fraternity in California and Hawaii and
urged each of them, as individuals, to take a more active part in his respective community's affairs and to make his influence known in his area. A
copy of my December 13, 1971 letter to this effect addressed to every Mason
in our jurisdiction is appended hereto as an exhibit hereof. I am happy to
report that this program and the suggestions in this letter were overwhelmingly approved by the Craft. As a matter of fact, after receiving my letter many
of our brethren who had never before thought of submitting their names to the
electorate determined to run for office and some were successful, an example
of which is our own Past Grand Master, Eugene S. Hopp, who ran for and
was elected this last June to the San Francisco School Board. To all of the
brethren who, in following the Grand Master's admonition to become involved in the civic affairs of their respective communities, have run for office,
I say "Thanks for a job well done. I salute you."
Each of us has the moral responsibility to take positive action by doing
what he can wherever he is to shore up the dike before the tide boils through.
I firmly believe that if each of us will become involved in his local, state or
national affairs, as his individual abilities permit and allow, and if each of us
will apply our Masonic precepts to the problems of his daily life, the effect
of such action on those around us will do tremendous good.

by your Grand Master on Grand Lodge business during this year. This extensive travel has given the Grand Master an opportunity to talk about Masonry with literally thousands of our brethren in all walks of life.
Some few of our Masonic Lodges are faced with difficult problems, but
by-in-large Masonry in the States of California and Hawaii is in a good condition and progressing. However, it is always well to ~emember that m~re
numbers are not the important element or goal, for the pinnacle of our attainment should be to accept the application of the best men in the community,
and then through our Masonic teachings, make them better men, even
though they be only a few in number.
Enthusiasm for and interest in Masonry, as well as the Officers' and
members' effectiveness in teaching the tenets of Freemasonry to our newly
obligated brothers, are good throughout the juris~ictio~. ~ con.tinuing p~r­
sonal commitment by each of us to apply Masonic prmc1ples m o~r da1l~
lives will assure the continued strength and growth of Freemasonry m California and Hawaii.
I compliment the members of the Grand Lodge of California for the fine
leaders they have selected for the future. I have worked closely with these
officers for the past several years and can personally attest to their great
ability and dedication to the Masonic fraternity and its principles. All of
these men have great capability, and in particular the incoming Grand
Master Right Worshipful William H. Price, the Deputy Grand Master, who
llas 1on~ well served the Grand Lodge of California. His level headed, saga-

cious judgment when requested from time to time has been of much assistance to your Grand Master. Bill will be an outstanding Grand Master.
The Senior Grand Warden, Right Worshipful Raymond A. Ebbage, has
also worked closely with your Grand Master and I know that he will be a
tower of strength to our Grand Lodge when eventually he takes office as
Grand Master.
The Junior Grand Warden, Right Worshipful Burton Meyer, Jr., although
serving his first year as a progressive Elective Grand Lodge Officer, long has
had a record of service as an Inspector and Appointive Officer of the Grand
Lodge. He, too, is a man of marked ability and in due course will lead this
Grand Lodge with great distinction.
Therefore, I am very pleased to publicly state that the future of our great
Grand Lodge for the foreseeable period ahead is assured of progressive
activity due to the tremendous leadership waiting in the wings to guide the
Grand Lodge of California when called upon to do so. I am very happy that
I have had the privilege and pleasure of working with these talented and
dedicated brothers for the last several years.
ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

Your Grand Master is deeply indebted to all of the members of the Craft
who have contributed their time and talents to the fraternity during the past
Masonic year. There are so many to whom I should pay special tribute for
their efforts in assisting the Grand Master in the various tasks which confronted him. The many who so loyally and graciously were of help to your
Grand Master are legion and if he tried to name tllem all, he would be certain
to overlook some. However, I do want to comment and state that I have
received the utinost cooperation from not only all of the progressive Grand
Lodge Elective Line Officers, but as would be expected from the Grand
Lecturer, Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary as well. The latter two have
been particularly helpful throughout the year in their many well thought
out suggestions.
In addition, I would be remiss if I did not tell you that every member of
the Grand Secretary's Office has cooperated and endeavored to help me
wherever it was possible for them to do so.
Verne Hendrix, the Assistant Grand Secretary, often has remained long
after dosing hours to discuss matters with the Grand Master and help in
reaching a proper solution thereto. His respectful criticisms and timely suggestions have been of great help to and much appreciated by me.
I am grateful to Mrs. Gladys Wraith, Secretary to the Grand Secretary, for
her attention to details and constant reminder of matters to be done by the
Grand Master in accordance with the proper procedure and schedule concerning the same.
Further, I must comment upon the loyal, able and gracious assistance I
have received all through the past year from those two outstanding and very

cheerful ladies in the Grand Secretary's Office who have acted as the Grand
Master's Secretary this year. I refer to Mrs. Pearl Hove and Mrs. Helen
Castellotti. Mrs. Hove has taken the Grand Master's stenographic dictation,
typed his letters, and made constant and helpful suggestions in regard to

Mrs. Castellotti, or " Helen" as she is known affectionately to the Masonic
