shall ever be grateful to both Mrs. Hove and Mrs. Castellotti for their very
able and considerate assistance to me during the past year.
While I have mentioned the Grand Secretary briefly above, I must state
that we in California are extremely fortunate to have a man of Ed Siems'
capability serving us as the Grand Secretary. He is the equal of any Grand
Secretary in North America and surpasses most of them in ability and dedication to his job. His loyal devotion to our fraternity is unsurpassed.
Ed and I have been friends for almost forty years. As young men we
served together in the Oakland Junior Chamber of Commerce; and over the
years our friendship has grown stronger. This is not to say, however, that
Ed and I always have agreed; for during the past year, we some times have had
very definite differences of opinion on matters involving the Grand Lodge.
However, this is not unusual when men with conscientious efforts endeavor to
make determinations which they consider best for the fraternity they love. At
no time, however, has any disagreement in any way diminished our friendship;
and I am very grateful that I have had the benefit of the counsel and suggestions of Ed Siems throughout the past year. His great knowledge of
Masonry and experience in office as Grand Secretary and as a Past Grand
Master have given him an insight and a sixth sense as to what is right and
good for the fraternity. As a result, he has been of tremendous help to all
Grand Masters with whom he has served, and in particular to your present
Grand Master. I know that when he assumes the office next February of the
Presidency of the Grand Secretaries' Association of North America, the latter
organization will have the finest administration it has ever had; for our
Grand Secretary is a great man, humble in spirit and very dedicated to the
principles of Free Masonry.
The camaraderie which has existed between all of the Grand Lodge Officers
during the past year, elective and appointive, has been the greatest. While
every Grand Master is proud of the line of Grand Lodge Officers with whom he
serves, I know that there never has been a finer or more loyal group of
Ofiicers to serve with any Grand Master than those with whom I have been
privileged to work during the past year. Each of them has my sincere thanks

61

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

for their loyal and helpful support. I never could have completed this year's
assignmen ts without their dedicated assistance and cooperation.
I can assure you, my brethren, that the duties and responsibilities of a
Grand Master are truly challenging and very demanding. However, the
fraternal support and assistance which are offered and were given to me on
every side, as well as the great many friendships made during the year, all
have served to make this past year one of the most pleasant, busiest and
interesting of my entire life. Now as I approach the termination of my year
as your Grand Master, I look back over this period as one which has added
much to my experience a nd the fullness of my life. I am the richer by far for
having had the privilege of knowing so many of you so well, and for this I
always shall be very thankful.
Your Grand Master earnestly hopes that each of you has approved of
his efforts to encourage the commitment of all Masons to the purposes, proper
effectiveness, and welfare of our great fraternity.
May the Great Architect of the Universe continually guide, bless and
watch over each one of you and our Masonic brotherhood.

Grand Master

REcoMMEN DAnoN ( S)
SELECTION AND NOTIFICAT ION OF JUNIOR GRAND WARDEN

Tlze Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recognizes that the
traditional, unwritten procedure long practiced for the recommendation of
a candidat~ for the office of Junior Grand Warden, on infrequent occasions
has met with resistance, and the delegates to Grand Lodge have seen fit to
elect to that office a brother other than the brother recommended for consideration. Such resistance can be proper and beneficial.
We recognize that confusion has sometimes (but not always) existed
during the Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge relating to the
identity of the individual recommended for consideration and we are aware
that the oral lines of communication respecting the n;mc of the brother
reco~mended have sometimes faltered, and tha t the biographical data concerning the brother is often lost enroute. Certainly it will be very helpful to
improve the lines of communication.
There are numerous questions to be resolved in the selection of a Junior
Grand Warden. The two most important are qualifications and availability.
These two break down into several subdivisions. Under qualifications, for
example, are knowledge of and devotion to Freemasonry, operation of Grand
Lodge, ~itualistic proficiency, administrative experience or ability, Masonic
lead~rsh1p ~h~racteristics, and condition of health. Under availability may be
classified w11lmgness to serve, necessary freedom from demands of business or
profession or other organizational obligations, attitude of immediate family,
~nd even to some extent economic independence or subsidization. Moreover,
m most cases, the brother elected usually must plan his business commitments and personal affairs well in advance ; and quite probably a well-qualified and otherwise available brother would decline to enter a contest for the
office.
We agree with the Grand Master that a study of the subject should be
made.
However, a special committee may not be necessary. We believe that the
incoming Grand Master may find it more feasible to request such a study and
report from one of the existing committees .
We, therefore, approve the Recommendation No. S of the Grand Master
if modified to leave it discretionary with the incoming Grand Master as to
the assignment of the subject to a committee already constituted or to a
special committee.
I move the adoption of Recommendation No. S but with the provision
providing the option to the incoming Grand Master as to selection of an existing or special committee, and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

Adopted subject to modifications in Committee's report.

RECOMMEN DATION ( 6)
CONDOMI NIUM OR OTHER PRIVATE HOUSING

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master has recommend ed that the incoming Grand Master
appoint a committee to inve~tigate the_ possibility of Grand .Lod~e establishing condominium or other pnvate housmg for Masons of Cahforma.
At the 1967 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge Past Grand Master
Ira W. Coburn, Chairman of a Special Committee on Masonic Retirement
Home Project, reported to Grand Lodge the results of that committee' s extensive investigations. The findings of this committee showed that Grand
Lodge would be confronted with a great many comple.'< problems if such a
plan were undertaken. Among these d ifficultie~ were: Corporate organ~za­
tion · should it be a profit or non-profit enterprise; Tax Status; the possible
eff~t on a non-profit organization; Government Control by such agencies as
the Internal Revenue Service and the California Departmen t of Social Welfare; means of financing.
The problems found by this former committee are primarily the same
today. In addition, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes
that the cost of constructing such housing would be so great that many
Masons desiring to live in such complex could not afford to do so. We are in
complete agreement with the 1967 committee that such a project should not
be undertaken.
I move the adoption of this recommendation and your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprude nce:
No legislation required.

Not adopted.

SALE OF CIRCUS TICKETS
D ECI SION No. 1

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

The Grand Master's Decision No. 1 relating to the sale of circus tickets
was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and we report as follows :
The portion of the decision stating that it was not a violation of Masonic
Law for a Shrine Temple, having obtained permission from Grand Lodge to
sponsor a circus, to send books of tickets for admission to its members requesting them to purchase the tickets is in accordance with Annotation 330
(b) of the California Masonic Code and is approved.
Annotation 330(b) specifically states that it is proper for a Lodge to
solicit funds from its own members.
However, we find no law to sustain the portion of the decision stating
that there could be no follow-up in case the tickets were not used and this
portion of the decision is not approved.
To say that a Lodge or other Masonic organization soliciting its members for funds to repai r a Temple or other proper pu rpose could only ask
for funds once and not follow-up with a second reminder of the need for help
is not in accordance with our law or practice.
We move the adoption of this report and urge a "Yes" vote.
(Not e: T lze Committees on Policy and Gen eral Purposes and on Commercialism concurred with the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence).
Adopted.
• USE OF LODGE REFRESHMENT F UNDS
DECISION No. 2

The Committee on Jurisprudence :

The Grand Master's Decision No. 2 was referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence for consideration :
In this decision the Grand Master held that " if members of one of our
Masonically affiliated Youth Orders were identified with a Constitution Observance Program, such as building a float to participate in a parade for that
observance, the reasonable use of Lodge refreshment funds for this purpose is
proper."
Your Committee finds that this opinion is contrary to Section 41 2 v of the
California l\,l asonic Code which provides as follows:
"Section 412v - A parade float or vehicle cannot be financed or sponsored from Lodge funds."
Your Committee therefore moves that said Decision No. 2 not be
approved.
( Note: The Committee on Polic y and General Purposes concurred).
Decision not approved .

LESTER 5. MCELWAIN

DECEMBER

13, 1971

GRAND MASTER

DEAR BROTHER:

Since assuming the awesome responsibilities of Grand Master of Masons
in California and Hawaii, it has been my desire to write to you personally
as a member of a Lodge of Masons and to request your active assistance.
I am sure you recall the charge given to you that "as a citizen you are
enjoined to be exemplary in the discharge of your civil duties ...." May I
stimulate your response to that charge and urge your participation in community affairs.
We know that the great majority of Masons are highly respected in their
comruunities because they were required to be good men before being accepted
into the Fraternity and, of course, the lessons and obligations of Masonry
have added much to each brother's stature.
The results of the efforts of our Masonic forefathers in their communities
are well known. The influence of such patriots as Washington, Franklin and
Paul Revere, as well as that of many of our present State Governors and
members of Congress who are Masons, needs no repetition. What you as an
individual Mason do may be just as important in the days ahead as that
which has been accomplished by Masons in the past. Remember that "nothing
results more in the triumph of evil over good, than for good men to do
nothing."
By separate letter I have asked the Master of your Lodge to form a committee on "Conununity Activities," and I would like every Mason who receives
this letter to notify his Master that he will serve on this committee, or support it to the best of his ability in his local community. Even if you should
be unable to attend Lodge regularly, there are many community activities
where you reside in which you could become involved.
The need for good men of character to participate in leadership has never
been greater. Your self improvement through increased knowledge and service
at local, state, or national levels will be satisfying and beneficial.
Please, my Brother, give your support to this important program. Personally contact the Master of your Lodge, or the Lodge closest to you, and
inquire about how your own efforts may be most effective. Let each of us seek
to improve government at every level, in our district, our city, our county,
our state, and our beloved country. Remember, becoming involved is the key
to the success of this program.
Sincerely and fraternally,
Attest:
LESTER s. MCELWAIN
Eow ARD H. SIEMS
Grand Master
Grand Secretary

PROCLAMATION
YOUTH ACTIVITIES WEEK
MARCH

13-17, 1972

The concern by adults of any society for the direction of its youth's
development has been evident since the beginnings of recorded history. The
greater the social pressures, the faster and more frantic the pace. of living,
the more difficult it becomes for young people to find a set of practical, moral
values upon which to rely. Never has youth been more severely challenged
by society. Never has it had greater opportunities to grow.
.
Concurrently, too, the quiet challenge by youth to our Fraterruty has
never been greater. Never have we, as adults, had greater opportunity to
assist. Each Mason owes an obligation to himself to act and assist our youth
in finding a basis upon which to develop a life philosophy for today and
tomorrow.
The lessons illustrating the work of our three fine Masonically oriented
youth groups, the International Orders of DeMolay, Job's Daughters and
Rainbow for Girls offer practical guidelines for character development.
Accordingly, t~ support the purposes of these groups, I proclaim the
week of March 13-17, 1972 as Youth Activities Week, and I urge each
member of every Lodge to make whatever reasonable effort he can to evidence
his personal interest in their welfare.
.
Further I direct that this proclamation be read at the Stated Meeting of
each Lodge' in March and, wherever practicable, that it be published in the
March trestleboard.
Let each of us, my Brethren, support these fine youth groups!
Dated: February 4, 1972

LESTER S. MCELWAIN

Grand Master

Attest:
EowARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

PROCLAMATION
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK-APRIL

PROCLAMATION

24-28, 1972

"OUR PUBLIC SCHOOLS, THE BASIS FOR FREEDOM AND
DEMOCRACY. KEEP THEM STRONG!"
The foundation of our nation rests upon the principles of freedom and
democracy but the security and future of its course rests entirely upon the
development and intelligence of our youth. The perpetual battleground for
freedom is in the minds of men and the ammunition of educated intelligence
must be continuously fostered and replaced.
The manifold blessings we enjoy through our democratic institutions,
and our own responsibilities toward those institutions, should not be lightly
as.sumed with complacency and self-satisfaction. Each of us should be aware
that responsibility for the maintenance of freedom demands not only perpetual vigilance and guidance by counsel of experience, but the constant
renewal and replacement of age with vigorous, knowledgeable youth.
The public school systems today provide the best possible assurance
for continuance of our American way of life anJ for the protection of that
way of life against foreign or domestic enemies. It equips our youth with tools
of information and judgment to become loyal, thoughtful, and responsible
citizens. In recognition of this, and because as individual Masons we are
involved in community affairs, I urge each of you to be concerned with the
direction of our public schools' growth, the personnel charged to administer
them, and the support of their educational programs in the search for truth.
To this end I proclaim the week of April 24 through April 28, 1972 as
P ublic Schools Week; and
That no Lodge programs or meetings be held during this period, other
than Stated Meetings or for purposes of this observance; and
That, wherever practicable, this proclamation be published in the Lodge
trestle boards; and
That this proclamation be read at the Stated Meeting of each Lodge in
March and April.
Dated: February 9, 1972
L ESTER S. McELWAIN

Grand Master
Attest:
EowARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

79

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMEN T MONTH

The Masonic Homes Endowment Fund has grown by our voluntary contributions and by gifts and bequests. Only the income, however, from this
fund may be used toward offsetting the costs of operating our Masonic
Homes.
Income from the fund is not yet large enough to cover all of such expenses
_ so each Lodge annually pays from its funds an assessment in proportion
to its size to offset a portion of the deficit. It is our goal that members'
voluntary contributions will sometime in the future increase the size of the
fund to the extent that income from it will be sufficient to cover the costs
of operation.
A visit to our fine homes makes us realize more clearly the need not only
to support this great Masonic charity, but to expand our giving commensurate with the additional needs and risin_g costs.
What a grand way for us as Masons to express our concern for those in
our care - for each of us to reaffirm our realization that these are our homes
and our loved ones. Let us not be found wanting in our desire to do our
share!
Accordingly I proclaim the month of May, 1972 to be
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

I direct this proclamation be read at the March and April Stated :Meetings
of each Lodge, and I suggest that wherever practicable copies of this proclamation be sent to each member of the Lodge.
Dated : February 17, 197 2
LESTER S. l\lcELWAIN

Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

Grand Secretary

EDICT-PATRIOTISM WEEK
PRocLAMA TION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

" Our Constitution - A Document for All the People" is a phrase representing the spirit of this year's observance of Constitution Month.
As citizens we tend to become acutely aware of the privileges we enjoy
under our form of government when we are involved in national struggles, or
when we observe from a distance the internal, social and political problems
of other nations. However, the very nature of the freedoms provided by our
Constitution tends toward personal complacency and carelessness of attitude
concerning the cuts and abrasions caused by the friction of human relationships. We often leave these wounds unguarded to subtle, persistent infection
and the siren song of the ever present enemies of our political system.
The need has never been greater for each of us (who are the people the
Constitution protects) to be ever grateful for the freedoms we enjoy under
our Constitution and to be vigilent in the prevention of its further erosion.
The love for our country should be a concern of all people, but particularly
of Masons. Let each of us remember our heritage and exercise this privilege!
I , therefore, proclaim the month of September 1972 to be Constitution
Observance Month and direct every Lodge in California and Hawaii to participate in an appropriate observance of the Constitution, and wherever possible to plan an open community type of program in which the theme of
patriotism is stressed.
I further direct that this proclamation be read at all stated meetings held
prior to your scheduled Constitution Month Program, and wherever possible
this proclamation shall be printed in the Lodge bulletin.
Dated: May 25, 1972
LESTER

s. M CELWAIN

Grand Master

Attest:

WHEREAS the members of our Masonic Fraternity particularly, as well
as all citizens, should continually renew an<l expand the spirit of patriotism
and love of country; and
WHEREAS appreciation of the wonderful heritage enjoyed by all citizens
of the United States constantly should be recalled ; and
WHEREAS our active participation in the affairs of our cities, states and
nation will tend to revive and increase patriotic spirit; an<l
WHEREAS there now appears to be much apathy by many of our citizens
concerning patriotism and love of country, and whereas there now is a great
need to bring these basic ideals to the attention of all of the citizens of our
nation;
NOW, THEREFORE, I direct that each Masonic Lodge in the States
of California and Hawaii set aside the week which next follows September 17,
1972 ( the anniversary date of the signing of the United States Constitution);
and this week shall be designated as " PATRIOTISM WEEK."
Masonic activities during this week shall be limited to Stated Meetings
only, if regularly scheduled during that :WC:k, or to progr~n15 dealing with
and promulgating the principles of pa_tnot1sm. Lodges which h~ve already
scheduled activities for that week, which cannot be changed without great
hardship, may in ·certain circumstances be authorized by the <?rand Master
to continue such activities (after written request therefor). It 1s hoped that
if such an exception is granted that the program involved will be supplemented
.
with a patriotic motif.
I further direct that this edict be read at the Stated Meetmgs of each
Masonic Lodge in California and Hawaii du.ring the months of July, Au~:t
and September, and that each Lodge immediately .make plans for a patnot1c
type of activity or program during the week followmg September 17 , 1972.
This week hereafter shall be known as "PAT RIOTISM WEEK."
Dated: June 23, 1972

E DWARD H. SIEMS

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
To tlze Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The report of the Grand Treasurer is based on the official audit statements
by Touche Ross & Co., Certified Public Accountants for each of the following
Masonic entities:
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California
Masonic Homes of California
California Masonic Memorial Temple
California Masonic Foundation
The period of the audit covered the year ending June 30, 1972 and contains a record of income and expense for the prior year. These official audit
statements are on file in the Grand Secretary's office for your perusal. All are
in proper form and, as stated by Touche Ross & Co., were made in accordance
with generally accepted accounting practices. A physical count was made by
Touche Ross & Co., and two members of the Grand Lodge accounting staff, in
the vault of the custodian, of all the securities owned by each of the above
entities.
The Statement for the Grand Lodge indicates a surplus, after expenditures,
of $41,519 .00 for the curren t year.
The Statement of the Masonic Homes of California Operating Fund indicates an excess of expenditures over income of $31 ,278.00.
The Statement of the California Masonic Memorial Temple indicates an
excess of expenditures over income of $126 ,615.00, which includes depreciation
of $158,419.00. An audit of California Masonic Memorial Temple's garage
receipts was made at the lessee's office - a continuing practice.
The Statement of the California Masonic Foundation indicates an excess
of expenditures over income of $21, 157 .00.
In the statement of appropriations the Grand Master was requested to
approve supplemental expenditures of $29,540.00 some of which are Mnrecurring.
On a personal note, the Grand Treasurer also serves on the Masonic
Homes Board, California Masonic Foundation Board, California Masonic
Memorial Temple Board as Treasurer and also as a member of the Grand
Lodge Investment Committee. It is my considered judgment that the work
of these Boards and Committees is accomplished in an exemplary manner.
Your Grand Treasurer is deeply appreciative of the outstanding cooperation of the Grand Master as well as the office staff of the Grand Lodge,
particularly in the accounting office. I cannot close this report without paying
great tribute to the Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems, whose knowledge,
affability and integrity have been an inspiration to your Grand Treasurer.
Respectfully submitted,

VETERAN BUTTONS

The rapid increase in Masonic membership immediately following World
War I continues to be reflected in the number of Fifty Year Veteran Buttons
which were awarded during the last year. At the 1971 Communication we reported that from September 1, 1970 to September 1, 1971, 1645 buttons bad
been presented to veteran members. Between September 1, 1971 to September
1, 1972 , the total number presented was increased to 1696.
Analysis of our membership records indicates that we can anticipate a
continuing high number of presentations for several years to come.
TAXATION ?\•I ATTERS

During the last several years the state and federal governments have
increased their requirements for tax reporting by both Grand Lodge entities
and the Constituent Lodges. With assistance from the Grand Lodge Committee on Taxation and the management section of Touche Ross & Co. a
brochure, consisting of tax report samples together with instructions to assist
the Constituent Lodges in the completion of the various forms, was forwarded
to each Lodge in April. Because of our desire to comply with requirements

89

of the laws and the penalties for non-compliance, we have encouraged prompt
and accurate filing of required tax reports by the Constituent Lodges.
ACCOUNTING RECORDS

Careful, progressive steps continue following thoughtful consideration of
bow to effectively apply modern mechanized techniques to our accounting
records.
Review of our own record requirements, as well as the many new recording
facilities which are available, has been made by our accounting staff in order
to keep abreast of new and economical techniques. Wherever, in our judgment,
new methods are practical we have made them effective. We are continuing to
make further analyses as they relate to our membership records. So far we
have been unable to justify a change from the present membership record
system but study of the matter continues.
CONSTITUEN T L ODGE OFFICERS

Our office by its very nature works closely with Masons, and particularly
Lodge Officers, of this as well as of other jurisdictions. As a consequence ~e
feel the pulse of the Fraternity. Where there is possible weakness we know it.
Where there is strength we are aware of its existence.
Sincere and continuous commitment to Masonry by many of our members
is one of the principal bulwarks against the eroding effects of complacency
by a few. No other group of Masons has greater personal devotion to the
purposes of Masonry than the Secretaries of o~r . Constituent Lodges.
should be a real satisfaction to every member, as 1t 1s for every employee m
our office to work with the Secretaries individually as a vital part of the
organizatlon. The \last majority of our Secretaries make the work load easier
for all of us with prompt correspondence and reports, but it is frustrati ng to
contend with the small percentage who put everything off until tomorrow or next week.
Only a few of our Lodge members and Officers are aware that many hours
of work are quietly expended by these devoted Brethren handling the mountain
of paper work necessary for the smooth operation of each Lodge. Theirs is
truly a labor of love !
In recent years the changes in our state and federal laws have increased
the burden of Lodge Secretaries because they are required to make out more
reports on your behalf.
Secretaries, like other Lodge Officers, are human beings and want to get
the work done and out of the way. In their haste, not only the Secretaries, but
particularly the other Lodge Officers, ignore the admonition " When in doubt
follow the directions." Much work and " wheel-spinning" could be eliminated
if time were taken to read the procedural steps outlined in the instructions.
We find this true not only in the Secretaries' monthly reports and other
related work, but also in the Homes applications and governmental reports
which involve the other Officers. What we are saying on one hand is "Con-

ns!"

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on By-Laws:
With its seven members present Saturday morning, October 7, 1972, your
Committee on By-Laws began its review of the matters referred to it.
Your Committee checked and re-checked ninety-live changes made by
constituent Lodges ... thirteen in change of Place of Meeting and eighty-two
changes in the By-laws. All of the reviewed amendments and resolutions were
found to be in order with the exception of one - Golden State Lodge No. 358.
EXHIBIT B of the Grand Secretary's preliminary report, to which members
of the Grand Lodge may refer, sets forth eighty-six of the changes. The nine
changes approved by the Grand Master, after said preliminary report was
sent to the printers, were found to be in order. Your Committee moves that
they be included in the Grand Secretary's final report.
Two Lodges adopted the Uniform Code of By-Laws (C.M.C. Sections 339
through 36S): Palestine-Craftsmen No. 3S l and Brawley No. 402.
One Lodge changing date of Stated Meeting (C.M.C. Section 343 Article III): Metropolitan No. 646.
Five Lodges - Increasing dues (C.M.C. Section 3S6 - Article IX) :
Tuolumne No. 8, Pasadena No. 272, Azusa No. 305, White Pine No. SSS and
Albany No. 686,
One Lodge - Change of Meeting Place (C.M.C. Section Nos. 372 and
373): Claremont No. 436.
As in the past, your Committee suggests that the Lodges review Article X
of their By-Laws which sets forth the maximum authority of the Charity
Committee of the Lodge during the interval between Stated Meetings. This
year two Lodges increased the authority of the Charity Committee and we
commend them for doing so.
Your Committee would like to point out that this is a very important part
of your by-laws and a ten dollar amount between Stated Meetings may not
be any charity at all.
Even though most of the amendments reviewed were approved, your Committee found that the matter of designating holidays in the By-Laws remains
troublesome. Article III of the Uniform Code of By-Laws, which permits
exceptions to the regular date of the Stated Meetings of a Lodge, limits the
exception to legal holidays and during the Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge.
With regard to legal holidays, these should be specifically named so that
there will be no misunderstanding as to whether a particular day is or is not a

94

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

holiday. Further, the particular legal holiday should be identified by NAME
and NOT by date; that is, New Year's Day is preferable to January 1 and
Independence Day is preferable to July 4, because such description leaves no
doubt that the exception applied when these days are celebrated on Monday
in a year when January 1 or July 4 falls on a Sunday.
Particular attention should be paid to this point of designation of holidays, and especially for 11onday night Lodges. By action of Congress, several
holidays will be celebrated on Monday even though they fall on another
day of the week. All :t\1onday night Lodges should contact the Grand Secretary's office before changing the holidays.
Also, a Lodge should provide for an alternate date in case its Stated
Meeting falls during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. While only
those Lodges whose Stated Meeting is during the second week of the month
are affected, the date of any Annual Communication may be changed for any
year, so the contingency should be provided for.
In reviewing the resolutions having to do with the change of meeting
place by various Lodges, your Committee found that in several cases a Lodge
moved to a new location without following the formal procedures set forth
in the California Masonic Code, and when the Lodge notified Grand Lodge it
was meeting at the new location, such notice was the first knowledge that
Grand Lodge would have of a move having taken place. Thereafter, the
Lodge would have to take the necessary procedural steps that it should have
completed prior to any move. The procedure for changing the meeting place
of a Lodge is set forth in California Masonic Code Section 372. We would
like to impress upon all the officers in attendance here that they should check
the Masonic Code and By-Laws of t heir respective Lodges before making any
changes in meeting places, so i hat the required formalities will be completed
before the move, rather than afterward.
This Committee wishes to commend the officers of the Lodges who so
carefully followed our Masonic Code.
We wish to thank the Grand Secretary and his staff for their efficiency
and diligence in guidin~ those who needed assistance in properly adopting
the changes.
Most Worshipful, we move that Grand Lodge approve the amendments,
and resolutions listed in Exhibit B of the Grand Secretary's report distributed
at this Communication with the additions herein-above specified, excepting the
Certificate of Amendment of Golden State Lodge Ko. 358 be denied and
returned to that Lodge, and the report of the By-Laws Committee be adopted.
Respectfully submitted,
ALDE N J. FULKERSON, SR., Chairman
ROBERT A. WERTSCH

CHARLES H. GRACE
DONALD M. BINKERD

JOHN B. MORGAN

LEONARD K. HERENDEEN

TRIAL RECORD No. 2007
This Trial Record raises a problem too common to many others. The
accused was charged with misappropriation of funds from a local Shrine Club.
He failed to answer the charges, whereupon a Trial Master was appointed and
called upon to make an investigation, a report of his findi_ng to
subordinate Lodge and a written report to Grand Lodge for review. This _latter
report consists of completing the forms furnished by Grand Lodge wherein the
Trial Master must declare the basis for bis findings. The Trial Master, as
happens in many similar cases, failed to state any fact upon which he made
his findings. It must be emphasized that the discretion and therefore responsibility of the Trial Master is exceptionally broad and the only check thereon
is the review of the Grand Lodge. Without ample records there can be no
adequate review. We urge, therefore that the Trial Master sho~ld fully state
the steps taken during his investigation and the result thereof in a complete
report in the forms provided with supplementary statements and documents,
if necessary. In the instant Trial Record for reasons heretofore stated we
offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: that the Trial Record No. 2007 be returned to the Lodge
and the Trial Master be directed to state the facts upon which he reached his
conclusions to allow proper review by Grand Lodge at the next Communication.

t?e

Adopted.

97

RESOLVED: that the Application for Restoration to Blackmer Lodge
No. 442 in Trial Record No. 1928 be denied.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1994
Th_e Accused, a member of Oak Grove Lodge No. 215, was charged with
the cnme of Grand theft, a felony for having taken money in excess of
two hundred dollars from three national banks. The plea nolo contendere
to o~e coun~ ?f grand theft. The court sent the Accused to the C.alifornia
Medical Fac1hty at Vacaville for diagnosis. On his return, sentence was suspended, and the Accused was granted probation.
. In 1_971, charges were filed and the Trial Master after investigation found
him gu!lty and fixed the penalty at expulsion. The Accused appealed and
stated that he had talked to the Trial Master on a number of occasions and
had told him t_bat, if h~ did not answer, be would only be suspended and not
expelled. Relying on this assurance, the Accused did not answer the charges
Becaus~ of this contention of the Accused the Grand Lodge, on the recom~
mendat10n of the Gri evances Committee, reversed the decision of the Trial
Master and s_ent the matt~r back to Oak Grove Lodge for further proceedings.
. I_n compliance therewith, new proceedings were commenced. A trial comnuss1on was properly convened and evidence presented. The Accused did not
appear. He was found guilty of the charge and of unmasonic conduct and the
penalty was fixed at suspension.
Your Committee feels that theft of funds from a bank is serious enough to
warrant the penalty of expulsion.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the findings of the Trial Commission in Record
No. 1994 be approved, but that the penalty be raised to expulsion, and that
the member be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

TRIAL REcoRD No. 2013
The accused, a member of Henry Clay Lodge No. 95, was charged with
two counts of unmasonic conduct. The first alleging that be did by the use
of undue influence upon an elderly invalid, a Master Mason suspended for
non-paymen t of dues, procure a gift of some 300 acres of valuable land, and,
second, that while employed at a chain supermarket, he did obtain merchandise
without paying for the same.
The evidence of the first was sufficiently strong to warrant a unanimous
verdict for conviction by the Trial Commission as to the first specification,
and a near unanimous verdict as to the second count. The penalty recommended was that of suspension.
In the opinion of your Committee on Grievances, the evidence was such
that a stronger charge as to count one could have easily been made resulting
in potential criminal charges being brought against the accused; none were.
We believe, however, that a brother who wilfully and intentionally seeks
to cheat, wrong or defraud a brother does not belong in our Fraternity and
that the penalty of suspension should be raised to that of expulsion.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
RESOLVED : that the findings of the Trial Commission in Record 2013
be approved, but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and t hat the member
be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

who would bring discredit to the Craft, and to knowingly and intentionally
aid and abet such person in making false and perjurous statements in his
petition to a Lodge of Masons, is so heinous and violative of the obligations as
to warrant expulsion rather than mere suspension.

Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 2014
The accused, a member of John Marshall Lodge No. 636, was charged
with unmasonic cond uct supported by four specifications. The first three
specifications, generally, were to the effect that the accused had knowingly
aud willingly sponsored, recommended and assisted an applicant for the degrees of Masonry in petitioning for the degrees and in executing said petition,
when the accused knew that tbe applicant had a long varied history of convictions of crimes and offenses of moral turpitude; and having such knowledge
counseled and assisted the applicant in answering the questions on the petition
in a perjurous manner. The fourth specification was dismissed for lack of
evidence. Trial before a Trial Master and seven Commissioners was duly and
regularly held in the form and manner required by Masonic law. The accused
was found guilty as charged in all three specifications and the evidence amply
supports that finding. The Trial Commissioners fixed the penalty at suspension.

Adopted.
Your Grievances Committee has carefully examined the entire trial
transcript. The record and the testimony amply and fully support the verdict
of guilty of unmasonic conduct. The serious nature of that misconduct, that
of a Mason recommending a man to be made a Mason, well-knowing such a
person to be unfit to be a Mason, who was not under the tongue of good report,

99

The Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and recommends
its adoption:
RESOLVED, that the finding of the Trial Committee finding the accused
guilty of three counts of unmasonic conduct be approved but the penalty
be raised to expulsion and that the member be expelled from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry. (See C.M.C. 683 Annotations an, ao).
Adopted.
TRIAL REcoRD No. 2015

The accused, a member of Estero Lodge No. 719, was charged with
unmasonic conduct supported by three specifications. The specifications generally allege that the accused committed bigamy on or about April 14, 1972,
and further that on or about )fay 11, 1972, he gave false information regarding the matter to a Past Master of his Lodge.
The accused was tried by Estero Lodge No. 719, and after evidence was
reviewed and the accused admitted that the offense had occurred and that he
had no defense, the Trial Master found the accused guilty and imposed the
penalty of suspension.
It has always -been the feeling of the Committee that after a member has
committed an act serious enough to be classified as a felony, he should be
expelled.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Master in Record No. 2015
be approved, but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and that the member
be expelled from all rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

LODGE ACTIVITIES AND CONDITIONS

To accurately report the condition of the Lodges in this jurisdiction, it is
necessary to carefully analyze the Inspector's annual report forms which are
filed with the Grand Lecturer in July of each year. An analysis of those
reports this year indicates a worsening of conditions within many of the
Lodges as regards availability of new Officer material, membership participation, membership loss and matters of finance. Several of our Lodges have
found it expedient this year to consolidate with others, and many more are
now tottering on the brink of extinction for lack of interested or qualified
Brethren who arc willing to serve their Lodge as Officers.
To quote directly from the Inspectors reports, out of 180 Inspectors who
filed reports, 13 2 report that the Lodges of their District are encountering
great difficulty in obtaining officers to fill the Stations. 13 2, - This represents
75% of all California Lodges who are having problems filling officers stations.
52 of the 180 report that they feel l\fasonry is not progressing within their
District, and practically all report lack of membership participation and loss
of members due to advancing age and lack of petitions for the degrees.
Activities within the Lodges seems to be generally down because of the lack
of interest on the part of the members to Lodge programs and events.
In the two previous Grand Lecturer's reports which I have been privileged
to deliver to this Grand Lodge, I have reported the existance of these problems
within the Lodges and made certain recommendations as to their solution.
Basically, those recommendations were that the Lodges should give serious
consideration to shortening their Officers' progressive line from the usual
period of seven or eight years, to the shorter period of four. This recommendation was based on a thorough study of the problems which beset the
majority of our Lodges, notable among which is the recurring problem of
finding young and qualified members who are willing to commit themselves to
the great number of years required to become Master of the Lodge. Most
business and professional men find it quite impossible to make such a commitment, consequently, a great number of our Lodges are being deprived of
leadership which could conceivably give them new direction and interest.
In view of an even further deterioration in this area, and at the risk of
belaboring the point, I again make the same recommendation. In the hope
that it will be given serious consideration by all of the Lodges, I most strongly

117

H AWAIIAN VISITATION

In February of this ye.ar, it was my privilege to visit the Lodges of H awaii
and to sample the wonderful Aloha Spirit which prevails in that beautiful
Island Paradise. I was accompanied on this trip by Brother "Use" Patropulos,
Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division three, and much good was achieved
in the Schools of Instruction which were conducted in each of the ten
island Lodges, and the two all day schools held on Saturday and Sunday in
Honolulu for all Officers, Officers Coaches and Candidates Coaches. A first
hand observation of the island Lodges disclosed that they are not immune to
those same problems indigenous to the mainland Lodges. Shortages of officer
material is a serious problem, and due to the nature of work requirements in
the islands, it is extremely difficult for members and officers alike to attend
meetings regularly. This has created Ritual problems and in an effort to
correct deficiencies in the Ritual, Brother Patropulos and I spent many hours
demonstrating the floor work of the three degrees. In my opinion our efforts
were well spent, for in each Lodge the Brethren exhibited an eagerness to
perfect their Ritual and dispel the problem areas. At each school we were
asked by the Brethren if it would be possible for these schools to be repeated
within the coming year. The answer of course was yes; these schools will be
repeated as often as required or necessary.
The three Island Inspectors are performing excellently under conditions
often aggravated by great distances which separate the Lodges in the island
chain. To these Inspectors, our heartiest appreciation for their devoted effor ts,
and to all the wonderful Masons of Hawaii: " Me ke aloha pau ale a hui hou."
Which, in the beautiful language of the island means, " With everlasting love
and affection until we meet again."

BUDGET

At last years Annual Communication, a budget appropriation in the
amount of $4 7,500.00 was requested by the Ritual Committee for the year
1971-72. Due to sharply escalating prices for travel and lodging, it was
problematical as to whether this amount would be sufficient to carry out the
assignments of the Ritual. Through the concerted efforts of the Assistant
Grand Lecturers and with the cooperation of all the Inspectors, we were able
to operate well within that budget limitation. Being persuaded that expenses
can be maintained at a level to offset continuing increases in costs, your Ritual
Committee is again this year requesting a budget appropriation in the amount
of $47,500.00 for the year 1972-73.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The Trustees of Masonic Homes of California respectfully present their
Eightieth Annual Report for the year ending June 30, 1972, with accompanying Reports from the Administrator of our Home for Children in
Covina and the Administrator of our Home for the Aged in Union City.
Masonic Homes of California is a charitable corporation, organized by
the Grand Lodge under the laws of the State of California. The corporate
powers are vested in the Board of Trustees. As provided in Section 221 of the
California Masonic Code, the Trustees are eleven in number: the Senior
Grand Warden and the Junior Grand Warden ex-officio and nine members
appointed by successive Grand Masters.

APPLICATIONS FOR RELIEF
Historically the function of the Masonic Homes is to assist the Constituent
Lodges in taking care of their bona fide chronic or permanent relief cases as
distinguished from temporary cases. Where appropriate, relief is extended by
means of admission to the Home for the Aged, the Home for Children or by
outside relief to the particular lodge. Individuals may not apply direct to
Masonic Homes. Applications for admission or assistance must originate with
the Constituent Lodge involved. The rules governing admission or assistance,
approved by the Grand Lodge, are set forth in the Appendix to the California
Masonic Code to which all Lodge Officers should refer whenever help is
needed.
The procedural steps are: ( 1) The Lodge Secretary writes or phones to
the Grand Secretary for the proper application form; (2) the Grand Secretary
immediately furnishes the application form which contains detailed instructions for completion; (3) the Worshipful Master appoints a 3-man
committee to investigate the circumstances of need and assist the applicant in
filling out the application which includes family, financial and medical information (under no circumstances should the application be completed by the
applicant); (4) the Lodge committee reports its recommendation back to the
Master for consideration at the next Stated Meeting; ( 5) by resolution the
Lodge approves or rejects the application; ( 6) if the Lodge approves the application, it is forwarded by the Secretary, over the seal of the Lodge, to the
Grand Secretary; (7) the Grand Secretary refers the application to one of the
Board's two Field Representatives: Mrs. Sue Collins in San Francisco, or Mrs.
Martha Quick in Covina; (8) the Field Representative contacts the Lodge
and the applicant and prepares a formal summary of the case, a Xerox copy
of which is mailed at once to each Trustee for study; ( 10) the Grand Secre-

123

iary schedules the case on the Agenda for the next regular monthly meeting
of the Board of Trustees; ( 11) the members of the Board vote upon each
application on the Agenda; (12) if the Trustees approve the application, the
Grand Secretary notifies the Lodge and arrangements are made administratively to implement the relief approved; ( 13) if the Trustees find it
necessary to deny relief, the Grand Secretary notifies the Lodge of the
reasons for the denial; (14) if further information is required, the application
is deferred to a subsequent meeting pending supplemental investigation.
These procedural steps have been outlined to emphasize the importance
of orderly and prompt handling of all applications, the essential role of the
Constituent Lodge and the fact that applications must be processed by and
through the Lodge before they can come before the Board of Trustees. Whenever the Officers of a Lodge have any question regarding procedures, we earnestly urge that they contact the Grand Secretary by letter or telephone. In
bis capacity as Secretary of the Masonic Homes, he will see that they have
a prompt answer to their problem.

OUTSIDE REIJEF
The record shows that as early as 1935 the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes were confronted with requests for assistance for those who
would not otherwise qualify for admission to the Homes. In their report to the
Grand Lodge under the heading of Outside Relief the Board recommended
'
and Grand Lodge approved, the following statement:
"Instead of admission to the Home, outside relief may be granted in
cases where, in the opinion of the Trustees, applicants can be better or
more economicAlly cared for outside the Homes."
Then they proceeded to give the circumstances under which outside relief
may be granted. Then follows the three conditions which are now stated in
the appendix, page 3 70 of the California Masonic Code. They further indica~ed "I.t is not the policy to give outside relief for temporary needs, such
rehef being the duty of the Lodge direct."
In Grand Master Herbert A. Huebner's message in 1971, he called attention to a special relief case for a physically or mentally impaired adult child
of a deceased Master Mason.
In checking our Masonic law it was obvious that no provision had been
made for such an emergent situation. The Grand Master ruled "that a Lodge
may, in its discretion, provide relief in exceptional circumstances to the adult
child of a deceased Mason where a need arises by reason of physical or
mental impairment."
The Grand Master further recommended that the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes be requested to undertake a study relative to the possible
amendment of its requirements which would permit outside relief to be
granted under exceptional circumstances.

124

Your Board has made such a study. It is the unanimous opinion that provision should be made for outside relief in cases similar to the one in point.
At its September meeting the Trustees unanimously adopted the following
resolution:
It was moved, seconded and carried that it be reported to the
next Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge and in accordance
with direction given to the Board of Trustees, (see page 77 of the
1971 Proceedings,) that it be the policy of the Board of Trustees of
the Masonic Homes of California to consider an application from a
Lodge for Outside Relief under exceptional circumstances for the
adult child of a deceased Master Mason who is physically or mentally impaired, and that there be added on page 370 of Calif.
Masonic Code Appendix, under the heading "Outside Relief,"
(d) Under exceptional circumstances the adult child of a deceased
Master Mason who is physically or mentally impaired.

The Resolution was unanimously adopted.

Prior to 1967 the Board of Trustees seriously considered the advisability
of moving the Home for Children from its location, on the outskirts of
Covina, to a more remote site. Several areas were investigated. It was recognized that the old two-story institutional brick buildings, constructed on the
dormitory philosophy, were outmoded and becoming unduly expensive to
maintain. Also, the accelerating growth of the city of Covina presented new
problems of administration for the staff at the Home.
After thorough investigation of possible alternatives, it was the decision
of the Board in 1967 to maintain the Home for Children at its present site. At
the 1968 Annual Communication a master plan of redevelopment of the
Home for Children was reported. Under the leadership of Donald G. Campbell,
then President of the Board, this plan proceeded toward completion. A.
Quincy Jones, F. A. I. A., and Associates, Inc. (formerly Jones and Emmons)
were engaged to prepare all plans necessary to convert the facility to a modern
residential community type of home for children. With their architectural
guidance the Master Plan for Redevelopment of the Home for Children has
been progressing as follows:

storage and the ultimate demolition of the old infirmary (presently being used
as a temporary dormitory pending completion of two cottages to be constructed beginning in December 19 72) .
From the testimony of our Administrator, as well as public and private
authorities on child care, your Trustees firmly believe that our Home for
Children, when fully redeveloped, will constitute the finest facility of its type
in the world. We are especially pleased that through careful and prudent
management the redevelopment of the Home will have been achieved without
any increase in the per capita assessment on the Lodges for the Homes.
However, development of the facility is not the real goal. The true goal is
the highest degree of perfection attainable in the care of the children who
are our responsibility. We have every reason to believe that the new plant and
equipment are proving to be most meaningful in the lives of the children, their
growth and development. This is evidenced in the accompanying report of
James C. Blaine, Administrator of the Home for Children, which you will find
most inspiring.

Trustees reported that it seemed advisable to move the Home for the Aged
to some other site in the ~ay Area and steps were being. taken for the stu~y
and survey of avai~able sit~. ?b~olescence, both. fu~ct1?nal and economic,

In the report of the Trustees in 1971 the Board again emphasized its
concern with the question of Decoto Redevelopment and annou?~ed that two
entirely independent studies had been made of the present fac1hty to determine if, based upon present requirements of law and building regulations, use
could be made of the existing site and buildings. One study was made by
A. Quincy Jones, F. A. I. A., and Associates, Inc. (formerly Jones and
Emmons), who have been the architects for the Covina redevelopment, and
the other report was prepared by the Community Health Planning Corporation of San Francisco. Both of these studies revealed that the Hayward
Fault extends along the western face of the Hayward hills through the
present site of our Home for the Aged and advocated a move to a different
site. (It should be pointed out that current studies disclose the Fault does
not pass under our buildings, but lies some distance from them.)
In the search for alternative sites the professional assistance of a real
property specialist was obtained who provided a summary of acreage which
might be available for development. Unfortunately, many of these proved to
be located on the San Andreas Fault and less desirable than the existing site.
Meantime, financial investigation has revealed that the cost of abandoning
our present Ho.me, the acquisition of a different site and the design and
construction of a completely new set of structures would thrust an overwhelming burden upon the financial resources of Masonic Homes of California
and the Fraternity. This would result in potentially sharp increases in the per
capita assessment on the Lodges and heavy borrowing. In addition an engineering analysis prepared by Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderson (a
Trustee of the Board, an outstanding engineer, and the author of the earthquake code for the State of California) pointed out advantages in the present
site and stated that redevelopment of the location would be feasible.
Trustee Anderson's analysis prompted the Board to engage Dr. Lloyd
Cluff, a principal partner in the firm of Woodward and Lundgren of Oakland
and San Francisco (an authority on the Hayward Fault), to conduct and prepare a geological survey of our site as rapidly as possible. This has included
extensive excavations on the property. Dr. Cluff's report was delivered to the
Board of Trustees at the September meeting. The report itself entitled "Geologic and Seismic Site Evaluation - Masonic Home of California, Union
City" is made up of 34 pages of carefully documented comments supported
by Exhibits, Maps, descriptions of 12 test trenches and a general discussion
of earthquakes and faultings. The test trenches were dug to a maximum depth

HOME FOR THE AGED
As changes have taken place in concepts of child care, so also changes
have occurred in concepts of housing, feeding, recreation and medical care of
the aged.
Prior to 1969 our Home for the Aged was licensed only for the admission
of ambulatory cases - those who in an emergency could make their escape
out of a building without assistance from others. This made it impossible for
the Trustees to approve admission of non-ambulatory cases - those requiring
assistance to leave a building in an emergency. Of course, once admitted, the
ambulatory case would remain in our care even though later becoming nonambulatory or a nursing case. Meantime, the incidence of needy non-ambulatory cases desiring admission continued to increase.
In 1969 through the research leadership of Past Grand Master Laurence
E. Dayton, a Trustee and legal counsel for the Iloard, Masonic Homes of
California succeeded in obtaining a license for admission of a limited number
of non-ambulatory cases. This was done by means of upgrading and improving
certain of the rooms and equipment in Adams Hall and the Administration
Building. While it has been possible to admit many non-ambulatory cases
since 1969, sufficient space is not available to meet the growing non-ambulatory need.

The "$502,978 short" is hopefully made up by funds from gifts, contributions and bequests received during the year and proceeds from residents'

On June 30, 1972, there was $26,489,962 in the Endowment Fund. Only
the income may be used to care for our guests. The 1973 anticipated income
from this source is $1,290,852.
On June 30, 1972, the general fund of the Homes consisted of $12,5 64,890.
This sum represents the emergency fund , the operating fund and capital fund.
The vital necessary income from these funds for operation of the Homes in
1972-73 is estimated to be $580,261.00.
In addition, the Masonic Homes Board has jurisdiction over funds, the
use of which has been restricted by the donor. The income, from that source
remains part of the corpus until spent for the special purposes specified by
the donor.
There are no other funds of the Masonic Homes!
Thus, it is crystal clear that there are no large sums available to redevelop our Home at Union City. To use most or all of the funds in our
operating account would be the height of folly. Any such proposal would
eliminate our r~serve operating fund; our emergency funds; and the necessary
income from investment of these monies.
The proper and orderly procedure is for the Hornes Board to do this
redevelopment as was done at Covina - on a priority basis over a period of
time.
It is anticipated that redevelopment of Decoto (Union City) can be
similarly programmed. All of us realize that we must continue to care for our
guests during the redevelopment program.
At our September Board meeting considerable time was given to the
discussion of how we could handle this proposed construction, or reconstruction, without placing an undue burden upon the Masons of California
who support the Home. In that connection the Grand Master, Grand Treasurer, Miss Birma Roush (our chief accounting officer), and the Chairman
of the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance together with two of his Committeemen joined in on our discussion and concurred in our findings.
It was brought to the attention of the Board of Trustees that, as the
result of a careful study our Accounting Office has developed a projection as
to the costs for "Life Care Committment" for the present residents of Decoto
and Covina. This material should be of substantial assistance in answering
our financial questions as we project the future of the Homes. For interested

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR
MASONIC HOME AT UNION CITY
It is with pleasure that I present my second report as Administrator of the
Masonic Home in Union City, for the fiscal year ending June 30th, 1972.
The population on June 30, 1972 was 397, including 32 married couples.
There were 168 men and 229 women, and the average age was 83.41 years.
For the second year in a row, the average age of our men residents, 84 years,
slightly exceeded the average age of our women, which was 83 years.
Ninety six residents were admitted from June 30, 1971 to June 30, 1972,
50 men, average age of 82 years and 46 women, average age of 79.52 years.
We laid to rest 54 residents, with an average age of 86.70 years. Six men were
withdrawn and four women withdrawn.

During the past fiscal year, our population has greatly increased. On
July 1, 1971 there were 365 residents, including 157 men and 208 women (32
married couples) with an average age of 83.43 years. Over the year our population has fluctuated, and we reached a new high on May 1, 1972 of 398,
and as of June 30, we were up 32 residents over the same period last year.
The total capacity of our hospital, including the 5th floor Adams Hall, is
167. On June 30, 1972 the hospital census was 155 patients of which 139 were
considered permanent. There were also 81 semi-ambulatory residents requiring
nursing care and 59~ % of the total population of the Home was under
nursing care. Because of the advanced age of the new residents entering the
Home (80.76 years) we can expect an even greater percentage of our population requiring nursing care in the future.
There were 3,593 visitors who signed our register, representing 460
Lodges in California, Hawaii and Alaska, 32 other states and 9 foreign
countries, Kwajelein, Marshall Islands, Scotland, The Netherlands, Canada,
Philippines, Belgium, Africa, Australia and Rhodesia. We were honored by
the visitation of Grand Commander Supreme Council of Belgium and the
Past Grand Master of Kansas, S. Allan Daugherty.
Our residents' Coffee Shop which was opened last year has been very successful and greatly appreciated by the residents. The Barber Shop, Beauty
Shop, Canteen and Post Office have been moved to the Fourth Floor North
Section. In due time all residents activities will be located on this floor and it
will be known as "Masonic Mall".
The Arts and Crafts Shop has been expanded and is now being used to its
fullest capacity. Last Labor Day week-end we held our first Masonic Home
Arts & Crafts Show. Over 250 exhibits which had been made by our residents
were exhibited. The BEST OF THE SHOW prize went to Mrs. Agnes Chamberlain, a permanent patient in our hospital. The Masonic Home Arts and
Crafts show will be an annual festival, with the public invited.
It is with regret that we report that Mrs. Annie Matthews passed away
this April at the age of 107 years. Mrs. Teresa Locke is now our oldest living
resident and will be 107 years on November 30th, 1972.

Our special thanks to the East Bay Past Matrons Association for their
59th annual visitation and reception for their Worthy Grand l\fatron and

permit me to mention the many Brethren, Lodges and friends who have made
various contributions of money, clothing, books, games, TVs, etc., which are
greatly appreciated and have been put to good use. Our Fraternal thanks to
all of you for your continued contributions.
We were honored on several occasions by visits of our Most Worshipful
Grand Master, Lester McElwain.
My personal thanks to the employees for their continuing cooperation and
effort in making our Masonic Home a better place to live.
To the Board of Trustees, the Grand Secretary and the San Francisco
Office, I express my appreciation and gratitude for all their interest in the
Home and for their cooperation and guidance during this year.

l917, has been demolished and replaced by a beautiful administration complex. This complex consists of (a) a modem up-to-date infirmary; (b) a
multi-purpose recreation, library, study hall room; ( c) a beautiful parlor;
(d) a completely new kitchen and dining hall; (e) a compact service building
consisting of repair shop and laundry; and (f) a suite of administrative
offices. This complex surrounds an open air patio which emphasizes our
DeMolay " Fountain of the Future." All our new buildings have been equipped
with new furnishings of bright, happy, colors that children enjoy.
Our children have been involved in many and varied supervised activities.
They have enjoyed special trips to cultural and fine arts exhibits in the local
community as well as par ticipated in baseball, football, DeMolay, Jobs
Daughters, Rainbow Girls and other groups such as Scouting, etc. Music
lessons are available for those who wish to pursue these studies. Weekend and
residential camping at Big Bear and the beach have been enjoyed. One of the
year's highlights was a trip to Decoto where our children enjoyed being hosted
by our elderly guests. Many "pen pals" have resulted from this visit.
Our Home Family has enjoyed good health this year. A few minor accidents have taken place but we have not suffered any serious illnesses. We have
continued yearly physical examinations which have included eye and dental
exams. Some of these in-depth physicals have resulted in glasses being
prescribed for some, and orthodontia for others. We are pleased to report that
there has been an increase in requests for visitations! Our children and staff
look forward to your visits. We sincerely hope that you and your Lodges
might be able to visit us in the near future. During your visitation our
children will be happy to serve as guides. Arrangements for visitations can be
made by calling the Home or writing for dates.
Please accept ·our sincere thanks for the many acts of kindness and
consideration extended the children under our care. A special thanks to the
Board of Trustees and our Masonic brethren in California and Hawaii whose
interest and efforts make possible our Masonic Home for Children.

Respectfully submitted,

INCOME FROM THE ENDOWMENT FUND

Our permanent Endowment Fund earned $1,212,979.43 this past year,
which amount has been transferred to the operating accounts of our two
Masonic Homes. It is significant that each member would need to contribute
$5.34 to equal this amount if we did not have the Endowment Fund working
for us. One can appreciate the wisdom of those early Masons who established
this permanent Endowment Fund.
BEQUESTS, GIFTS AND MEMORIALS

Bequests in the amount of $245,382.91 were received into the Endowment
Fund this past year. In addition, $768,117.67 were received by the Homes
in bequests from estates where the Endowment Fund was not specifically
mentioned in the will.
Organizations and individuals made gifts in the amount of $9,64 7.29.
Memorials added $39,791.72 to our funds, making a total of $1,062,939.59
received during the past year in the form of bequests, memorials, and gifts
from organizations and individuals. One can readily see the importance of
stressing the value of bequests and wills for the benefit of our two homes.

RECOGNITION TO lNSPECTORAL CORPS

RECOGNITION TO LODGE SECRETARIES

We extend our special thanks and appreciation to the Grand Lecturer and
Inspectors who as a body enthusiastically support the endowment program.
This support is invaluable to our success.

The secretaries play a vital role in disseminating information and literature
to the members of the lodges. It is through their efforts that we bring our
message to those who do not attend Lodge on a regular basis. Our special
thanks to each of our Lodge Secretaries for their wonderful help.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

143

Our thanks to the Grand Lodge officers, Past Grand Masters, and Grand
Lodge Committeemen who have always looked out for our Masonic Homes.
To the Grand Lecturer, Assistant Grand Lecturers, Masters and Wardens, and
Endowment Committeemen, our thanks for helping to encourage the Brethren
to share in the satisfaction of helping our elderly at Union City and our
children at Covina.
It has been a pleasure to work with our Grand Lodge office. The leadership
of our Grand Secretary Edward H. Siems and Assistant Grand Secretary
Verne W. Hendrix, along with the efficiency of their staff, made it possible to
handle the many details associated with the work of this Iloard.
We are most grateful to the 111,479 Brethren who contributed $959,157.90
for our permanent Endowment Fund.
Your chairman commends the members of this Board for a complete
dedication and a total effort.
My Brethren, this is a fine monetary record of which we are proud. However, in a deeper sense this is also an expres~ion from the Brethren of this
Grand Lodge of understanding and love for their fellow men. When we look
to our two Homes, we see the results of our efforts in happy, secure people
who are in their declining years; and the joy of seeing children who are
maturing into healthy young men and women preparing to take their places
in a complex society.
Respectfully submitted,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
KERMIT A. JACOBSON, Chairman
BOARD MEMBERS

CERTIFICATES OF MERIT

Your Board has recognized for some time that our $2 .00 goal for Honor
Roll status has been of little incentive for so many Lodges which have exceeded this mark. For several years we have separately displayed those
Lodges making an average of $3.00 or more. It is our plan to design a plaque
or certificate which will be laminated on its own backing and will have adequate space to add the designation each year. We feel confident that those
Lodges which have far exceeded even the $3.00 minimum will continue to
strive for their own new goals and that those which have been below $3.00
will put forth every effort to meet and to pass this minimum requirement.
CONCLUSION
Special mention must go to our Grand Master, the Most Worshipful
Lester S. McElwain, who has given us his full support. We have gained by
his warm and enthusiastic leadership and his stimulating addresses throughout
California and Hawaii.

IN GRAND LODGE
MORNING SESSION- Tuesday, October 10, 1972
Grand Lodge was called on at 9:30 A.M., the Grand Master presiding.
Past Masters Eugene R. Gilbertson and Earl C. Lowe, Inspectors of the 606th
and 610th Masonic Districts respectively, raised Grand Lodge. The invocation
was delivered by the Grand Chaplain. The minutes of the morning and afternoon sessons of Monday, October 9, 1972 were read and approved.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
As of June 30, 1972 there were 19 Masonic Service Bureaus representing
335 Lodges and approximate ly 136,208 Master Masons of California. The
Bureaus vary in size from 4 Lodges to the largest with a membership of 98
Lodges.

*The six Bureaus in Los Angeles County received financial contributions of
approximately the amount of their approved budget from the Masonic
Board of Relief of the City of Los Angeles, a corporation. These Bureaus
did not have a per-capita assessment. Prior to the receipt of the financial
contribution, Long Beach collected per-capita funds and the amount of
$1511.00 has been refunded to the member Lodges of that Bureau.
Bureaus having a surplus fund, derived from per-capita assessment, in
excess of 125% of their approved budget have been requested to reduce or
suspend assessments until such time as the surplus is in compliance with the
Rules and Regulations.
It should be noted that the Santa Barbara and Richmond Bureaus operated without an assessment to their members and without other sources of
financial assistance.
Typical of the caliber of Masons acting as officers and employees of the
Service Bureaus are Executive Secretaries, Del May of Santa Barbara and
Anthony Taylor of Southern Alameda County, who served without pay. It
is also reported that Gene Bloomfield, Bakersfield Executive Secretary, extended financial relief out of his own pocket.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Special recognition must be given to the East Bay Bureau. Under the
leadership of President Keith Abshire, the budget has been reduced approximately 43 % .
VISITATIONS AND MEETINGS

By pre-arrangement with the Bureaus, inspections of the operations and
records of the San Jose, Stockton, and San Gabriel Valley Bureaus were made
by the Board of Control.
Executive Secretaries, Herman Little of San Jose and Edwin Arnold of
Stockton, maintain excellent and detailed records. The officers and members
of these Bureaus are to be commended for their outstanding operation. They
are a credit to Masonry and the area they serve.
The San Gabriel Valley Bureau was found to have adequate and accurate
accounting methods for their particular operation. Minor recommendations
were made for record and operational procedures.
Every visitation was an enjoyable and enlightening experience to the
Board. We were received very cordially and every effort was made by the
officers of the Bureaus to cooperate and comply with the Rules and Regulations.
Additional inspections were planned to the Bakersfield, Fresno, and
Orange County Bureaus. Arrangements had not been completed at the time
this report was prepared.
Representatives of the Board have met with Lodges or Bureaus on 18
other occasions to discuss Service Bureau matters.
Implementation, on an experimental basis, of seminar type meetings with
Bureaus in the Northern and Southern part of the State, to discuss and review mutual problems and procedures, was delayed due to the time required
to revise and rewrite the Rules and Regulations.
The Board held four business meetings since January of this year, two in
the Los Angeles area and two in Oakland. Detailed minutes of the meetings
and reports of interim activities of the Board were sent to the Grand Master.
All recommendations and decisions of the Board were submitted to the
Grand Master for approval prior to implementation.
RULES AND REGULATIONS

As the result of legislation enacted at the last Session of Grand Lodge and
changes deemed desirable through experience, it was ncessary for the Board
of Control to devote much of its time and effort to the rewriting of the Rules
and Regulations for the Operation of Masonic Service Bureaus.
Suggestions and recommendations were solicited from Bureaus and interested brethren. The only reservation made by the Board was that the change
must be for the benefit of all Bureaus and not applicable to only one Bureau
or an isolated situation. The response was most gratifying. Typical of the

171

cooperation and willingness to assist was President 1\-Iel Nahin of Los Angeles
who appointed a special committee.
The revision was completed in June and approved by the Grand Master
and his Elective Line Officers. The Board is most appreciative of their guidance, counsel, and complete understanding of Service Bureau operations.
Through the expeditious efforts of the Grand Secretary and his staff, printing and distribution to the Bureaus was accomplished by the Grand Lodge
office early in July at a considerable financial savings. Circulation to Lodges
and Bureau representatives wa. ;iccomplished by the Bureau offices. A copy
was provided for insertion in the Lodge Manual of each member Lodge. Additional copies, if required, may be obtained through the Grand Secretary's
office.
The Board is deeply indebted to the Most Worshipful Leo Anderson, Past
Grand Master, for his unselfish service during our efforts to rewrite the Rules.
His advice and wisdom were both good and timely.
All Bureaus have been encouraged to meet with representatives of the
Board to review and discuss the new Rules and thereby eliminate any misinterpretation. To date we have held such meetings with San Diego, Glendale,
San Gabriel Valley, San Francisco, and jointly with East Bay, Richmond, and
Southern Alameda County Bureaus.
TAXES

The complexity of tax laws prompted the Board to send inquiries to each
Bureau to determine if Federal and State tax exemption status forms had
been filed and what, if any, income tax forms were being filed with the government agencies. Further discussions with Tax Committee will be necessary
to clarify the status of the Bureaus and provide the Board with information
that will result in uniform and concise instructions to the Bureaus.
FORMS AND STUDIES

The Board continued its study and up dating of forms, compacts, and
procedures. Forms required to report Bureau activities have been revised to
reflect the change of name from Boards of Relief to Service Bureaus and also
changes in approved operations. The assistance of former Chairman Jim
Wellet in preparing and donating mats to expedite and reduce printing cost
is gratefully acknowledged.
The Standard Practice Bulletin manual , dated July 1, 1963, was determined to be hopelessly out dated. Bureaus have been advised of its discontinuance and to develop their own methods within the concept of the Rules and
Regulations.
Standard forms for reporting funeral data and mileage payments have been
designed for use by the Bureaus in 197 3.
An in-depth audit of Uniform Compacts, the contract or agreement between Lodges and Bureaus, has been completed. What at first appeared to be

173

a routine assignment became two years of Herculean research for the Secre·
tary of this Board. Upon finalization of the program, a complete file of active
compacts will be in the Grand Lodge archives. New compacts should be obtained to clarify the records of 12 Lodge consolidations. Copies of 14 other
compacts are necessary to complete the file.

To provide a safe, central, and permanent location of records, all Board
of Control minutes prior to 196 7 and other surplus records will be delivered

REALIGNMENT

The Board continued realignment of membership as outlined at the 1971
Session of Grand Lodge. Recommended changes were consistent with the
Rules and Regulations and established policies. There were 13 withdrawals,
5 transfers, and 5 new memberships approved.
Florence 423 was approved as a member of the Los Angeles Bureau on
3-14-72 to clarify its membership status as the result of Lodge consolidation
of non-member Florence 649 and Bureau member York 423.
Realignments are still pending in the Santa Ana, Anaheim, and Santa
Monica Bay areas. Meetings with the representatives of Ledges in these areas
have been held and it is the opinion of the Board that this program will be
completed prior to the close of the 1972-1973 fiscal year.
The Board appreciates the cooperation it has received from the Lodges,
Bureaus, Inspectors, and Grand Lodge Officers in accomplishing membership
changes with the minimum of confusion and misunderstanding. It is suggested and hoped that the mechanics of a system can be set up so that any
necessary change in Bureau membership will be made at the time approval
is given to relocate, consolidate, or create a new Lodge.
