EXPANSION

Two Bureaus indicated a desire to expand the area serviced under their
present jurisdiction. Both Bureaus were instructed to maintain a six month
record of service requests beyond their normal jurisdiction and forward the
same to the Board of Control for study.

To the M ost Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Catifornia:

Your Committee on Commercialism herewith submits its report for the
year just ending.
Infractions of our laws, rules and regulations under the jurisdiction of
this committee have been minor in nature. No Masonic trial resulted from
any matter of violation.
The infractions or violations have been handled through discussion and
an understanding. Those in violation have agreed to cease and desist. Several
examples of items referred to the Commercialism Committee are as follows:
Several of the clandestine bodies were in violation of using the Square and
Compass in advertising. Those in violation were instructed that the Sq uare
and Compass is the property of the Grand Lodge of California and that permission to use same must come from the Grand Master of this body.
A color photography company was soliciting the Job's Daughters, Rainbow
Girls and DeMolays fo r installation photos, again the Square and Compass
was used in the solicitation, it was the concern of the Committee that a
possible Masonic roster was being used to promote their photo business.
A number of the charitable athletic events were reviewed by the committee. The audited fi nancial statements of the Shrine football games in California and Hawaii were submitted to the Grand Master and examined by the
Committee. Recommendations and conclusions were reported to the Grand
Master.
Over a period Of years considerable money has been raised by the Shrine
foo tball games for the hospitals for crippled children as well as the burn
centers. During this year your Committee has had considerable conversation,
both in meetings and in letter form, regarding the conduct and operation of
some of these games and as a result of those meetings a clarification of the
195 7 Annual Communication with relation to game proceeds was felt to be
justified. The 1957 Proceed ings read that, "No division of the proceeds shall
be made with any institution, organization, group, or individual other than
payment of necessary expenses." This was approved by the Grand Lodge in
195 7 and has been stringently observed ever since.
Although application of this procedure, was intended for Masonic Lodges
or masonically affiliated groups, the restriction has been used with respect to
all parties or institutions concerned.
Periodically the strict observance of this rule, particularly with nonmasonic groups, such as schools or universities has been inconvenient.
Hence the Committee proposes the following r ecommendation be added
to the language quoted above: " Except that permission for a division of game
proceeds could be approved by the Grand Lodge under the recommenda tion of

178

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the Committee on Commercialism, providing such a proposed co-sponsored
game's contractual plan be submitted to the Grand Lodge for approval ten
months prior to the date of the game."
A second important item was the subject of Masonic advertising during
our year.
The cost of mailing, publishing and printing of masonic bullet.ins, as well
as charity football programs, has reached proportions that are not commensurate with the amount of dues received by the various masonic organizations.

In order to mainta in the quality of bullet.ins and to offset printing and
mailing costs, your Committee has been asked to review and give their recommendations on the subject of masonic advertising.
Herewith are the recommendations of the Committee:
Advertising would be allowed in the monthly bulletins, publications, newsletters, as well as charity football programs, of the following named organizations: any group, chapter, order, club, association or organization, requiring
Masonic affiliation or sponsorship, including but not limited to:
York Rite Bodies
Scottish Rite Bodies
Shrine
Scio ts
Grotto
Eastern Star
White Shrine of Jerusalem
Job's Daughters
Rainbow Girls
DeMolay
Masonic Clubs and Associations
Provided:
( 1) That all funds received from advertising be used only for the printing,
publication and mailing of such bulletins or charity foo tball programs.
(2) That such advertising be strictly voluntary and of a Mason's own
free will and accord and that no solicitation be used to secure such ads.
(3) That the advertising be limite<l to twenty-five p ercent of the usual size
of the monthly publications as long as the monthly publication is not reduced
in size from its average size over the last two years from the date of acceptance of this recommendation by Grand Lodge.
( 4) That the Masters of the Blue Lodges, the four Masters of the Scottish
Rite, the Divan of the Shrine and the Grand Commander of the Commandry
shall be jointly and severally responsible for the proper conduct of their respective Lodges for such allowed advertising program and the budgeting of
funds. An accounting of such advertising funds shall be submitted each year
to the Grand Secretary for approval of the Grand Lodge.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

179

( S) Penalties for infractions of this recommendation :
A. First infraction, for a period of one year no advertising will be
allowed.
B. Second infraction, a three year cease and desist order will be issued.
C . Third infraction , such organization shall be permanently restricted
from advertising under this recommendation.
Investigation of such infraction to be conducted by the Commercialism Committee.
The criteria of the type of advertising allowed has been taken from the

1966 Proceeding of the Grand Lodge of Indiana, Page 79, paragraph 3 e and f
and are as follows :
( 1) Advertisements must not contain direct or indirect appeal to Masons
to do business with other Masons.
(2) Liquor advertising, political advertising, advertising any lottery or
game of chance are forbidden (advertising of taverns and liquor stores are
taboo).
(3) The words "Mason," "Masonic" or any other word associated wi~h
Freemasonry must not be used in advertising, nor can Masonic emblems, m
particular the Square and Compass with or without the letter "G,'' be used.
Brethren, this concludes the Committee Recommendations.
Your committee does not initiate investigations. Its activities originate
with complaints which are referred to the Committee. A member of the Co~­
mittee is assigned each complaint an d after investigation the final report is
forwarded to the Grand Secretary. Continual education of the Brethren will
help to reduce the·number of complaints. If in doubt as to the legality of an
affair a letter to the Committee asking recommendations will further reduce
violations a nd infractions.
Your committee appreciates the helpful cooperation of the Grand Master,
the Grand Secretary and The Grand Lodge Officers. It has been a privilege to
have worked with each of them.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The report of the Special Committee on Commercialism was referred to
tl1e Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The first recommendation proposes to remove the present restriction on
the division of the proceeds of Shrine games for "necessary expenses" to
permit the division of proceeds on recommendation of the Committee on
Commercialism. Since the games are charitable endeavors we can see no need
for payment of other than "all proper expenses."
The second recommendation is much more distressing, far-reaching and
disturbing. It has been a source of great pride among California Freemasons
that our publication, the California Freemason, is recognized internationally
as one of the most outstanding of Masonic publications. It has been equally
gratifying to note that the brethren have uniformly opposed, whenever the
matter has been presented, the opening of that publication to advertising. The
recommendation of the Special Committee would go even further and permit
advertising in Lodge Bulletins, newsletters, and other publications. While
provision is made that no solicitation of advertising be done, your Committee
believes such solicitation would be unavoidable and inevitable. Even more
concern is occasioned by the recommendation that a joint committee composed
of "Masters of the Blue Lodges, the four Masters of the Scottish Rite, the
Divan of the Shrine and the Grand Commander of the Commandery" shall
determine "advertising program and the budgeting of funds." This would
remove lhe decision making process from the body of Freemasonry, the Masonic Lodges, where your Committee strongly believes it properly belongs and
must always be kept.
We recognize that some Grand Jurisdictions permit advertising in their
publications but your Committee does not believe we should emulate their
less desirable characteristics but that we, in California, should be able to
continue in the finest tra<litions of Masonry.
I move the adoption of the recommendations in the report of the Special
Committee on Commercialism and your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes strongly urges a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

The Report of the Special Committee on Commercialism was referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence, and we have conferred with representatives
of the Committee and there are two recommendations to be considered:
The first recommendation simply proposes a change in a regulation of the
Committee which is in the 1957 proceedings as part of the Committee Report
and is not law contained in the California Masonic Code and, accordingly,
no legislation is required.
The second recommendation proposes changes in Section 334 of the California Masonic Code, but we are not certain as to exactly what legislation

181

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

should be prepared and it would take more time to do this than we have
available at this Communication.
We, accordingly, move that if the recommendation of the Committee on
Commercialism as to advertising is approved by this Grand Lodge that the
preparation of the necessary legislation be referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence and the Committee on Commercialism for their report thereon
at the 1973 Annual Communication.
We move the adoption of this report.
(NOTE: By separate action of Grand Lodge a majority voted against
the recommendations made by the Special Committee on Commercialism
relative to advertising.)

REPORT OF TAXATION COMMITIEE
1972
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

At the 19 71 Grand Lodge meeting the scope of your committee was extended from payroll taxes to include other taxes and tax reports required from
our Lodges. In April 1972, the Grand Secretary issued detailed information
to all lodge Secretaries regarding their tax and reporting responsibilities.
For reference purposes, this report will summarize the various requirements at the present time. You should be cautioned that summaries cannot be
complete and you should refer to the government instructions
additional
information. You also should understand that the laws are sub1ect to continual change.

ro:

RETURNS
Lodges are required to file returns with the U. S. Internal Reve~ue Service
and the California Franchise Tax Board by May 15 each year. Failure to file
may result in severe penalties.
U. S. Internal Revenue Service Form 990, "Return of Organi:iation
Exempt from Income Tax," must be filed if the lodge has gross receipts of
more than $5,000.
FEDERAL UNEMPLOYMENT TAX (FUTA)
Lodges are subject to this tax if they paid wages of $1,500 or more in any
quarter or had one or more employees at any time in each .of twenty weeks.
Wages are taxable if $50 or more is earned by an e~pl~yee m ~ quarter. The
tax is 3.2% reduced by a credit of 2.7% for contributions paid to the Sta~e
unemployment fund or a net of .5 % applied to the first $4,200 wages paid
each year to each employee. This is a tax on employers.
CALIFORNIA UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE TAX (CUI)
Lodges are subject to this tax if an employee earned $50 or more per
quarter of taxable wages (the same as for FUTA), or if total wages of $100

182

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

or more are paid in some quarter. If the lodge is not subject to Federal Unemployment Tax, then wages paid to an employee will be exempt from CUI
unless total wages paid exceed $100 per month. The amount of tax is based
on employment experience and varies from 1.4% to 3.5% (which includes
the balancing fund account) applied to the first $4,200 wages paid each year
to each employee. This is a tax on employers.

Real or tangible personal property owned by Lodges or other groups that
is located in California on March 1st is subject to local property tax. A personal property tax statement may be required by the local assessor.
Lodges may be responsible for sales tax on receipts from furnishing of
meals unless furnished exclusively for members and not more frequently than
once a week. If the Lodge furnishes meals to nonmembers or to members more
frequently than once a week, all receipts are subject to tax whether furnished
to members or nonmembers. Meals paid for by members are considered
furnished to them even though consumed by guests who are not members.
The tax reports now required from Lodges have increased to a considerable
burden, however the laws must be observed. Failure to conform to the law
will result in penalties and possible unfavorable publicity. The Grand Secretary and your Committee on Taxation will assist whenever possible.

CALIFORNIA DISABILITY INSURANCE TAX (SDI)
Employees are subject to this tax on the same wages subject to the
employers tax for unemployment insurance. The tax is l % of the first $8,000
of wages paid each year to each employee for 1972. For the years 1973 and
thereafter the tax is 1% on the first $8,500 of wages paid each year. This is a
tax on employees only.
California Franchise Tax Board Form 199B, "Exempt Organization
Annual Information Statement,'' must be filed by all lodges with gross receipts
and assets under $5,000.
California Franchise Tax Board Form 199, "Exempt Organization Annual
Information Return,'' must be filed by all lodges with gross receipts and
assets of over $5 ,000.
lNCOM.E TAX WITHHOLDING
All wages paid to any lodge employee (secretary, tiler, organist, soloist,
etc) are subject to U.S. and California income tax withholding. The amount
to be withheld is determined by U. S. Form W-4 "Employee Withholding
Exemption Certificate" which must be obtained from every employee. Withholding tax tables may be found in the Internal Revenue Service Employer's
Tax Guide Publication 15 (Circular E) and in California Department of
Human Resources Development, Employer's Income Tax Withholding Guide,
Publication DE 44.
Lodges that have not registered with the Department of Human Resources
Development for state disability or unemployment insurance contributions
must register within 15 days of becoming subject to income tax withholding.
SOCIAL SECURITY (FICA)
Any employee who has gross income of $50 or more in each quarter is
subject to this tax, regardless of whether the employee is already collecting
Social Security payments. At present, the amount deducted from gross wages
is 5.2% on the first $9,000 of wages paid each year to each employee. The
same amount is paid by the employer.
OTHER TAXES
Temple Associations and other Masonic groups are subject to various
returns and taxes. Some Lodges may be responsible for funds held in a fiduciary capacity. Reporting and tax requirements should he reviewed periodically.

w. STANLEY DAVIS

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
PUBLICATION BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The publicatio~ and distribution of the California Freemason is administered by a board comprised of the Grand !\faster, the Grand Secretary, such
advisors as may be desirable, and an Editor-in-Chief, who is appointed by the
Grand Master.
Next year will be the Twentieth Year of publication. The magazine has
maintained its position as one of the outstanding publications issued by Grand
Jurisdictions. It has been distributed at regular quarterly intervals to all
members of California Lodges.
Each issue is diversified to s11pply its readers with Masonic information
and inspiration. Some space is allotted to Grand Lodge so that Masons may
know about state-wide activities. Long, scholarly articles, excellent in themselves, are avoided because they lack appeal for the majority of our quarter
of a million readers.
There has been a gratifying number of paid subscriptions from sojourners
and from interested persons in other stales and countries.
The present per capita of 35 cents has not been sufficient to cover the cost
of preparing, printing, distributing and mailing. There is the possibility of
higher postal rates. However, we ask the continuation of the present rate for

another year. We will exercise every possible economy consistent with maintaining the quality of the magazine. An effort will also be made to increase the

report.

REPORT OF COMMI TIEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Warshipfu l Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The twenty-five members and two consultants comprising your committee
this past Masonic year wish to express their gratitude to the Grand Lodge
official line and, in particular, the Grand Secretary and Assistant Grand
Secretary, for their counsel and assistance during the past twelve months.
Our two consultants, Brothers Oscar E. Anderson and Richard R. F. Lehmann, are also due a special " thanks" for their endeavors.
Although "Public Schools Week" continues to be an important function
of the committee and a summary of our activities appears later in this report,
much time and effort has been devoted to other problems and challenges involving public schools. The amount of anti-public school legislation submitted
to the state legislature is increasing all the time. Your committee is fortunate
in having two members who serve as a sub-committee acting as watch-dogs
over the voluminous amount of bills submitted, advising the committee of all
legislation involving pu~lic schools.
Under the direction of the committee, many concerned citizens have responded to the call by contacting members of both H ouses of the State Legislature expressing their individual views concerning anti-public school legislation. It is most difficult to estimate the amount of mail that has been sent on
our behalf, but reliable sources report the number to be in excess of 25,000.
This has materially helped in defeating to date all, but one minor bill, that
have been presented.
The next legislati\'e threat to public schooh1 in California is Assembly Bill
No. 1724. This bill passed the State Assembly in June and is set for a hearing
before the Senate Finance Committee when it reconvenes in November. This
bill would allow to parents earning up to $15,000 annual adjusted gross
income, a tax credit of up to $ 125 per child attending a non-public school.
This $125 would be deducted directly from the parents' income tax and would
funnel into the non-public schools. The cost to the taxpayers of California
will start at fifty million dollars the first year increasing each year thereafter.
Your committee urges that you contact your State Senator expressing your
views on this bill.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Your Committee on Lodge Financing respectfully submits this report
describing the activities of the Committee during the past year. As will become
apparent from the report, this Committee again has been busy replying to tbe
numerous applications as submitted by various Lodges and temple associations

188

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

within the jurisdiction. Activity continues within the jurisdiction in respect
to the acquisition of property, as well as the construction of new temples and
the improvement of existing temples.

like to express appreciation for the support and encouragement given by our
Grand Master, Lester S. McElwain and his officers. We also acknowledge the
c~ntinuing coopera~ion and assistance of the Grand Secretary, Edward H.
Siems and the Assistant Grand Secretary, Verne Hendrix as well as their
most efficient and accommodating staff. With such assistanc~, cooperation and
encouragement from everyone concerned, the privilege of serving Grand
Lodge is most rewarding.

Your Committee has also received and reviewed Financial Reports as submitted by the majority of the temple associations within the jurisdiction in
accordance with Section 200 of the California Masonic Code. These reports
indicate a continued awareness on the part of the officers and directors of the
various Masonic Temple Associations of a need for an improvement in the
financial affairs of said corporations. Every effort is made by your Committee
to assist the Temple Associations in putting their affairs on a sound financial
basis and counseling is provided on matters of concern to the officers of these
Temple Associations and Lodges such as matters of taxation and the establishment of reserves for depreciation, which reserves are so important in the future
repair, rehabilitation or replacement of Temple property.
During the past year the Committee has received and acted upon some
34 applications relating to the jurisdiction of the Committee. Specifically, the
Committee has considered some 15 applications for the transfer of funds from
Lodges to Temple Associations for use in matters relating to Temple construction, operation and maintenance ; some S requests for the purchase of
property for future Temple sites; 3 requests to initiate construction of new
Masonic Temples; 7 requests for capital improvements, expansion, renovation
and repairs; 1 request to borrow money; 1 request to form a Masonic Temple
Association for the purpose of conducting the financial affairs of the Lodge;
1 request for authority to enter into satisfactory leasing agreements; and
1 request covering other miscellaneous matters . .These requests, together with
other miscellaneous inquiries required action of the Committee in more than
SS situations.
In addition to the above applications which have already been acted upon,
there are pending before the Committee on Lodge Financing for action before
the said Committee at this Annual Communication an additional 19 matters.
These involve additional applications for the transfer of sums, application for
the purchase of property, applications for capital improvements or repairs,
applications to borrow money, applications to lease property and other miscellaneous matters.
Numerous visitations were made to Lodges at their request to advise and
counsel with the brethren concerning particular problems respecting Lodge
and T emple Association matters. Your Committee is always most happy
to be of assistance in this way, and it is anticipated that in the ensuing year
even more such visitations will be made.
Your Committee and particularly, your Chairman, would like to take this
occasion to express appreciation to Brother I van T. Crase who, during the
early part of the year, acted as Chairman of the Committee in order to permit
your present Chairman to spend additional time in completing his assignment
as a member of the Special Committee on Code Revision. We would also

Yearly activities of the Committee including actions at this Annual Com~
munication are contained in detail on the following pages of this report and
will be included in the published proceedings.
A review of this report will, we are sure, convince all concerned that masonry continues to grow in California and will continue to make its mark in
the community so long as its members have the determination and desire to
build and maintain Temples illustrative of the strength of the fraternity.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Mosl Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:

The members of this Committee wish to express their appreciation to the
Grand Lodge and to our Grand l\Iaster, Lester S. McElwain for the privilege
of serving. The cooperation of the Grand Master and the Grand Lodge has
made this year a pleasure.
We have been continuing our work of cataloguing and photographing
the Masonic buildings of this Jurisdiction. We have added several new photographs and histories to our growing library in our slide lecture series, "Some
Came by Land and Some Came by Sea." These slides with their commentary
have again, this year, been in use by the Lodges and by Masonic Districts
throughout the State to show the history of Masonry in California. Any
Masonic group can have them for a showing by contacting the Chairman of
this Committee. He will see that they are sent or brought to your meeting.
I am sure that all who see it will enjoy this fine history of the Fraternity in
California. The section on the Lodges of the Mother Lode is especially well
done.
Through this work we have been adding to the library of the Committee
on the over-all history of the Lodges and the Grand Lodge in California.
This information will be on file and ready for use in an up date of the written
history of this Grand Jurisdiction.

In tracing the history of the various Lodges there are times when the
personality of one member seems to dominate the scene. In our study of the
records the personality of one such man seemed to stand out. His name was
Lieutenant George Horatio Derby.
Derby was born in Dedham, Massachusetts in 1823. He chose the army
as a career and graduated from West Point in 1846. He fought under General
Winfield Scott in the Mexican War where he made a distinguished mark for
himself. After the War he returned to Washington, D.C., where in 1848 he was
made a Mason in Federal Lodge No. 1. The next year he was elected Junior

196

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Warden of that Lodge. That same year he was transferred to Benicia, California as an army engineer. He affiliated with Benicia Lodge before it joined
the Grand Lodge of California in 185D. His stay there was of short duration
as he was transferred to Sonoma in 1851 where he became one of the
organizers of Temple Lodge No. 14. He was the charter Senior Deacon of
that Lodge.
Shortly after, Lieutenant Derby was transferred to San Diego to take
charge of diverting the waters of the San Diego River into Mission Bay, then
known as False Bay. On March 7th, 1853 he visited San Diego Lodge, then
under dispensation. He was asked to preside as Master for the evening. He
enjoyed the privilege so much that on April 23rd he affiliated with the Lodge.
He was then asked to represent the Lodge at the next annual Grand Lodge
Communication to try to obtain the Charter for the Lodge. He did go to
San Francisco and he did straighten out the differences between Grand Lodge
and San Diego Lodge and the Charter was issued.
Derby was a forceful character and made a profound impression in Grand
Lodge. When the Grand Officers were named that year Derby became Grand
Sword Bearer. Also during the first year of operation of San Diego Lodge
under its new charter he acted as both Master and Secretary.
Derby was really a man of distinction and wit. In fact, he was sent to
California by Secretary of War, Jefferson Davis, for allowing his wit to get
the better of his discretion. It seems he was very proficient at sketching, which
he did for the War Department. Some of these sketches, which were interjected with the Lieutenant's wit, brought the displeasure of Mr. Davis and
Derby quickly found himself in California.
For a while Derby lived in San Francisco and wrote for a paper called
the "Alta California" under the pen names of "Squibob" and "John Phoenix."
He also wrote under these names for the San Diego Herald. The articles he
wrote were noted for their humor and wit. They were copied in newspapers
all over the world. They were published in book form under the name of
Squibob Papers and Phoenixiana. They gained Lt. Derby the reputation of
being one of the foremost humorists of his day. Such men as Mark Twain,
Artemus Ward and Bill Nye called him the first American humorist.
He was an inveterate practical joker and kept his friends and acquaintances
on edge waiting for his next move. For instance, when John Judson Ames,
Publisher of the San Diego Herald, and member of San Diego Lodge No. 3S,
went to San Francisco to get funds from the Democratic party headquarters
there, he left Derby in charge of the paper. As soon as Ames was out of sight,
Derby changed the newspaper's politics from Democratic to Whig. John
Bigler had been nominated for Governor on the Democratic ticket, and Derby
ran a big headline in which his name was spelled, "Wiggler,'' instead of
Bigler. This paper reached San Francisco ahead of Ames and naturally spoiled
his chances of getting any campaign funds.
When Ames returned to San Diego an alleged fight between the two was
described in the paper as being along the lines of the fight between David

and Goliath (Derby was at least a foot shorter than Ames). In his article in
the Herald, Derby stated that by the careful insertion of his nose between
~mes' t.eeth he held the latter at bay while he succeeded in saving the only
1mpress1on of that week's paper - on the back of the white shirt be wore. This
story of combat was, of course, purely mythical, as the two were always the
best of friends until Derby's untimely death in 1861.

197

We write of this man here to give recognition to this outstanding Mason.
Besides belonging to at least three Lodges in California he was instrumental
in organizing several others. All his adult life he was an ardent supporter of
the Craft. He was a world known figure whose humor will live in the annals
of history.
This year your Committee has again been contacted by Benicia Lodge
No. 5 in regards to their historic temple building. Resolution No. 21 this year
~sks f?r a !oan to h~lp them preserve this, the first Masonic Lodge building
m Cali forma. We believe some means should be found to preserve this historic
si te. We can only reiterate the stand we took at the last Communication of
Grand Lodge. We suggest that the recommendation of the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes in response to Resolution No. S at the 1971
Communication is the proper course to be followed.

Homer Glick, who has added many new, or should say old, artifacts to our
exhibits. We have added a new three-tiered showcase, many fans for added
comfort additional first aid equipment , and a flag of the United States of
Americ; which had been flown over the White House and which was presented
to us by Robert Finch.
During the past year over 1200 visitors from thirty stat~ of ~e Union
and eleven foreign countries have been conducted through our historic Temple.
The Brethren of the many Lodges have been inspired within its sacred
walls when holdina various degree meetings in our Temple. It is surprising
to note the numb~r of Job's Daughters Bethels that have used our "old
temple,'' but, even more surprising is the ~umbe: of .Lodge~ that DO N?T
avail themselves of the splendid opportunit y to inspire their brethren with
a deeper reverence for Masonry.

RALPH W. WINTERS, Grand Orator

Most Worshipfu l Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters,
Distinguished Guests, and my Brethren:
Nearly one year ago, I approached this appointme nt with a feeling of
anticipatio n, humble gratitude and high honor. I looked forward to a year of
pleasant association with many dedicated Masons from whom I knew I
could learn still more of the truths of our Fraternity , to meeting and renewing
friendships with the many Masons throughout our jurisdiction. Our Grand
Master, Most Worshipful Lester S. McElwain, has been a great leader to all
Masons; he has shown me the way when the way was less than clear; he has
offered wisdom when a word of encouragement was needed and above all, he,
himself, has been a Mason from whom all could see the Light of Masonry. I
am deeply grateful for the short year that has just passed. It will live long
in my memory as a year of challenge and accomplishment.
When the possibility of being your Grand Orator became a reality, my
uppermost thoughts were how best could I tell the story of a subject that I
have long felt was so important and yet was one that most of us take for
granted. It is the story of Patriotism , of Freedom, of Truth, of Dedication , of
Love of Country, and above all a story of the fulfillment of contributio n as an
American Citizen. The story has unfolded over the year in many small
ways, . . the story of the Liberty Bell, of the Tomb of The Unknown Soldier,
of our Dedicated Forefather s and the story we must tell our sons and daughters, of the country we are leaving to them. Today, I would like to capsulize
some of these thoughts that we may share together, truths that may have been
covered by our own efforts in other directions.
God gave each of us a life to live; and each life has purpose; and each
purpose is a contributio n to our society. Thus we must make our contributio n,
large or small, that will fulfill the purpose of our existence. Each life is a
very important, God-planned and integrated part of society and by making
that life contributor y, wholesome and unselfish, we will begin to see a light
where our contributio n has purpose and meaning. If each one of us did our
best in everything we attempted, our best as we alone honestly see it, the
responsibilities to maintain a healthy and progressive society would be automatically taken care of and Dependability, Truthfulne ss, Integrity and Sincerity will again be an integral part of the contributio n each life gives for the
whole.
The foundation of every honest act is Truth. " Truth is a divine attribute
and the foundation of every virtue." Every Mason has heard those words and
is taught throughout his masonic education to search for and believe in this,
the most important of the fundament al virtues. No act can have factual meaning without Truth. Falseness may be likened to the house built on sand where
truth is built on the solid and unmoving foundation of rock. The one consuming passion of all time has been to know the truth. Truth is the prevailing

200

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mystery which lures us into continuing adventure. Truth is timeless. It exists
from the moment consciousness is born. One of the things I remember my
father telling me as a child was that you always had to remember a lie but
you did not have to remember a Truth. It would not change.
We, as masons, throughout our teachings are given pathways . to follow,
where we may find the virtues to live our lives according to the will of God.
We believe in these virtues, virtues that have meaning, not only for the
fulfillment of our own individual contributions but give us the basis for fulfilling the purpose of our lives in the society. of ~merica. '~hat ar~ some of
these virtues that we take for granted? .. Smcenty, Integnty, Faithfulness,
Dependability, Honesty and Plain-dealing. These are important ?ut they
could not be attained without Truth. Jn addition, we must recognize other
virtues that are equally necessary: Morality, Patriotism, Responsibility and
many, many more.
Jn the so-called "good-old-days", and maybe not too long ago at that,
many of us can remember the time when a man's word was as good as his
bond. In those days men were ridiculed, if not outcast, for backing away
from their promised ~ord. Today, however, the neglect of moral principles and
the unwillingness to accept individual responsibilities in society, bas decayed
the virtue of integrity to where it is even considered by some to be a weakness
of character to stand up for the "old-fashioned" ideas of Honesty, Truth and
Consideration for Others.
Are we willing to analyze our own lives and judge the merits of integrity
we have lived by? Can we, each of us, say that we live a life of Integrity?
Can we really? When each of us fails to live up to our word or turn away
from our responsibilities, no matter what they may be, my brethren, no matter
what they may be, we lose our Integrity. We believe in Truth and Sincerity.
Many of our fundamental teachings would have been lost centuries ago had
not these virtues been founded on, and built around, Truth, Honesty, and
Sincerity. All of these are an integral and inseparable part of Integrity.
We cannot change Truth any more than we can change nature. Yet we turn
away from real, honest Truth and accept half-truths for the sake of avoiding
discomfort hardship or hurt. Is it not true that we have been weakened by
our own c~nsuming anxiety to be comfortable ... more than being right? We
are growing weaker by reason of the deterioration of our importances. Yes,
the Things we think are important. Charles Malik of Lebanon, once said:
"The trouble is, that you in America, who have a great spiritual message ~o
give the world, are simply not giving it. You give the impression that 1.n
America only material Things count. You forget that human greed is
insatiable."
And that's exactly where we're weak. Yes, that's where we're weak!
What can we do? Well . . . we can begin as upright citizens to straighten
out our own lives and live disciplined lives when it comes to material Things.
Look closely at Morality and to high moral values. It is one of the important

virtues we are given in our Masonic lessons. Morality is a force ... Morality
is a force. It is the magnetic attraction of the heart toward Truth and Virtue.
Let us look at the bible. There are many examples of Integrity which can
be lessons for making order out of our lives ... if we but put them to practice.
One outstanding example is that wherein Job, in his last words, protested
his innocence to the accusations of his three friends when he said: "My lips
shall not speak wickedness nor my tongue utter deceit. God forbid that I
should justify you; till I die I will not remove my Integrity from me."
The greatness of our country was inspired and developed by men whose
Integrity was devout. Brethren, the most important thing to them was their
Integrity. We can look to these founders and learn from their example. Had
not Thomas Jefferson been steadfast in his belief in Truth and Right, we may
never have had the Declaration of Independence.
We can look to and follow the example of our great civic and Masonic
leaders, for whom we hold such high respect, for they are surely the bulwark
against our growing weaknesses.
Why should we even be concerned about our own individual Integrity ?
Wouldn't the world go on just the same? The answer, of course, is a loud
and resounding ... NO! The contribution each of us makes is meant to be a
very important and integrated part of the progress our society is making. By
making that contribution wholesome and upright, each of us will have done
our part in making society pro-gressive and not re·gressive.
Men honor all who stand up for Truth and Right .. men who never shrink
from that stand. The world builds monuments to its patriots but the unjust
man fades away into obscurity.
It then becomes a matter for each of us to determine the degree of effort
we are willing to put into living a life of Integrity.
The society we live in is a society called the United States of America.
Not a very old society by world standards, but our society nonetheless. The
pride and patriotism you have for this country is a matter for your own
conscience, but the manner in which you exercise the liberties and freedoms
given to you by this society is a matter for everyone you come in touch with
throughout your entire life. That is what society is. Man was never intenrled
to live alone. From the earliest records we know that man on this planet has
banded together for many reasons: surviYal, companionship, the need for
understanding and all the comforts that are part of society living. In a society,
therefore, there are many responsibilities that are shared by all according to
their abilities and talents.
Each one of us must face the bold and bare-faced fact that "someone
else" cannot carry our load for us. Especially when it comes to preserving
the heritage of Freedom. Since nearly 200 years ago, when the freedom we
know today was born, men have literally given up their lives, fortunes and
homes so that we, today, can live in a security that our country provides us.
But we must accept our responsibility and do our very best to see it carried
out successfully. Josiah Stamp said: "It is easy to dodge our responsibilities,

201

203

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

but we cannot dodge the consequences of dodging our responsibilities." Easy
enough said and the meaning is clear - if we don't accept our responsibilities,
the payment for the results will be very dear indeed. Nor can we satisfy the
duty by explaining to ourselves that our little bit won't help. It takes a great
number of individual efforts to make an effective army. If each of the
soldiers felt that his little bit wouldn't help, that he could dodge his responsibilities and let his buddy carry his load, look where we'd have been in
any of the conflicts this country has endured ... to preserve that precious
gift we each are given . .. Freedom.
What gives us this heritage? First of all it was the Declaration of Colonial
Rights, drawn up by the First Continental Congress in 1774. The Second
Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776, and
also the Articles of Confederation in 1778. This same Congress was destined
to endure until finally superseded in 17 89 by the government organized under
our present Constitution, that great document having been adopted on
Sept. 17, 1787.
It took great men, dedicated to the purpose of Freedom and Liberty, to
write, discuss, amend and finally adopt each of these four great documents.
Yes, there were many Masons among them, some about whom you may have
heard: Benjamin Franklin, John Hancock, Joseph Hewes, William Hooper,
Robert Treat Paine, Richard Stockton, George Walton, William Whipple and
of course, George Washington. And there were many, many more too numerous to mention.
What kind of men were these people who had such a common purpose of
freedom; who carved a nation of United States from a wilderness? They were
influential men. They were men of distinction - lawyers, jurists, merchants,
wealthy plantation owners, etc. They were men of means and well educated,
but they prepared and signed their names to these great documents, particularly the Declaration of Independence, knowing full well that the penalty
would be death if they were captured by the British. The stories of these brave
men are stories of sacrifice, hurt, anguish and, in some cases, horrible death.
Yet they knew this could be their fate but accepted their responsibility with
Sincerity and Integrity. These were men that ga ve their worldly possessions,
willingly, for the belief that this Country must be free from the oppression of
dictatorship, that the people of the Thirteen Colonies, the people themselves,
be given the right to determine their own destiny.
That is exactly what the Declaration of Independence did for us and the
culmination of that supreme effort was the birth of our Constitution, which
spells out the rights and liberties each of us now enjoys.
Today these two pieces of our history are the very foundation of the
mightiest republic in the world. It took brave men, who had full confidence
in their convictions, and Integrity in their every action, to give us the
heritage of Freedom. Let us not overlook, also, the countless thousands of
equally brave men who have stood up to a would-be conqueror and fought for,
yes, even gave their lives for the preservation of the Freedom they believed in.

Vol~mes have. been written on the reason for the fall of the Roman Empire,
but 1t can easily be summed up in just three words ... lack of Patriotism!
Can each of us look at our own lives and believe that we could stand
alongside t?ese _great ~m.erica~s and be counted as they were? Can we say
that. we believe m Patnot1si:i with such a dedication that we would be willing
to give our worldly possessions, fortunes or even our lives to preserve F reedom ? '."1re we willing to sacrifice our comforts fo r this heritage? Can we truly
P~~clarm to the world that we, each of us, are willing to accept the responsi.
b1hty to practice what we belie\·e?

REPORT OF BOARD OF LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Acting as your Board of Library Commissioners under appointment of
the :Most Worshipful Lester S. McElwain, Grand Master, it has been our
pleasure and opportunity to serve the Grand Lodge and brethren within the
jurisdiction in accordance with the Grand Master's wishes and the policies
of the Grand Lodge in the administratio n of our Library and Museum.
During this past Masonic year we have been pleased to receive 164 books
donated to our Library from Masons, their families, or other concordant or
related organizations. Forty-eight items of Masonic and historic significance
were also donated to our Library from similar sources during the past year.
Each of these items is carefully indexed, filed, and then takes its place
among an ever-growing number of volumes, and an ever-increasing collection
of historic and Masonic memorabilia. Our sincere thanks to those who continue to remember our Library and Museum in this manner.
During this year we have purchased thirty-two new volumes of Masonic
significance as well as renewed or continued our subscription to periodicals
and other publications of special import to our area of concern. Also we
acquired two additional sets of book shelves which were installed in everdecreasing available wall space to accommodate our book stacks.
Our lending library continues to be a source of activity to the Commission
and our volunteer staff, for which we are very grateful. This year over 200
volumes were loaned for reading and research to members of this jurisdiction.
'Ve have recently completed an up-<late of our reading list which indicates a
sample of various books in a wide variety of subjects currently available in
our Library. We urge each Lodge to acquire a supply of these reading lists to
be kept available f9r the use of their members.
During this year with the cooperation of the Grand Master and the Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility, we were able to insert two
articles in the "Grand Master's Monthly Letter." We trust that these brief
bits of information about our Library and Museum found their way into the
Bulletin or Trestleboard of a goodly number of Lodges.
As the Report of the Trustees of the Masonic Memorial Temple indicates,
plans for the expansion of our present structure include therein very adequate
and suitable space for the expansion and further opportunity for growth of
our present wholly inadequate physical setting of the Library and Museum
as it is now located. It is not the purpose of this Board to unduly involve
itself in matters that pertain to the responsibilities of the Temple Trustees, or
of the Grand Lodge as a body, however, it is surely evident, and appropriate
for us to urge a careful consideration of the proposals set forth by the Temple
Trustees as they relate to the Library and Museum and its future growth and
usefulness to this Grand Lodge and the Craft in general. Our ability to serve
our brethren and contribute to the growth of our fraternity is in the final
analysis dependent upon our having sufficient space, readily available to our
clientele, Masonic and non-Masonic .

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our request for funds in the amount of $1, 750.00 for the ensuing year is
the same as this year. This request has been forwarded to the Finance Committee in accordance with their request and should be considered a part of
this report.
In conclusion, we desire to express our sincere thanks to our Grand Master
for affording each of us this opportunity to serve our brethren in this capacity,
as well as thank him personally for his interest and support of our endeavors.
Our Grand Secretary also has the title and responsibility of Grand Librarian ;
in both capacities be has lent us the strong right hand of encouragement and
abiding interest in our work. Our volunteer staff continues to be the mainstay
of our effectiveness. Assistant Librarian William H. Scott and his group of
loyal assistants deserve and have our gratitude for a job well done, and thanks
for another milestone of Masonic service passed.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:

I
An eloquent and fitting tribute has been paid to our late Past Grand
l\faster Phil N. Myers, and I would like to add to his memory by e:qxessing
my grief at his passing. Phil appointed me to this Committee in 1958 and he
served as its chairman from 1959 throu gh the 1965 Communication. Grand
Lodge can well be proud of its representative to our sister Grand Lodges in
the United States and abroad. We remember his unruffled urbanity, his imposing intellectual and physical stature and his dedication to the highest ideals
of our great Fraternity.

II
In last year's report, mention was made of the severing of relations be-

tween the United Grand Lodge of England and the Grand Lodge Alpina of
Switzerland. I am happy to be able to report that the prompt and uncompromising action by the latter to insist that its subordinate lodges adhere to
basic Masonic principles have had salutary effect, and harmony now prevails
between these important Masonic powers.

207

III
Grande L oja do Maranhao:
This Grand Lodge was constituted the 27th day of March 1960 by a
charter issued by The Grand Lodge of Para. It is the only legitimate and
regular masonic power for the State of Maranhao, which, geographically,
faces the Atlantic Ocean and is bounded on the west by Para, on the south by
Goias and on the cast by Piaui. We recognize all three of these Grand Lodges.
The Declaration of Principles submitted by the Grand Lodge of Maranhao
completely satisfies our Tests for Recognition and could well serve as a model
for such a document.
Carlos Jorge Francis is the Grand Master. The Grand Secretary for Foreign Relations is Dr. Jose Anselmo dos Reis Freitas, and the Grand Secretary
is Nonato Francisco Barbosa. The address of the Grand Lodge is Rua Henrique Figueredo N. 311, Caixa Postal 4, Codo, Maranhao.
I therefore move that the Grand Loja do Maranhao, whose seat is in the
City of Codo, be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.

IV
Gran L ogia Occidental 111 exicana:
This Grand Lodge has its seat in the City of Guadalajara, Jalisco, l'vlexico,
and is the Grand Lodge for that state as well as Nayarit, Colima and
:Michoacan. It was constituted the 5th day of February 1912 under a charter
issued by the Gran Logia Valle de Mexico and the Grand Logia Unida
Mexicana de Vera Cruz, both recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.
There are at present nineteen subordinate lodges under its jurisdiction and
it is a member of the Confedracion Masonica Interamericana. It is recognized
by its sister Grand Lodges in Mexico and at least ten Grand Lodges in the
United States, including Massachusetts, Michigan and Texas.
Jose G. Zuno is Grand l'lfaster and Joaquin Yanez Albarran is Grand
Secretary. The temple is at Lopez Cotilla No. 111, apdo. Num. 1-9, Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico.
Based on the foregoing, I move that the Gran Logia Occidental Mexicana
be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.

v

The other matters before the Committee concern requests for recognition
by the Grand Lodge of Haiti and La Peninsular Oriental in Yucatan. Adequate information is lacking, so it is our recommendation that further consideration be given to these requests, and our surveillance of these Grand
Lodges continue.
I therefore move the adoption of this report, suggestions and recommendations.
Respectfully submitted,
\VILLIAM RHODES HERVEY, JR., Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDE NCE

A number of Grand Lodges not only support DeMolay, Job's Daughters
and Rainbow for girls, but carry out extensive vacation-time programs for
youth, such as sponsoring baseball, softball, golf and other types of activities.
The regulations on Masonic funerals in California, a few years ago, was
changed to permit the services for entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts.
The Grand Master of the District of Columbia sets aside Sunday afternoon to visit Brothers who are ill.
Mississippi's Grand Master, on being informed that New Jersey had
appointed a Negro as Grand Chaplain and that New York had sanctioned the
transfer of Negro memberships and had initiated Negroes, issued an edict
breaking fraternal relations between 'Mississippi and the two j urisdictions.
A Missouri petitioner of the Moslem faith requested the Lodge to replace
the Holy Bible with the Koran during his initiation. The Grand Master ruled
that the Koran could be placed alongside the Holy Bible, but that it could
not be placed upon it nor replace it.
The Grand Master of New Hampshire corresponds with each New Hampshire Mason serving in Viet Nam.
The chairman of New York's Committee on Masonic jurisdiction is undoubtedly very popular with the Brethren. Before starting his report, he said
" You are itching, so am I , the candles at the altar are abou t to go out, and
we haven 't any more so we will make this very, very brief. "
The Grand Lodge of North Carolina approved a resolution providing for
the issuance of a Grand Lodge publication, "The North Carolina Mason."
North Dakota followed the lead of the Grand Lodge of South Dakota by
eliminating the office of Grand Treasurer and combining it into one office,
Grand Secretary--:C:reasurer.
The Grand Master of Ohio ordered a sign removed from the T yler's room
of a Lodge which stated, "The ~laster Mason Degree without the Royal
Arch Degree is a story half told and a song half sung."
For the past two years, South Dakota's Grand Secretary has written
letters to those suspended for non-payment of dues when names and addresses
were furnished by Lodge Secretaries. H e reported writing 214 such letters
the past year and that of that number, 187 sent their dues to him.
Vermont's Grand Historian reported finding in the minute book of an old
Lodge dated August 1821, the following: " Voted that after the present dues
of this Lodge are paid, the sum of $1 S.00 to be taken from the Lodge fu nds
to purchase a cow."
In his address, Georgia's Grand Master itemized a three-point program for
Masonic living - "a faith to serve by," "a self fit to live with" and "a
purpose fit to live for."
The famous Irish wit was displayed by the Grand :Master of Ireland on

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your committee on Correspondence respectfully submits the following
report for Lhe fiscal year 19 72.
Proceedings of the different Masonic Jurisdictions of the United States
and who have forwarded their proceedings for the current fiscal year 1972
bave been reviewed. A brief summary of our review appears in the 1972
California Freemason. Due to the limited space available in California Freemason, many interesting items of interest to California Masons have been
eliminated from the individual reviews.
New York has Lhe largest membership, and Utah, the smallest.
Problems in other jurisdictions are similar to those in California , such as
lodge attendance, suspensions, population shifts, and reducing the resident
memberships of some country lodges.
Several Grand Masters stressed the answer to the shifting of population
was a concentrated drive for the new lodges in the new outlying metropolitan
centers.
The liquor problem continues to bob up in a number of jurisdictions, but
wherever it did, there was no deviation from the accepted rule that liquor and
the Masonic Lodge does not mix.
A new controversial subject appeared in several jurisdictions with mixed
emotions, that of Lhe apparent effort of the Roman Catholic Church and the
Knights of Columbus to better their relationship with the Masonic Fraternity.
Generally speaking, where a Catholic pass ·was marle at the Masonic Fraternity, it was accepted for its apparent face value and the Grand Masters
cooperated. One southern jurisdiction indicated it wanted no part of a relationship with the Roman Catholic Church, which the Philippines welcome
providing the church refrained from attempting "to gain control of the public
educational system of the land."
Sentiment for statewide concurrent jurisdictions seems to be gaining in
favor. Wisconsin, for instance, tried it for a year and voted to try it for
another year. Several jurisdictions brought up the matter for general discussion.
Masonic education and public information activities have been greatly
expanded. Grand Lodge publications are necessary, and in a number of them
the publications are mailed to all members. Committees to promote the
disposing of Masonic news to newspapers, rarlio and television have been
established in a number of jurisdictions.
Participation of Masons in the promotion of the public schools is steadily
increasing. A number of jurisdictions made awards for scholarships and
promote local Lodge public schools week activities as well as urging Masons
to get acquainted with public school teachers, visit schools, and become active
in other ways to show that Masonry is interested in youth and youth organizations.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
INFORMATION AND RESPONSIBILITY
To the Most Worshipful Gran.d Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Following is the combined report of the Committee on Masonic I nformation and Responsibility, and its Subcommittees.
Grand Master's Bulletin: Chairman John R. Nocas. This Bulletin, in new
format has been mailed to each Master and each Senior Warden via each
Secretary throughout the Jurisdiction. The material contained therein is a
monthly message from the Grand Master, material compiled for the use of
the editors of the Lodge Trestleboards, longer material for use of the Masters
for the edification of their Lodge members, and a monthly calendar of Grand
Lodge events and activities to make them accessible to the constituent
Lodges.
Inter-Grand Lodge Research: Chairman John L. Cooper III. This operation is a continuing correspondence with other 'Cnited States Grand Lodges.
Through this work, we share California experiences and developed material
with them and are recipients of the same from them. As such material comes
to our hands, it is either shared with interested Grand Lodge Committees or
transmitted to the Grand Lodge Library for reference. Most of these contacts
are with the Grand Secretaries or designated Education Committee Chairmen.
All are cleared through the Grand Secretary's office. We currently are in
communication with 44 jurisdictions.
Masonic Widows: Chairman Herbert W. Cahn. The Lodge acceptance of
the program has more than tripled this year. The participation now enrolls
over 100 Lodges. A considerable number of non-committee members has
joined this activity to maintain the contact required by the interested Masters.
It has also been necessary for budget reasons to make a partial North-South
division of the jurisdiction. Emile R. Laversin, P.M. ( 1) is supervising in
Northern California and Albert Brotherton, P .M. (242) in the South.
Information kits have been prepared and sent to all inquiring Masters.
The purpose of this program is to assist Lodges in broadening their own
programs of Masonic responsibility by sharing other Lodge's successful ideas.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITIEE ON CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Cemeteries submits the following report of their
activities for the Masonic Year 1971-1972.
Brother John R. Wise of East Belt Lodge No. 391 was appointed Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Cemeteries in October 1971 by the
Most Worshipful Grand Master Lester S. McElwain. Because of serious
illness in his family it was necessary for him to resign in April of this year and
I was again asked to take over the duties for the balance of the term.
Columbia: The Masonic section of the cemetery located in the Columbia
State Park near Sonora is in fair condition except for some broken headstones
caused by vandalism, a problem that seems to be increasing each year. The
Future Farmers of America of Sonora Union High School, again this year,
performed their usual good job of spraying and weecling. A Square and Compass wreath was placed in the cemetery again this year on Memorial Day.
Much favorable comment is received from this gesture.

Michigan Bluff: As reported last year, Grand Lodge has acquired title to
the Michigan Bluff Masonic Cemetery in Placer County. It was hoped that
we would get started clearing the area and making it presentable as a
Masonic Cemetery should be. However, due to circumstances beyond our
control work could not be started. We are again requesting the sum of $250.00
for the next Masonic year with the hope that we can get started this fall or
early spring. This cemetery is in a rather remote area and getting competent
people to do the work is quite difficult.
Peter Lassen Grave: No reply was received from Brother William E.
Bolton of Lassen Lodge No. 149. Therefore, no report can be made of the
condition of the Peter Lassen Grave at this time.
FaUhrook: :Much of last year's report of this committee to Grand Lodge
was devoted to a rather bad situation that has existed for a number of years,
between Fallbrook Lodge No. 317 and the former President and Directors of
the Masonic Cemetery Association of Fallbrook.
Following is the report received from Brother William G. Alford, past
master of Fallbrook Lodge No. 317 and received by me on Friday October 6 1

of this annual meeting was published in the local newspaper for three
weeks previous to the meeting. As far as can be ascertained, this was the
first legal stockholders meeting since 1953. At this meeting was Brother
Jack Levitt, attorney-at-law, who guided them in the proper procedure.

is the sole owner of the Fallbrook Masonic Cemetery. Five new hoard

The old corporation expired on September 13, 197 1. Attorney Levitt
drafted new corporation papers and the period of duration of this
corporation in now perpetual. These papers are registered with the
Secretary of State.
The cemetery is now registered with the California State Cemetery
Board. This was never done before. It is registered as an endowment
care cemetery, and as such they have deposited, in a special fund in.a
local Savings and Loan Association, an adequate amount to be m
compliance with the California State Regulations. An inventory was
taken of each lot sold and one dollar ($1.00) per square foot has been
placed in this endowment fund.
Attorney Jack Levitt has now been appointed a Superior Court Judge
and he has turned this matter over to one of his staff, a Mr. James
Shannon who is an expert in corporation matters. With his help and
guidanc~ a new set of by-laws was drawn up. At the July business
meeting the cemetery board voted to repeal the old by-laws and adopt
the new ones.
The treasurer has adopted a new report system, and at every monthly
meeting he has an up-to-date financial report on all accounts controlled
by the Cemetery Board. This report will of course be furnished to
Grand Lodge at the close of the year, and will also be read to our own
Lodge. This has never been done before.
W ith the assistance of their attorney they have adopted a new form
to be used when lots are purchased. The old forms were not correct
and very ambiguous.
They have had a new stock book printed. To date no shares of stock
have been issued.
They are at the present time re-vamping the water system. The system originally installed was copied along the lines of an ayocado grove
system and caused them to waste too much valuable water. It will be
necessary to spend several hundred dollars, but feel confident that it
will resul t in considerable sa vings and be much more efficient.
At the suggestion of the local mortician and other interested person~,
several beautiful trees and decorative shrubs were planted. The pubhc
response to this has been most gratifying and a nursery friend of the
cemetery has offered more for planting.

pictures about the cemetery. They were most complimentary in their

11. About six ( 6) acres of the cemetery property is not used for that

portion of the property was leased in 1966 to Brother Earl Hedrick and
his son D avid. According to the terms of t he lease they were to care
for the cemetery portion. This was never done and it was necessary
for the Lodge and Cemetery Association to assume the responsibility.
The new board reviewed the lease on the avocado grove and came to
the conclusion something had to be done to protect the Cemetery Board,
and in fact, Fallbrook Lodge. Brother H ed rick and his son appeared
at several of the board meetings. The president of the board informed
the Hedricks that arrangements, as such, could not continue and a new
lease would have to be negotiated. The Hedricks re fused and walked
ou t of the meeting with their attorney.
All of the grove management firms were invited to submit sealed
bids for the care of the grove. Several bids were submitted. After
careful consideration and discussion by the board, a bid was awarded
to a grove management firm that is a neighbor to the grove. This firm
is doing an outstanding job. All funds to be received from the avocado
grove will be put in the Cemetery Association account.
12. Late Friday night, October 6, 19 72, word was received by phone from
Brother Alford that a law suit for breach of contract had been filed by
Earl and David H edrick against Fallbrook Lodge and the Fallbrook
Masonic Cemetery Association. The attorney for the Lodge and the
Association feel they have a very strong position and should have no
trouble winning the suit.

Brethren, a ~reat many of us belong to other Masonic prerequisite bodies,
many of which have philanthropic projects, and we are sure that each of you
are aware of them.
But what do we as Master Masons do ? Oh yes, we all, well many, no some
of us, say we support our youth. Yes, we give lip service, " we support our
you th." How many of you visited a Bethel meeting last month? How many a
DeMolay function this las t summer? Or when did you last visit a Rainbow
Installation? I'll bet if I were to ask for a show of hands, not only would I be
embarrassed, but each of you would have to look to see if your shoes were
shined!
That is not even lip service ! They are our youth! Are you thinking?
Some food for thought. If I may do a little mathematics, I'll show you
what the youth are doing for you. Yes, what the DeMolays, Rainbow Girls
and Job's Daughters are doing for you Master Masons.
I..et's say for this exercise there are 28,000 J ob's Daughters, 12,000 DeMolay, and 10,000 Rainbow Girls for a total of 50,000 members. Now giving
50 members to an average Chapter, Bethel or Assembly comes to 1,000 local
units. These 1,000 units pay as high as $75 plus per month rent and a lucky
few, very few, as little as nothing. For this situation let us say the average rent
is $40.00 per month paid to the various temple associations. Now the multiplication ; $40.00 per month X 12 months X 1,000 you get a fig ure of $480,000
per year. Yes, my brethren, !ji480,000 per year these youth pay to help support
our temples.
Where do they get the money? Dues you say. Not hardly. $40.00 per
month rent and the unit has 50 members. That comes to almost $1 per member
per month just to pay their rent or $12 .00 per member per year dues. How do
they pay for their other ac tivities? Sell donations to the Master Masons.
Brethren, they <lo it! Yet they really do not show hard feelings. These are
our Youth! To a one they are proud to say they meet in a Masonic Temple.
Are you proud to have them there ? Are You?
I t would only take a small increase in your dues to pay for their rent.
Oh, Oh, I see that l\Iaster back there thinking to himself, "many of the members of my Lodge are retired and on a fixed income." "How can I possibly
raise their dues ?" "What does that guy want ?" "Blood?"
Yes, my brethren what do I want? No not blood, just a little support. You
know, the green, folding support.
Speaking of blood. T o the Master of the Lodge that has many retired
members on its rolls: To you Worshipful Sir. These men are beyond the
blood-giving age and the Red Cross will no longer accept their donations. But
on the other hand it is their generation that tends to have the greatest drain
on the blood supply.
No, I do not want blood. But do you know what our Youth want to give?
Do you? Blood that is what! Yes, their blood, they want to donate it to the
Masonic Blood Banks. Their blood to you Master Masons.

The report of the Audit Committee was referred to your Committee on

To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The DeMolay Liaison Board is the eyes and ears of the Grand Master in
relation to DeMolay. It operates only on the executive level through Melvin A.
Pixley, Executive Officer of the Jurisdiction of Southern California, Order of
Del\folay; John L. Wixon, Executive Officer of the Jurisdictio n of Northern
California, Order of DeMolay; Kenneth L. Look, Executive Officer of the
Jurisdictio n of Hawaii, Order of DeMolay; and through the Kansas City
office of The Internation al Supreme Council, Order of DeMolay. It is not
the function of the Liaison Board to deal with the chapters directly. The
Board has reported to the Grand Master what it considered an improper use
of DeMolay funds where a Lodge had appropriat ed DeMolay money to build
a fence around Lodge property. Recommendations were made and accepted
by the Grand :r.faster to return the funds to DeMolay.
Unlike the Charters Committee which exists for the growth and expansion
of Masonry, it is the desire of the DeMolay Liaison Board to die for lack of
things to do. When there are no DeMolay problems to be solved that require
the action of the Grand Master the Board will not be necessary but let me
explain: This Board was established as a result of a problem that arose in the
southern part of the state and which ultimately resulted in a Masonic trial.
Our then Grand Master, Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner, established
the Board and appointed the Senior Grand Warden and Junior Grand Warden
as representatives from Grand Lodge, along with representatives from the
Southern Jurisdiction, the Northern Jurisdiction and Hawaii. Unfortuna tely,
there is still work that.the Board must do and so a request for $500.00 to be
appropriat ed for the continuance of the Board for the ensuing year is hereby
made.
Respectful ly submitted,
RAYMOND A. EBBAGE, Chairman
BURTON MEYER, JR.

REPOR T OF COMM ITTEE ON INSURA NCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
As stated by the Grand l\laster, "the purpose of the Insurance Committee
is to assist the Grand Secretary and to advise the Grand Master in regard to
Grand Lodge insurance matters."
As requested by the Most Worshipful Grand l\faster Lester S. McElwain,
the Special Committee on Insurance has completed a study and evaluation of
the entire insurance program of Grand Lodge an d its entities, and has instituted and maintained a "Loss Record Register" to reflect any losses.
The insurance committee hereby submits its summary of activities:
Committee members, with representatives from the insurance brokerage
firm of Thompki ns and Company , held several meetings at 1111 California
Street, San F rancisco. \Ve met to review and discuss the various insurance
policies applicable to Grand Lodge and its Constitue nt Lodges, Masonic Homes
of California, California Masonic Memorial Temple, and California Masonic
Foundati on.
The meetings resulted in a better understanding of the insurance needs of
the fraternity , and of the adequacy of each policy, particula rly, in regard to
the purpose for which it was issued and the amount of coverage that it
provided.
A report to the Gran<l Master was respectfully submitte d. This report
outlined the various Grand Lodge policies, including related entities. Each
section of the report dealt with a specific policy and outlined the insurance
coverage provided therein. Recommendations and/or suggestions to improve
or clarify the coverage afforded by the policies were also included in the
report.
In addition to the survey, a loss summary record is being maintain ed, as
requested. The information contained in this register will prove to be invaluable in future insuran ce negotiations, as well as to alert Grand Lodge to possible areas where unsafe conditions may exist which may result in loss of
property, or injury to others.
A sincere "thank you" to the Grand Lodge office staff and to all others
who have been so helpful to this committe e during the past year.

REPOR T OF RETIRE MENT PENSIO N PLAN COMM ITTEE
To the M ost Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . .M. of California:
. In our report to Grand Lodge at the October, 1971 Annual Communication, we presented three ( 3) specific amendments to the Retireme nt Income
Pia~ de~igncd to improve benefits for employees of the Masonic Homes of
~aliforma and of the Grand Lodge of California and Component Orcranizations; and an amendme nt changing the name of the Plan from l\Iasonic
~o mes of California - Retirement Income Plan to California Masonic Retirement Plan.
We al_so recomm_ended an amendment to the Trust Indenture clarifying and
transfem ng authority for the making of investments from the Trustee to the
Pension Plan Committee, such actions on the part of the Committe e to be in
accordance with provisions of Sections 245 and 246 of the California Masonic
Code. Section 245 of the Code empowers the Investme nt Committe e of the
Grand Lodge to inves~ a~d re-invest t~e various funds of the Grand Lodge
and compone nt orgamzau ons named m Section 245 and to authorize the
pu rchase and sale of securities held in their portfolios. Section 246 controls the
manner of investments.
The amendmen ts referred to above have been submitted to the Internal
Revenue Service for required approval. The Committee expresses its thanks
to Brother Varnum Paul for his legal assistance in the preparati on of the
amendment to the Trust Indenture .
Your Pension Plan Committee referred the portfolio of investmen ts belong~ng to the P lan to the Grand Lodge Investme nt Committee and to Alliance
Capital Management Corporation in January of this year and a number of
changes haYe been made in the Portfolio - designed to reduce the total
number of securities held and to improve the quality and over-all yield of
investments.
The actuaries for the Plan, Coates and Crawford, have presented their
Ann ual ~e~orts covering the calendar year 1971 and an analysis of the
Reports mdtcates an overall strengthened financial position. As of Decembe r
31, 19 71, Trust Assets totaled $ 1,2 2 5, 979 .00 on a cost basis. The bond portion
of the Fund showed a market value of approximately $50,000.00 less than
cost v~lu:. Ho~e.ver, with no need to sell the bonds prior to their maturity
dates, 1t 1s ant1~1pated that the bonds will ultimatel y be redeemed at par.
Currently, a satisfacto ry yield is being obtained from this particula r segment
of the Fund's assets.

In 1970 net investment income was $17,882.00 and we are pleased to
report that for 1971 the net investment income amounted to $63,795.00.
During the calendar year 19 71, while still under the management of the
Trustee, the Pension Fund exp<!rienced a realized gain of $30,719.00 from
security transactions and for the first six months of 1972 the net realized
gain from security transactions approximated $ 18,000.00.
Last year, the rate of contribution for the employers (Masonic Homes
of California, Grand Lodge and its component organization s) was predicated
in part on an interest assumption of 4 % on a cost basis, an increase of 0%
from the 3 0 % interest assumption used in prior years. On a cost basis the
yield in 1971, including realized net gains from security transactions and
expenses charged to the Fund was 3.61%. On a market basis, again including
realized net gains and expenses, the yield for 1971 was 4.58 %.
It is anticipated that interest/divid end earnings will improve in subsequent
years. Expenses incurred in connection with amendments to the Plan resulted
in somewhat heavier charges for the year under review.
For the Masonic Homes of California, the number of participating members in the Plan increased during 19 71 from 106 to 108. In accordance with
Grand Lodge approval of the In-Depth Study Report which was reported
to Grand Lodge at the 1970 Annu al Communicat ion and adopted by Grand
Lodge at the 1971 Annual Communicat ion, three employees stationed in the
Grand Lodge office, formerly classified as Masonic Homes employees, have
been transferred to the Grand Lodge payroll. There are now 32 employees
retired and receiving benefits from the Pension Plan, an increase of 2 over
last year. The annual covered payroll increased $45,504.00 to $720,923.00 and
the average annual salary increased :$303.00 to $6,675.00. Annual pensions
being paid increased $5,161.00 to $24,461.00.
For the Grand Lodge of California and its components, the number of
participating members in the Plan increased from 15 to 18. There are now
16 employees retired and receiving benefits from the Pension Plan, a decrease
of 1 from last year. The annual covered payroll increased $25,205.00 to
$133,868.00 and the average annual salary increased $ 193.00 to $7,437.00.
Annual pensions being pairl decreased $657.00 to $21,333.00.
To maintain the Plan in sound financial condition, continuing the employee contribution rate of 3%, assuming a 4% return on investments, and
considering the portfolio of investments at cost value as of D ecember 31, 19 71,
our actuaries have calculated an employer's contribution rate this year of
9.17% for the Masonic Homes of California and 10.83% for Grand Lodge
and its component organizations . These rates represent a decrease of .03%
for the Masonic Homes and an increase of . 73 % for the Grand Lodge.
Shortly after the close of the 1971 Annual Communicat ion, our committee
suffered a great loss in the sudden and untimely death of Alfred W. Odle.
Brother Odle was a most valuable member of the committee and was one of
the members representing the Masonic Homes Board. We were fortunate to
secure as new members, also representing the Homes Board, L. Harold Anderson and Ralph H. Head. These Brothers were members of the Special Com-

which was adopted by Grand Lodge in 1955.
