REPORT OF COMMITIEE ON PAY OF MEMBERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Pay of Members submits the following report covering
the I 23rd Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to mileage compensation are the l\laster, or in his absence,
the ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly
Elected Representative and Past Grand Masters, if they attend Grand Lodge
in s uch capacity only. However, when a Master and Warden from the same
Lodge are present at an Annual Communication, and one of said Officers serves
on a Grand Lodge Committee entitled to travel and expense reimbursement, he shall be reimbursed accordingly; the other Officer shall receive
reimbursement und er Section 174, California Masonic Code, as the Officer
representing his Lodge on the floor of Grand Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San
Francisco has been taken from the published records of the California State
Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii to San
Francisco has been taken from the published reports of air lines, in accordance
with Sections 174 and 176, California Masonic Code. No compensation is
allowed to members from San Francisco or the immediate vicinity. Compensation of members from the State of California has been computed on the basis
of ten ( 10) cents per mile, the rate fixed by the Committee on Finance.
Compensation of the members from the State of Hawaii has been figured on
the basis of published first class round-trip air rates of regularly scheduled
major air lines, from Honolulu to San Francisco, plus inter-island air fare to
Honolulu when necessary.
The payroll has been checked with the registration records as submitted
to us by the Committee on Credentials, and the amounts required to meet the
transportation costs for the 1972 Annual Communication are as follows:
80.60

Representatives of Lodges . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 35,994.48

Checks will be ready for distribution at the Registration D esk on Friday
morning immediately following the election of the Junior Grand Warden.
Brethren, if you are the Master or Warden representing your Lodge, or the
duly Elected Representative of your Lodge, the Pay of 'Members Committee
urgently requests you to promptly pick up your check.
Arrangements have been made so that those who desire to cash their checks
may do so at the United California Bank, Fairmont Hotel. Your Grand Lodge
Credentials will serve as suitable identification.
We wish to express our sincere appreciation to members of the Grand
Lodge Office Staff for cooperation shown throughout the year in assembling,
preparing and computing the detail necessary for the functioning of this
Committee.

The California Masonic Memorial Temple with its great Auditorium is a
landmark of San Francisco. Its beauty and structure are symbolic of the
functions it serves-those of Masonry, and the cultural, intellectual and entertainment interests of San Francisco and the Bay Area. The Temple attracts
visitors from all parts of the world; this past year guests from thirty-fi ve
countries viewed our Temple and signed the register.
PUBLIC RELATIONS, CIVIC AFFAIRS AND OCCUPANCY
Our Manager continues to maintain diversified contacts with theatrical,
convention, business and ethnic groups. His association with these groups has
proved to be most rewarding.

many contracts which carry into 1973 and beyond. These include, for example,
high school and college graduations and State bar and accounting exam-

agreement which will protect the Temple not only as to its future expansion
but also from an aesthetic standpoint.

opinion of both Committees and of the Board of Trustees of the Temple that
the Grand Lodge should not proceed with this plan at the present time. While
the project is estimated to be ultimately self-liquidating, the initial financial
contribution and obligation on the part of the Grand Lodge of California
would be very substantial and would seriously limit the borrowing capacity
of the Grand Lodge unless a number of very large contributions were made to
help finance the program, or unless a comparatively heavy addition to the
per capita tax was effected.
While it is recognized that moneys have been expended for the procurement of schematic drawings, a model of the Memorial Temple with the
proposed addition, and for a very competently prepared feasibility study, it
is the belief of the Board and the Committees that th.is expenditure has been
both wise and timely. A feasibility study is just that - a study to produce
facts and projections from which a judgment as to the feasibility or nonfeasibility of a project can be made. Thus the recommendation to not proceed
at this time is based on a sound and thorough study. The presently proposed
plan, as portrayed in the schematic drawings and the accompanying model,
does not need to be and should not be cast aside. It represents one answer, an
ideal answer in fact, to the question of what to do about adequate Museum
and Library space at the Memorial Temple and the need for expanded exhibit
and garage space at the T emple. Obviously there can be other plans to achieve
part or all of the desired additions.
While it may be argued, because it is true, that construction costs continue to rise at an alarming rate and thus delay in starting to build is an added
cost, it is more important to be certain of the right course of action. An error
of judgment occasioned by not having had the opportunity to secure all of the
facts and study all of the possibilities could easily be more costly than an
increased increment in construction costs.
The Trustees of the Temple continue to seek alternate plans, and they are
confident that such plans can be prepared and completed for presentation and
decision at the 1973 Annual Communication.
The goal is to find the best use of the property owned on Pine Street,
behind the Memorial Temple, for the benefit of Freemasonry in California.
The answer should not be found in haste. There must be full satisfaction that
all possibilities have been thoroughly explored, and there must be the combined and thoughtful judgment of the Trustees, of the Finance Committee,
and of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes before an endorsed
proposal is presented to the Grand Lodge for its decision. The investment
by this Grand Lodge in the Pine Street property must be protected by the
best possible use of the property for the benefit of the Fraternity. Receipt
of the present study has been the sensible start of the development of an
ultimate and final plan. The time of decision has not yet arrived, but the
work needed for decision is well under way.
We therefore request that the Grand Lodge authorize the Board of
Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple to continue its work

On recommendation of the Deputy Grand Master a Budget Committee
was established. Subsequent meetings held by the Committee resulted in a
Preliminary Budget and Forecast being presented to the Board at its meeting
on December 9, 1971. The preliminary suggestions for a revised budget were
presented to the Board at its meeting on March 1, .1972: After p~oper revi~w
and study the Final Budget and Forcast of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1973, was presented to the Board
of Trustees on August 24, 19 72. A copy of this report is on file with the
Grand Secretary.
PLANNING AND ECONOMIC FEASIBILITY FOR THE
PROPOSED EXPANSION OF THE TEMPLE

In the Report of the Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
presented to the 1971 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge it was pointed
out that the architect estimated the erection of a new structure, such as that
proposed by him, would involve a total expenditure of approximately
$6,000,000. This structure would not only house the Library and Museum but
provide us with the additional space needed for our own operations, as well as
revenue producing facilities. The report further pointed out that the Board
of Trustees did not desire to incur the additional architectural expenses for a
feasibility study or for a graphic report, illustrative material, etc., until Grand
Lodge expressly authorized such expenditures.
The Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes to the same
Annual Communication of Grand Lodge recommended "that the Trustees of
the California Masonic Memorial Temple be authorized to proceed to secure
a feasibility study and such related reports as in their judgment are necessary to enable this Grand Lodge to make a careful decision in the future
concerning the development of the P ine Street property owned by Grand
Lodge, and that the costs of the study and reports be provided from T emple
funds." The Report of the Conunittee on Policy and General Purposes was
thereafter approved by Grand Lodge.
Pursuant to the above mandate, the Board of Trustees retained Milton T.
Pflueger, AIA, to prepare a feasibility study together with preliminary plans
for the erection of the structure. The feasibility study is marked Exhibit A
and is attached hereto and made a part of this report. All working papers
and drawings are on file in the Grand Secretary's office.
The feasibility report, as well as the schematic drawings for the expansion
of the Memorial Temple, has been carefully studied and reviewed by the
Trustees of the T emple. The Conunittees on Finance and Policy and General
Purposes have also studied and reviewed the report. They have also met with
the Temple Trustees for discussion of the proposal. It is the unanimous

of procuring alternate plans for the development of the Pine Street property
with the understanding that no construction will be authorized or commenced'
nor any obligation incurred for any construction, until expressly approved

We further request that an additional per capita of fifty cents per member

to provide necessary funds for whatever professional services are required and
to establish a building fund ; it being understood that in the event no project

I am authorized to state that the Committee on Policy and General

Second, I move that an additional per capita of fifty cents be included in
the budget for the purposes outlined in this report.

ECONOMIC CONSULTANT

1. The Project

To consider the expansion of the T emple, providing a Library-Museum
complex, additional Office Space and such other space which would
complement, enhance, and expand existing Fraternal facilities ; and to so
plan such other space so that when not used by t he Fraternity, it will
produce increased revenue, thereby making the project viable in all
respects.
2. The Directive
In essence, the directive by the Board of Trustees was to make ( 1) a
Feasibility Report involving Usage, Expenses, Income, and Economic
Study; (2) a Graphic Report involving basically conceptual planning
with appropriate drawings, slides and a scale model. Both parts are
coincident and must by their nature relate in all aspects to the other.
This report is in accord with the intent of services first discussed with
the Board in August 1970, subsequently proposed in September, 197 1
confirmed and accepted by the Board in December 1971.
The Architects employed URS RESEARCH COl\IPANY as their consultants to make a market analysis, testing the feasibility of t he Project.
The projected usage, cash flow calculations, etc., based upon " with"
expansion and "without" expansion, are the results of research, market
studies, consultations, and conferencing with every available source.

3. E xpansion Property
The proposed Project envisions the expansion of the Temple southwest to
Pine Street. This Report deals with property described as follows :
Starting at the southwest corner of the existing Temple Building, running
southerly 13 70 feet to the Pine Street Property line ; thence easterly
1370 feet on Pine Street, then northerly 75' to abut the existing
Temple Building. The land area of the "Pine Street Proper ty" equals
17,343 square feet including 1875 square feet (25 feet on Pine x 75 deep)
which was part of the original T emple property.
The existing T emple pr operty, wi th a frontage of 275 feet on California
Street, and 200 feet on Taylor Street equals 4 7,968 square fee t.

242

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

4. Planning Factors and Criteria
There are certain basic premises which set the parameters of the Concept.
They include the following:

a. Property Configuration.
At the midpoint of the Pine Street Property, the curb elevation is
222' -6". The elevation of the existing 11ain Floor is 294'-9" and the
elevation of the existing Ground Floor (Exhibit-Dining, etc.) is
276'-9", which is 54 feet or 5 stories, above the Pine Street elevation.
In the existing building there are S floors of Garage in this height,
with an inconvenient egress drive to Pine Street which is also used as
the service drive. There is a definite need for a generous, convenient
garage entrance and exit from Pine Street, it being a wide 3 lane
one-way street. There is also the need for the Service Drive, and a
Temple Lobby from Pine Street. These 3 elements however, need not
be 5 stories high, and open space with columns 5 stories high would
be a poor use of valuable property, as well as being most unsightly
and unclean. Consideration was given to commercial use and also a
"strip" of apartment units along the Pine Street frontage. Both of
these uses are incompatible with the principle of the Temple and
would involve unrelated income destroying the tax structure. Commercial use would also necessitate rezoning of the property which is
now R-3, but which, with a Conditional Use Permit, would allow a
"Lodge" building and other facilities directly related thereto. Expanded garage facilities is therefor the proper use for this cubage
and is feasible as shown in the report.
The usage of the property above the garage floors, follows rather
naturally.
b. Expansion of Ground Floor.
The existing Exhibition Space on the Ground Floor is not as desirable
as it should be for several reasons. It has numero us columns which
inhibit sight lines and flexibility. It also is of a size, approximately
16,000 square feet, which is insufficient for many of the ExhibitConvention requests and needs. An expansion of over 14,000 net
square feet in the " new" property area, free of columns is an obvious
gain. The new space may serve as an independent unit, or by nature of
its contiguity, as an adjoining expansion of the present space.

c. Expansion of Main Floor
The existing Main Floor, entered from California Street now contains
the Memorial Foyer, the Main Floor of the Auditorium, and auxiliary
rooms such as Recep tion Office, Checking Room, Reception and
Robing Rooms.
With the desire for additional Fraternal Facilities, such as the
Library-Museum Complex, etc., another factor which prompted the
purchase of the new property was the preservation of natural light

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

243

through the endomosaic window of the Grand Lobby. This leads to
the concept of an inner court, skylighted, or as we may choose to
call it, the Atrium, which in early Roman History was the central
daylighted room around which other rooms were disposed, and in
early Christian church structures was the large open court or meeting
place in front of the Church itself, and thou gh not so called, one may
think of it in connection with the great Court of King Solomon's
Temple.
The Atrium here, 52 feet in width, the full width of the window,
80 feet plus in length and 60 feet high, to the roof of the Third Floor,
serves a noble purpose, featuring the endomosaic window, and with
its su rrounding spaces can be a general meeting area for those functions which would not be thought suitable in the Memorial Lobby.
As an adjunct to the Auditorium its uses are manifold. The expansion
area in total is over 14,000 net square feet. It serves as the third unit
of the Exhibit-Meeting areas and is connected by a large open stair
to the Exhibit space below.
d. Upper Floor Expansion.
The upper floors of the expansion which ring the Atrium are most
suitable for the Library, the Museum and of course, the office expansion on the existing office (the third) floor.
They are thus private, for Fraternal use, but readily accessible for
visiting, educational purposes, and uses compatible with the principles
of the Order.

e. Other Planning Criteria .
The above basic premises may be considered those which primarily
set the parameters for the Concept.
Other important design features include the following:
1. In order to provide a complete "ring" of circulation around the
Atrium, tliree new passenger elevators would be installed within
the boundaries of the " new" area. The location of the two existing
passenger elevators would preclude the " ring" which is functionally necessary and a Building Code requirement. Three elevators
will of course improve the elevator service and they are required
with the expansion.
2. The existing freight elevator now serves only the Ground Floor. It
cannot, by reason of location, be extended upward to the Main
Floor. It will be retained ; however, a new freight elevator will be
installed to serve not only the Ground Floor, but also the Auditorium and the new Main Floor areas, a very necessary requirement.
3. A section of the Main Floor expansion, namely, a space along
the Pine Street frontage, approximately 12 6 feet by 74 feet in
depth, all south of the Atrium, could be partitioned off with

244

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

sliding walls, to serve as a multi-media, multi-use room with
tiered removable seating which may be used for presentations,
meetings, exhibits, museum expansion , or other uses as the Fraternity may see flt. This room, with its 700 - 800 seat capacity,
offers another example of flexibility, which is the key-note of the
concept.
4. The integration of the existing and new is mandatory. While the
expansion offers new dimensions and potentials, th ere must be no
sacrifice or diminishment of the existing; instead, improvement
and enhancement.
5. During construction of the expansion there must be no interruption in the use of the existing facilities. Use and revenue produced by the existing is required in this period.
CONCEPT SUMMARY
The P roject is one which excites the spirit and the mind. New dimensions
are added which will thrill not only the members of the Masonic Fraternity
but the public who will be privileged to use the Temple, in whole or in part.
With the expansion, The Temple will be unique, affording facilities not
provided by an existing or planned project.
The concept envisions much more than a series of rooms. The Temple can
be the place, a place of meeting.

APPROACH

The attached cash flow calculations were prepared to test the feasibility of the proposed expansion of the Temple. The general approach has
been to contrast the average annual net cash flow for a ten-year period with
the new facility, with that expected without the expansion. The ten-year
period selected was FY 1976-85 inclusive and all figures are in 1975 dollars.
A 15% inflation factor was used to escalate from 1972 to 1975 dollars.

For the year ended J une 30, 1972 satisfactory results were again obtained from the investment of securities under the control of the Investment
Committee. T otal investments increased to a record high of $40,690,615 from
the total o f $3 7,446,790 at June 30, 1971. T he increase of $3,243 ,825 is accounted for by contributions and other funds received of $2,022,098, plus net
realized and unrealized gains in the portfolio totaling $ 1,2 21, 72 7.
Activities of t he Committee are regulated generally by the Masonic Code,
which se ts forth the three major categories (as groups) of securities allowa ble
for investment. These categories may be summarized as follows:
(1) Group I-Consists of cash, savings accounts, obliga tions of the United
States, obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions, and
such other securities as are legal for savings banks in California and Hawaii.
In general, Group I may be said to consist of the hi gh est grade an d most
conservative securities. At least 20o/o of the funds a vailable fo r investment
must be maintai ned in such securities.
(2) Group II-Consists generally of bonds, debentures, and other
evidences of indebtedness which do not meet the qualifications of Group I.
It also consists of preferred stocks which are listed on a National Securities
Exchange and the preferred stocks of corporations whose common stocks a re
eligible for investment in Group III.
(3) Group III-Consists of common stocks, which must be fully listed
and registered on a national exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, bank·and insurance company stocks, shares of investment
trusts, and savings accounts with savings and loan associations. Total investments in Group III securities are generally limited to 60 % of the total
portfolio.

During the past year we have continued to switch from federal agency
bonds to comparable quality corporate issues with an increase in yield to the
portfolio. The holdings of convertible debentures has increased during the
year, even though $1,250,000 par value of convertible debentures was converted into common stock. Two of the conversions were $950,000 par value of
real estate trust issues where the increased dividends on the common shares
now exceeds the interest income from the debentures. We continue to believe
that convertible securities offer a unique opportunity to combine a satisfactory
yield with potential capital appreciation.
Common stocks now represent 55.48% of the total portfolio and are
represented by 41 issues, a decrease from 64 issues a year ago. Alliance
Capital Management's recommendations of common stocks are confined to
those of well capitalized companies which are highly marketable and meet
statutory requirements of standards of prudence. Investments are concentrated principally in companies possessing above-average earnings growth
potential over the longer term. Details of the individual securities making up
the various funds are spelled out in the Grand Treasurer's report and are
accordingly not repeated here.
It continues to be the policy of this Committee to consider the safety and
preservation of capital as its primary goal. We recognize the need for increasing income to provide major financial support for the two Masonic Homes and
at the same time provide a measure of protection against the spiraling costs
of inflation. The estimated annual income from the portfolio is $1,898,660
against an estimated annual income last year of $1,751,122. This is a current
yield of 4. 7% on the market value of the portfolio.

ASSETS RECEIVED FROM THE ORDER OF THE AMARANTH
During the past fiscal year, the Foundati on was the very fortunate recipient of substanti al assets from the Order of the Amaranth . This came
about through the fact that the top officers of that organizat ion had decided,
and were supported in this decision by a majority of their members, that they
neither had the facilities nor the desire to adopt new charitable -giving programs or to continue with the type of charitabl e activities which they had
engaged in the past. These had consisted primarily in the operation of a home
for minor females, and when the demand for such a facility decreased , the
home was sold, leaving the Order of the Amarant h with assets valued at some
$217 ,000, of which approxim ately S11 S,000 was in cash and the balance was
in the form of a promisso ry note secured by a first trust deed on the real
property. After a court hearing before the Los Angeles County Superior Co~rt
at which represent atives of the Order of the Amaranth and of our Foundati on
appeared and .a D eputy Attorney General of the State of Californi a, was
present and approved the transactio n, the Court approved the transfer of these
assets to us and made its Order according ly.
We now have these assets in our portfolio as is shown in the financial
statemen t of the Foundati on on file in the Grand Secretary 's office, and several
awards have already been made therefrom, although under the terms of the
Court Order (which was based upon the terms of the original Order of the
Amaranth Trust Agreeme nt), only the income can be used, and awards are
limited to worthy females under age 21 , who are Californi a residents.
We cannot express too strongly, our deep and lasting appreciat ion to the
Order of the Amaranth , their officers and directors for the wonderfu l gift of
these assets, and assure them that our Board regards this as an exception ally
high trust obligation , and will extend every effo rt to use the funds to the
greatest benefit of everyone concerned , including all members of the Order
of the Amarant h, the Grand Lodge, and the young women who will become
beneficiaries of the awards made therefrom .

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTE E
TO PREPARE GRAND LODGE HISTORY PUBLICATI ON
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
At the last Communication of the Grand Lodge in 19 71, Grand Master
Herbert A. Huebner r~comm~nded and Grand Lodge approved the preparation
of a Grand Lodge history, m popular reading style, revolving around the
Grand Lodge, to be available in time for any Masonic observance of the 200th
anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
. The new Grand Master, Lester S. McElwain, appointed a Special Committee to Prepare a Grand Lodge History Publication. The committee has met
three times during the present Masonic year.
. The committee set as an approximate deadline for publication of the
history October I, 19 75 - the 12 5th anniversary of the Grand Lodge, or not
later than Jan. I , 1976.
Members estimated that a volume of 400 pages, well illustrated, would
cost $10 or more per copy. The estimated cost of publication, from $7,000 to
$10,000, would, to a large extent, be recovered from sales to the constituent
Lodges.
The committee also agreed that it favored publication of a single volume
covering the history of the Grand Lodge from 1850 to 1975 rather than on~
volume covering only the 25-year period from 1950 to 1975 a~ the fif th volume
of the four-volume One Hundred Years of Freemasonry in California.
The committee also voted to request the Grand Master to ask the Line
Officers, th~ough the present Junior Grand Warden, to commit themselves, so
far as possible, to an. under~tanding that they would support the publication
of a ?ra~d Lodge H1s_tory m the year 1975. The committee further agreed
that !t Will proce~d wit~ the gathering of material and writing the history
only 1f, and when, 1t receives assurances from the Line Officers of their support
of the project.

SPECIAL REPORT ON PRIORITIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In his message to the Grand Lodge on October 11, 1971, Grand Master
Herbert A. Huebner recommended "that the incoming Grand Master appoint
a special committee for the Study of Priorities. This committee should invite,
from all pertinent committees and boards, and from all interested Lodges as
well as individual brethren, suggestions for programs and projects, evaluate
their importance, study probable costs together with funds currently available
or possible sources to provide the same. The committee should report in detail
its findings and recommendations, with particularity as to priorities which
should be accorded."
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which this recommendation of the Grand l\faster was referred, reported, "We endorse the
Grand Master's recommendation concerning the need for a Study of Priorities.
We suggest that the first step in such a study program might properly be
a request to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes for a determination and proposal as to basic priorities and categories thereof, prior to the
appointment of a special committee and/ or the issuance of a general invitation
for the submission of suggestions for particular programs and projects. To do
otherwise provides the possibility of priorities being set on the basis of proposals at hand whether timely or not. At the proper time the Grand Master
should issue the invitation for the submission of programs and projects." This
report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes was adopted by the
Grand Lodge.
The Committee an Policy and General Purposes, after consideration and
with recognition of the importance of determining priorities, now reports as
follows:
We propose that matters involving priorities can be segregated into four
basic categories. These categories are: A. - Intra-fraternal Communication and Relations
B. - Programs and Special Events
C. - Physical Facilities
D. - Historical Prcserva ti on
We suggest no order of rank or priority for these basic categories; rather
they should all be considered as of equal importance to this Grand Lodge
and to Masonry in this jurisdiction. For illustration we list herewith some
definite programs and projects under what we regard as their appropriate
categories: Category A. - Intra-fraternal Communication and Relations
- Masonic information and communication to Masonic-youth organizations
- Adequate explanation of the role and authority of the Grand Lodge in
its relation to the individual 1\faster Mason

260
-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Better explanation and instruction concerning the relationship between
the Lodge of .Masons and the Masonic-related organizations wherein
membership is dependent upon Masonic affiliation

Category B. - Programs and Special Events
- Proper advancement of the stated purposes of the California Masonic
Foundation
- Modernization of the program of support of the Public Schools
- Renovation of the Constitution Observance program
- Financial support to Masonic-related youth organizations
- Participation in the USA Bicentennial (1976)
Category C. - Physical Facilities
- Modernization of facilities of the l\fasonic Homes of California
- Enlargement of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
- Establishment of a Grand Lodge Museum and Library in Southern
California
Category D. - Historical Preservation
- Marking, restoration and preservation of historical buildings and sites
- Publication of an up-dated California Masonic History
A special committee for the Study of Priorities should be able to "sift and
sort" proposals made to the Grand Lodge into the four basic categories suggested. Priorities within the categories can then be suggested and recommended for determination by the Grand Lodge. There must be recognition
that priorities within the categories must be flexible enough to allow for
existing conditions at the time proposed for implementation of a particular
project or program. No order of priorities should be so rigid as to foreclose
a worthy undertaking when unforeseen or changing conditions may clearly
indicate that the undertaking should be immediately commenced. Nor should
any order of priorities be regarded on a "one-thing-at-a-time" basis; for,
dependent upon the resources and time involved, more than one undertaking
may be in progress at the same time.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes now recommends that the
incoming Grand Master appoint either the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, or a special committee as recommended by Grand Master H~e~~er
to study priorities and with the instruction to develop and propose pnont1es
within the four basic categories proposed in this report.
Respectfully submitted,
THEODORE MERIAM, Chairman

Of the physical qualification of Candidates for the degrees of Masonry -

PHYSICAL QUALIF ICATION
(NOTE: By action of Grand Lodge at the 1971 Annua.l Communic ation,
the Grand Secretary was directed to distribute copies of the reports made by
m embers of the Special Committee on Physical Qualifications. These appear
on pages 249 through 264 inclusive of the 1971 Proceedings. Distributio n was
made to Lodges prior to this Communic ation. Following are reports by Grand

by Grand Lodge.)
The Committee on Ritual:

Reporting on Physical Qualifications, your Committee on Ritual has the
following to offer:
We feel that both sides of this question have been exhaustively explored
and all arguments presented.

267

How can there be a difference of opinion on this subject? Let any Mason
ask himself whether the Candidate who is blind or deaf, or who has lost an
arm or leg is capable of acquiring a knowledge of Masonry so as to impart
the same to another : Whether he is capable of making himself known as a
Mason under all circumstances; in the dark as well as in the light? His answer
to these simple questions, as answer them he can but in one way, will supersede all argument upon this subject.
'We move the adoption of the report but very strongly urge a "No" vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

This section of our report is directed to the subject of physical qualifications. Such subject has been before Grand Lodge in one form or another for
several Annual Communications.
It now comes before Grand Lodge as unfinished business, held over from
the 1971 Annual Communication. The exploration and study has been painstakingly and thoroughly prepared and presented. The opposing views of an
evenly divided committee were printed not only in the 197 1 Proceedings
pp. 249-264, but pamphlet reprints were distributed to the constituent Lodges
in April, 1972, and a foJlow-up mailing just concluded.
There has been ample time for quiet and prayerful consideration, absent
emotional oratory and thrust of personality.
The subject now comes before Grand Lodge in form suitable for action.
The Report and Re~lutions on Physical Qualifications define a fundamental
question in paragraph 1, and legislation provisions in paragraphs numbered
2 through 8.
The fundamental question is "Do you desire change in present regula tions
concerning physical requirements of candidates which would necessitate
change in the ritual?"
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the opinion tha t the
fundament al question is one which should be resolved by the membershi p of
this Jurisdiction without any committee persuasion. It is a question of basic
importance. The legislative sections, paragraphs 2-8, stand or fall with the
vote on the fundamental question.
Every Lodge has had opportunit y to consider the subject and instruct its
representatives or delegates. It is time now for a vote.
To bring the matter before Grand Lodge I move the adoption of the
Resolutions numbered I through 9 and the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes makes no recommendation concerning the vote thereon.

California Masonic Code to change the required Physical Qualifications which

California Masonic Code which set forth the requirements for forming a
Lodge under Dispensation and, among other things, provide that a Dispensation terminates at the next Grand Lodge Communication, and
vVHEREAS, the representatives of the Committees on Jurisprudence,
Policy and General Purposes, and Ritual feel that the proposed amendments
should be revised to make them more workable and accordingly have rewritten said proposed amendments, and
WHEREAS, those opposing any change in the requirements for physical
qualification propose that a question be submitted to Grand Lodge reading
"Do you desire change in the present regulations concerning physical requirements of candidates which would necessitate change in the ritual, or do you
oppose such change?"

Sec. 510. PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS. The physical qualifications of a person shall not necessarily make him ineligible to file an application for the degrees if he is otherwise worthy and well qualified. The

the Lodge, and if an applicant is elected who could not conform substantially to what the several degrees respectively require of him, the
degrees must be conferred by qualified ritualists as hereinafter provided.

Sec. 511. MORAL AND PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS. An applicant for the degrees of Masonry must be a man ; a believer in God and a

Sec. 512.
4. RESOLVED , that Sec. 512 be amended to read:
Sec. 512. PROCEDURE FOR PHYSICALLY HANDICAPPED
APPLICANTS. Before the application of an applicant who has a physical
handicap which would prevent him from conforming substantially to what
the several degrees require of him can be received and voted upon by the
Lodge, it will be necessary for him to appear before a special committee
of not Jess than 5, appointed by the Master of the Lodge to which he
wishes to make the application. This committee shall consist of not less
than two of the principal officers of the Lodge, and other members whom
the Master may appoint. The date of the meeting of this committee shall
be so set as to enable the Inspector of the District in which the Lodge is
located to attend and advise the committee. The committee shall request
that the proposed applicant appear before them at the Lodge hall in a
private room suitable for the occasion, and with dignity and as little
embarrassment to the applicant as is reasonably possible, view the extent

The Committe e on Policy and General Purposes:
The purpose of the proponen ts of this Resolutio n is to foreclose aid and
support to subversiv e individua ls or groups which provision of the use of the
facilities of the Grand Lodge, constitue nt Lodges or Masonic- related organizations might provide.
The Committe e on P olicy and General Purposes recognizes the laudable
purpose apparent in the thinking of the proponen ts. It is the opinion of the
Committe e, however, that the classification of the motives and activities of
persons and groups and the determina tion of what constitute s subversio n
under all conditions by the persons or organizat ions seeking use of the facilities could possibly create legal hazards of extremely serious proportio ns.

278

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

It is also our opinion that the Grand Lodge Temple management, the
Lodges and concordant organizations in this Grand Jurisdiction , currently
and consistently make every reasonable effort to serve the purposes of this
Resolution without there being a formal provision in the Code as the basis of
decision. We belie\•e that the best interest of all concerned will be best
served by the continuation of the current procedures.

I move the adoption of this Resolution. The Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This resolution proposes that the Grand Lodge an<l its constituent Lodges
refrain from allowing individuals or groups, who are known to be subversive or
who would advocate the violent overthrow of the government or our democratic way of life, to use its facilities.
The following is offered to implement this resolution:
RESOLVED : That Section 332.3 be and it is hereby added to the
California Masonic Code.
Section 332 .2 - Use of Facilities by Subversives. The Grand Lodge, a
constituent Lodge, or an organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a
condition for membership shall not give aid or support by permitting the
use of its facilities by any business, project, or scheme to advance the
cause or causes of any individual, group, or concern known to be subversive or who would advocate the violent overthrow of our national government, or our democratic way of life.
There is no question that the purposes proposed by the proponents are
exemplary. Our Grand Lodge and its constituent Lodges are presently striving
diligently to investigate each applicant who wants to use the facilities to
make sure that the use will conform to those p rinciples that we, as Masons,
are bound to uphol d.
However, your Committee on Jurisprud ence believes that the resolution
as presented is unenforceable because the terms therein are vague and uncertai n. For example, "democratic way of life" involves political philosophy.
And there can already exist a justifiable divergence of political philosophies
between and within the Lodges.
Further it is a dangerous resolution because it could result in charges
being preferred against a Mason or the charter of a Lodge being revoked
because of what was said or done at the meeting, even though the Lodge had
done all in its power to investigate the group prior to the meeting.
For the above reasons, we offer this resolution but strongly recommend a
"No" vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

WILLIAM

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes :

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution state that it is not always necessary or
practical to have five members serving on the Board of Control as now required by the California l\Iasonic Code. 1t is their recommendation that the
first sentence of Section 261 be amended to read : " There is hereby created a
Board of Control to consist of not more titan five to be appointed by the
Grand l\Iaster."
Section 262 provides that " The Board of Control shall have control and
supervise the activities of Masonic Service Bureaus now existing or hereafter
to be created under the authority of the Grand Lodge of Cali fornia."
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is keenly aware of the
enlarged and added responsibilities of our Masonic Ser vice Bureaus, the need
for adequate record keeping including appropriate statistical data, the broad
expanse of these Bureaus across the State and the necessity and obligation o f
the Board of Control to evaluate, supervise and control the activities of the
Bureaus.
The term of office of the members of the Board of Control, unlike that of
other committees, is specified for three years, with staggered appointment .
In recognition of the foregoing and the tenure of appointment as members
of the Board of Control, it is necessary that the number of members be
maintained at five. To reduce the number of members in this instance \Vould
be to curtail the service required of our Committees and Boards and defeat
the Purpose for which they were created. It would be impractical and in the

280

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

event of difference among members could result in lack of decision for failure
of a majority vote.
I move the adoption of the Re!\ol11tion and your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This Resolution, reciting that "it is not always necessary or practical to
have five members serving on the Board of Control," proposes that the first
sentence of Section 261, C.M.C . be amended to read:
" There is hereby created a Board of Control to consist of not more than
five members to be appointed by the Grand Master."
In the opinion of your Committee on Jurisprudence, the language of the
proposed amendment adequately covers the intent of the proposers.
However, your Committee on Jurisprudence points out that under the
language of the proposed amendment, namely that the Board of Control shall
"consist of not more than five members," there is nothing whatever to prevent
the immediate reduction of the Board to a single member. This is so because
the proposed amendment sel5 a ceiling of five members but states no minimum
such as two, three or four.
For these reasons, your Committee on Jurisprudence moves the adoption
of Resolution No. 5 and recommends a "No" vote thereon.
A majority voted against the resolution.

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes :
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes;
Resolution No. 7 proposes that all sections of the California Masonic
Code prohibiting the serving of alcoholic beverages at Masonic functions be
repealed. The proponent also proposes that there be one exception, in that
"alcoholic beverages shall not be serYed in Lodge meeting rooms while the
rooms are being used as such."
Essentially the proposal is that this Grand Lodge place no restriction upon
the serving and use of alcoholic beverages except during a Masonic Lodge
meeting in a Lodge room.
Reference is made in the proposal to the fact that State law does not
prohibit the ser\'in~ of alcoholic beverages at Lodges, Clubs and Associations
if pertinent State laws are followed. Lack of a prohibition in State law does
not represent permission to do that which is not in accordance with decorum
and propriety. There is a time and place for everything.
Our present regulations concerning the serving of liquor were made after
much careful study and consideration, and it is the belief of your Committee
on Policy and General Purposes that the existing regulations reflect not
only current social practices and customs but also the dignity, the serious
purpose, and the recognized quality of the institution of Freemasonry. Again,
there is a time and place for everything; there are also times and places
where some things are clearly inappropriate.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 7, and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes unanimously recommend and urges a "No" vote.

Resolution No. 7 has been referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence for
attention and Consideration.
Your Committee presents the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that Section 324.2 of the California Masonic Code be
amended as follows:
After the word "establishment" in line 7 add the following "and except
as hereinafter provided, alcoholic beverages may be served at Masonic
functions held in Masonic Temples and buildings owned by organizations,
the prerequisite wherein is that a person be a Master Mason, pro'vided
that all pertinent laws of Federal, State, and other Governmental Organizations are complied with," and be it further resolved that the last ten
lines of said Section 324.2 commencing with the words "provided, however" in the seventh line be deleted and in lieu thereof the following is to
be substituted: "provided, however, that, except for ritualistic purposes,
no liquor, wine, or beer may be seryed in a Lodge Meeting Room while it
is being used for a Lodge Meeting."

WEARING OF APRONS

(8)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS the Grand Lodge Communication of 1971 approved and more
closely defined the wearing of aprons by Officers and Past Masters in Section
328.1 of the California Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS the Officer's apron is the symbol of his rank and the Officer's
jewel is the symbol of his station, as evidenced by the Officer appearing for
installation in his apron as the symbol of his rank and being presented his
jewel upon installation in his individual station; and
WHEREAS it has been a practice for an Officer working in either an
advanced or lesser station to retain his apron, but assu me the jewel of the
advanced or lesser station; and
WHEREAS it has been a practice for a brother about the Lodge working
in an Officer's station to retain his apron, but assume the jewel of the Officer's station; and
WHEREAS on an evening when two or more candidates are receiving a
degree, the changing of Officers' station assignments by Officers and brethren
about the Lodge makes the exchange of more than jewels both inconvenient
and detractive from the dignity of the occasion; and
WHEREAS it would not be possible for a brother about the Lodge or a
sojourner to recognize an Officer who has given up his apron except by such
personal knowledge of the Officer or his rank; and

284

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Section 328.l be amended
to read as follows:
328.1 Wearing of Aprons. The apron appropriate to one's Rank or
Station may be worn at any gathering of Masons at which Officers of
Lodges are authorized to wear the apron of their respective Stations,
and further, that those who hold the Title and Rank of Past Master
as defined in Section 490 of the California Masonic Code, may wear a
Past Master's Apron having the Jewel of a Past Master upon it. An
Officer relinquishing his Station during the conferral of a degree must
surrender his Jewel, but should continue to wear his Apron as the
badge of his rank.

Furthermore, it conforms to the practice of the Grand Lodge Officers at Grand
Lodge ceremonies, at which the man filling the office customarily wears both
jewel and apron indicating the office.
It has been pointed out on prior occasions that there is no authority in
our law or regulations for so-called officers' aprons, and no regulation governing color, design or insignia to be placed on them. They exist in contradiction
of the instruction given to Candidates to the effect that the white lambskin
apron is the badge of a Mason. If we are to adopt an amendment to section
328. l to prescribe the practice with respect to aprons, we should first adopt a
regulation specifying the color, design and insignia to be placed thereon.
There is neither law nor precedent for the contention that the apron belongs to the installed Officer. It is merely part of the equipment belonging to
the Lodge, just as is the jewel with which the officer is formally invested at
installation. It must also be remembered that in the installation service it is
made quite clear that the jewel is the especial badge of the station, and no
reference whatsoever is made to the apron.
The officer who is selected to act in any station or place during a degree is
selected by the installed Master: However, for the purposes of the degree, he
is the officer of the Lodge which is convened to confer the degree. The Junior
Warden acting as Master in a Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons is for all
purposes the Master of that Lodge. He must be addressed as Worshipful
Master. He wears the Master's J ewe!; he wears the Master's hat and he wields
the Master's gavel, which incidentally, is the distinct emblem of the Master's
authority. These are all surrendered to him without question. So also, we
think, must the apron be surrendered if it designates the office.
If the installed Master is to sit on the sidelines with the Master's apron,
then by the same token he should retain the hat and his gavel.
If the rule suggested in this resolution were adopted, the result would be
at best, confusion , because if the apron of the station were to be worn only
by the installed Master or other Officer, then half the officers conferring the
degree might be clothed in officers' aprons and half of them clothed in white
aprons. Where then, is the uniformity required by our law, and what purpose
could possibly be served?
Since our law requires under section 554, that each degree conferred must
be in conformity with the ritual now taught by the Grand Lecturer and recognized by the Grand Lodge, and fur ther, since this resolution would destroy the
uniformity required by this section, we suggest that it purports to amend this
section and would require a five-sixths vote of this Grand Lodge.
We move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a "No" vote.

Respectfully submitted,

As to that portion of the resolution which refers to the Grand Lodge, it
should be noted that without exception the Pledge of Allegiance is recited at
every Grand Lodge opening ceremony. This is a matter of policy which is
never deviated from.
It is the opinion of this Committee that love of flag and country is best
demonstrated voluntarily and not as a mechanical requirement.
Jn discussing this resolution with members of other Grand Lodge Committees your Grand Lecturer has projected the following points regarding the
pledge of allegiance to our country's flag:
We of the Ritual Committee agree that our allegiance and respect should
be shown our country's flag at all gatherings of Masons. We encourage the
formal presentation of the flag at all Lodge meetings, not just those annual
meetings at which it is req uired by l\fasonic law. We are fearful that the
adoption of this resolution will discourage the formal presentation of the flag
by those Lodges which now make it a regular practice.
This Committee will pledge its efforts in the coming year, through the
Ritual Chain of Instruction, to urge all Lodges to pay proper respect to the
flag at every meeting either by its formal presentation , or by having the
Master of the Lodge reques t that the members repeat the pledge of allegiance
at the appropriate place in the Lodge opening ceremony, which place will be
instructed to the Masters by the Inspectors.
We move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a " No" vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Manifestatio.n of the love and respect of all Masons for our National
Emblem is not a result of recent wars or the current international problems.
The display of our Flag at all Communications of the Grand Lodge and at all
meetings of the Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction has been a provision of the
Code since 1927. The Monitor and Officers' Manual specifies the floor work
and ritual for occasions when the Flag is formally presented at the altar, which
ceremony includes the Pledge of Allegiance. There is no ritual provision for
meetings when the Flag is informally posted in the East prior to opening.
It is the opinion of this Committee that the unfailing display of the Flag
as required by the Code at all meetings may well have created a mental
tolerance a nd its presence at our meetings a matter of mere unconscious
acceptance.
The rigors of the times, the scornful references to "flag waving" and the
frequ ent and callous instances of the desecration of this revered emblem makes
it most important that Masons do not merely "accept" the presence of our
Flag as a ma tter of no particular significance. We should consciously and
reverently honor it ! My Brethren, we are American Masons.
The Committee on Ritual has indicated that every effort will be made to
encourage the use of the Flag Ceremony already provided. We believe that
continuous and direct contact through Inspectors to Lodge Officers may be

288

more effective than provision in the Code. For this reason the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes concurs with the report of the Committee on
Ritual to that end.

The C()mrnittee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 11 has been submitted by our Grand Secretary for the
purpose of amending the California Masonic Code so that it will not be a
Masonic offense for a non-Mason to audit the books of a Lodge.
This Resolution is necessary in order that Lodges may comply with National and State regulations, which under our civil law, may require an audit
of the records of a Lodge. Some of the government auditors may be nonMasons. Thus, by adoption of this proposed amendment, Lodges will not be
con_imiting a Masonic offense when a non-Masonic government employee is
assigned to make such an audit. Essentially, all auditors for governmental
bodies are prevented by law from divulging information received from such
audits.
I move the adoption of this Resolution No. 11 and your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 11 was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence which
reports as follows:
This Resolution proposes to rescind Annotation h. of Section 493 and add
legislation to permit non-Masons acting as authorized representatives of
Governmental Agencies to audit Lodge records, and to limit that audit to
only those records pertaining to that specific subject or Lodge report being
audited.
Your Committee believes that the intention of this Resolution would be
carried out by the adoption of the following:
RESOLVED, that Annotation 493 h. should be and is hereby deleted and
that Annotation 493 1. be added as follows:
For a Secretary to allow a non-Mason to see the Lodge books is a Masonic
offense, but it is not an offense to have the Lodge books audited by a Master
Mason who is a member in good standing of some other Lodge or to allow
authorized representatives of Governmental Agencies to audit the Lodge
re:ords, b~t only those records which pertain to the subject or Lodge report
bemg audited by such Governmental representative.

Section 493j, C.M.C. states that the minutes should recite which of t he
elected and appointed officers are present. Actually, this annotation is a recommendation as to form and completeness of the minutes of a Lodge. There
is no direct requirement that the Secretary, in reading the minutes, must read
aloud the names of all of t he officers, elected and appointed, who are presen t.
He might properly read, " There were present the officers and members as
their na mes appear on the Tiler's Register, and Brother John Doe served as
Junior Deacon and Brother Richard Roe as Senior Steward f?r the mee~ing."
We also suggest that the word "recite" is not confined to the smgle meamng of
repeat ing aloud; it also means to enumerate. Quite possibly this was the
intent of Grand Master Leo F. Anderson in 1958 when this annotation was
added to t he California Masonic Code.
Consideration should also be given to the possibility tha t Brothers Doe and
Roe may look forward to hearing their names read, as recognition that they
have actively participated in the work of the Lodge on a given occasion.
\Ve also would point out that a Lodge is indeed fortunate if, due to
activity an extra period of t ime is needed to read the minutes.
Sectlon 493a., C.M.C. presently permits the reporting of bills previously
paid to be grouped in a single statement; for example, "The bills as audi ted
and reported were ordered paid." Such an expression is not in conflict with
Section 493a. We therefore see no reason for the proposal in Resolution No. 13
with respect to audit ed bills.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 12, and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 13, and your Committee on Policy

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 15 proposes a change in the present regulations concerning
the jurisdiction of a Lodge as that jurisdiction pertains to the receipt of
applications for the degrees of Masonry. The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends rejection of the proposal because a special study by

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution was referred,
reports as follows :
This Resolution proposes to increase from ten to twenty-five miles from
the Lodge room the territorial limits of residential qualification of an applicant for Degrees .
The amendment of Section 522 of the California Masonic Code is required,
substituting for the word "ten" the word "twenty -five."
In addition, Annotations b, c, d, e and g to Section 522 contain law which
is still applicable, but use the words "ten miles." Because of the value of the
law contained in them, the Committee does not believe these Annotations
should be deleted. It does believe, however, that a parenthetical explanation
should be made in each of said Annotations so that any reader would know
that as of 1972 the limit bad been changed to twenty-five miles.

proposed:

as amended it will read :

VOTING BY TILER
(17)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, by Decision No. 3, the undersigned, as the Grand Master,
construed the California Masonic Code to require that the Tiler, if a member
of the Lodge, and is present, must vote upon a ballot for the degrees or for
affiliation, and for such purpose attendance at bjs post in the Tiler's room
constitutes presence at the meeting. The Decision prescribed procedures for
enabling such ballot to be cast, and also for relieving the Tiler if he desires to
debate or vote on questions before the Lodge ( 19 71 Proc. p. 63, adopted by
Grand Lodge, p. 81); and
WHEREAS, it has been reported that compliance with the requirement
that the Tiler must vote upon a ballot for the degrees or for affiliation, has
unduly prolonged stated meetings in numerous Lodges where the Tiler would
have been content to remain at his post and his lack of a ballot be interpreted
as a favorable vote; and
WHEREAS, any member, including the Tiler, has the right to object to
the election of an applicant for the degrees or for affiliation, the objection to
be made orally or in writing privately to the Master (C.M.C. Section 540 and
540a), and the Tiler's privilege of a negative vote thus may be preserved;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 534 of the
C.M.C. be amended by inserting in line 2 after the words "when present," except the Tiler, - , same line after the word "must" inserting-, and the
Tiler may,-; so that the entire section as amended will read:
Sec. 534. Members present must vote. Every member of a Lodge when
present, except the Tiler, must, and the Tiler may, vote upon a ballot for the
degrees or for affiliation.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 323h of the C.M.C. Supp.
be amended by striking the word "obligation" in line 1 and substituting the
word - privilege-; in the second paragraph line 2 after "voted", insertin.g
the phrase - and the Tiler having informed the Master in advance of his
desire to vote,-; so that the entire section will read:

300

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Sec. 323h. To discharge his privilege to vote, the Tiler may make arrangements in advance with a visiting brother or member of the Lodge to relieve
him that he may be in the Lodge room for the entire balloting procedure.
If there be no visitor or member who will volunteer for this purpose, after
all members present have voted, and the Tiler having informed the Master in
advance of his desire to vote, the Master shall order a member of the Lodge
to relieve the Tiler for the purpose of casting his ballot.
Upon entrance of the Tiler, the Master shall repeat the purpose of the
ballot and the announcement of the report of the investigating committee. The
Tiler shall then vote and return to this post. Re-entrance of the brother who
relieved him shall be optional. Huebner, G.M. 1971, pp. 63, 81; 1972.
Not approved.
Respectfully submitted,
HERBERT A. HUEBNER, P.M., No. 445
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Resolution No. 17 proposes that the Tiler may, but is not required, to
vote upon a ballot for the degrees or for affiliation.
At the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge in October, 1971, the then
Grand Master, 1\1.".W.".Herbert A. Huebner, by his decision No. 3 ruled that
it was mandatory for the Tiler if present, to vote upon all ballots for the
degrees and for affiliations.
The Committees on Jurisprudence, Ritual, and Policy and General Purposes agreed with the Grand Master. Grand Lodge concurred by the adoption
of this decision.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is still of the opinion
that Grand Master Huebner's Decision No. 3 was correct. We believe that
Resolution No. 17 would take away from the Tiler his right and privilege
to cast a secret ballot, either favorably or negatively, on an applicant. This
proposal recommends that the Tiler make his objection to the Master if he
disapproves of the applicant. If he voluntarily remains at his post his lack of a
ballot would be interpreted as a favorable vote, thus saving the time it takes
to read all the pertinent information on an application a second time.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the opinion that
very little consideration should be given to the time saved on rereading applications for the Tiler's benefit in proportion to the importance of the effort to
protect the right and privilege of his secret ballot. Also that there may be
occasions when it is not feasible for the Tiler to make his objections to the
Master, either because of business or personal reasons. If the Tiler were to
vote only upon requesting this privilege, it might seem to other members of
the Lodge that he is doing this for the purpose of casting a negative ballot.
We feel that this challenges the secrecy of his vote.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

301

I move the adoption of Resolu tion No. 17 and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 17 was referred to the Committee on J urisprudence. The
Committee reports as follows:
The purpose of the resolution is to change the provisions pertaining to
voting by the Tiler. Then Grand Master Herbert A. Huebner, by Decision 3
rendered in 1971, construed the California Masonic Code to require the
T iler, if a member of the Lodge and present at his Tiler's post, to vote upon a
ballot for the degrees or for affiliation. That decision (incorporated into the
C.M.C. as Annotation 323h ) prescribed procedures for enabling the Tiler's
ballot to be cast.
The Past Grand Master has now proposed a change which would permit,
but not require, the Tiler to vote upon a ballot for the degrees or for
affiliation.
The language of the proponent presents in excellent form the legislation
required to carry out his intent; howe\'er, the Committee believes it is not
proper to preserve Annotation 323 h by modifying it, and that that Annotation
should be deleted and a new Annotation 323 i should be substituted therefore.
Using the language of the proponent, a proper form for the proposed
legislation would be as follows:
BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 534 of the C.M.C. be amended by
inserting in line 2 after the words "when present," the words "except the
Tiler," and on the same line after the word " must" by inserting now the
words", and the Tiler may," so that the entire section as amended will read :
"Sec. 534. Members present must vote. Every member of a Lodge when
present, except the Tiler, must, and the Tiler may, vote upon a ballot for the
degrees or for affiliation."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 323 h of the C.M.C. Supp.
be deleted and that a new Annotation Section 323 i be adopted in form as
follows:
"Sec. 323 i. To discharge his privilege to vote, the Tiler may make arrangements in advance with a visiting brother or member of the Lodge to relieve
him that be may be in the Lodge room for the entire balloting procedure. If
there be no visitor or member who will volunteer for this purpose, after all
members present have voted, and the Tiler having informed the Master in
advance of his desire to vote, the Master shall order a member of the Lodge
to relieve the Tiler for the purpose of casting his ballot.
Upon entrance of the Tiler, the Master shall repeat the purpose of the
ballot and the announcement of the report of the investigating committee.
The Tiler shall then vote and return to his post. Re-entrance of the brother
who relieved him shall be optional."
We move the adoption of the Resolution.

A majority voted against the resolution.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, Section 579 C.M.C. permits the Secretary to send notices
to members, either by registered letter or certified mail, with return receipt

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the first paragraph of
Section 546 C.M.C. be amended to read as follows:
546. FORFEITURE OF FEES. If a candidate does not present himself
qualified for the Second and Third Degrees within a period of five years
from the date of his initiation as an Entered Apprentice, the Master shall
direct the Secretary to forward to such candidate, either by registered letter
or certified mail, with return receipt requested, deposited in the U.S. Post

D. W. MALTBY, P.M., No. 542
R eferred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 18 seeks to revise the first paragraph of Section 546 of the
California Masonic Code which now directs the Secretary to forward to a
candidate, by registered mail, to his last known address, a notice advising him
that unless he shall present himself for advancement on or before a specified
date his fees for the unconferred degrees and all his previous contributions
will be forfeited. This resolution would permit such notification to be addressed to the candidate, either by registered letter or certified mail, with
return receipt requested, deposited in the U. S. Post Office. The proposed notification procedure is similar to that followed in the execution of Sections 579
and 707 of the California ~Iasonic Code.
It is the opinion of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes that
the amendment as proposed would establish definite proof of receipt of notification of forfeiture and eliminate possible misunderstanding or ignored verbal
or written communication. Further, the amended Section would establish
greater uniformity in notification procedure to candidates and members in
matters of grave importance. The word "properly" should be inserted after
" himself" in the first line of the subject paragraph.
I move the adoption of this resolution and the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

REMISSION OF DUES IN ADVANCE

(19)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, one of the most prized possessions we l\Iasons carry in our
pockets is our Paid-up membership card in the Masonic Lodge; and
WHEREAS, our present law provides for the remission of dues in advance
to brethren who are in the Masonic Home, thus providing them with the
same prized possession; and
WHEREAS the same privilege is denied those brethren who are not in
the Home, but' unable to pay, and deserving, as our law permits only the
remission of accrued dues for such brethren; and
WHEREAS, this means that these unfortunate brethren have a Paid-up
dues card only until the end of the quarter in which the remission is made,
and that for a period of 9 to 11 months they must carry a card that shows
them to be in arrears, thus making them second-class Masons; and
WHE REAS it is true that a member can visit a Lodge with a dues card
up to a year in' arrears, but very few Masons realize this fact, and even if
they did, no Mason wants to d isplay his dues car? that is in arrears, and
thus show that he is a member who does not pay his d ues; and
WHEREAS,. Masonic charity demands that we give these unfortunate
brethren who are deserving, but unable to pay, the same Paid-up receipt we
proudly carry, as we do fo r our brethren in the Home;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that our laws be amended to
provide that Lodges may remit dues in advance to the end of the calendar
year fo r brethren who are unable to pay them, and that Lodges should not
be subject to Grand Lodge per capita tax on members whose dues are so
remitted, if they have received no dues from the member for twelve months
prior to the date of the remission.
Respectfully submitted,
CHARLES B. MACKEY, P.M., No. 348

FUNERAL RITUAL - INVOCATION

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 19 is essentially a renewed proposal to provide that Lodges
remit dues in advance to the end of the calendar year for brethren who are
unable to pay them, and that Lodges should not be subject to Grand Lodge
per capita tax on members whose dues are so remitted, if they have received
no dues from the member for twelve months prior to the date of the remission.
Section 577-a permits the remission of dues in June, the effect of which is
remission in advance for a period of six months.
It is the opinion of this Committee that such action may well be taken
at the January Stated Meeting instead of the June Stated Meeting.
There appears to be no substantial reason why remission of dues in advance for a twelve months' period is not justifiable or practical. The Committee concurs in the sentiments expressed by the proponents that Fraternal
spirit requires Fraternal consideration in cases where remission is necessary.
I move the adoption of this resolution and the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "Yes'' vote.
The Committee on Finance indicated its concurrence with the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
WHEREAS , upon first entering the doors of Freemasonry we were informed that " no man should ever enter upon any great or important undertaking without first invoking the blessing of God,"
WHEREAS, as Masons we practice the foregoing by preceding Masonic
business at hand by an invocation to God, whether it be at a Lodge dinner,
a dedication ceremony, a service pin presentation, or a Masonic program or
meeting,
WHEREAS, the funeral service for a departed brother is truly one of the
greatest and most important of our undertakings ,
NOW, IBEREFOR E, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Masonic Funeral
Service be amended to include an invocation to God to be delivered by the
Chaplain just prior to the beginning of the existing funeral ritual, except that
for a joint Masonic/ Religious service the participating clergyman be invited
by the Master to deliver, if he so desires, either the Masonic invocation or
one of his own design.
Respectfully submitted,
CHARLES H. WELSH, P.M., No. 243
JoHN C. SPEIGHT, P.M., No. 243

Tlte Committee on Jurisprudence:
This Resolution proposes to amend Section 577 of the California Masonic
Code, and Section 283-Sth-(a), to provide that Lodges may remit dues in
advance to the end of the calendar year for brethren who are unable to pay
them.
The Committee on Jurisprudence offers the following:
RESOLVED that Section 577 of the California Masonic Code be
amended to read as follows:
"A Lodge may annually remit the accrued dues of those of its members
who are unable to pay them, and at that time may remit the dues of such
members to December 31st of the then calendar year."
DE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 283-Sth-(a) be amended
as follows:
provide
to
" Master Masons whose accrued dues for the preceding 12 months
or until the end of the calendar year have been remitted by Lodge action
at the June Stated meeting."
We offer the Resolution without recommendation.

The Committee on Ritual:
Your Committee on Ritual to which has been referred resolution No. 20,
reports as follows:
No exception is taken by this committee to the proponents' contention
that no man should enter upon any great or important undertaking without
first invoking the blessing of God: However, it must be noted that the composition of every Ceremony or Ritual service conducted in this Grand Jurisdiction is prefaced by appropriate opening remarks followed by a prayer.
Our California ?\fa.sonic Funeral Service is no exception. Your Committee
on Ritual believes that this beautiful ceremony as presently written, is adequate to comply with the requirement of invoking the blessing of God before
entering the body of the service.
It should be noted that the California Masonic Funeral Service is Ritual,
for which reason a participating clergyman could not he invited to deliver an
invocation of his own design. This would in effect produce an optional Ritual
which would be in violation of the requirement of Sec. 554 of the California
Masonic Code.
'Ve move the adoption of the resolution but strongly urgt> a "No" vote.
I am authorized to report that the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes concurs in this recommenda tion.

Adopted 5/6 vote.

The Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 21 proposes that the Grand Lodge provide financial assistance to I3enicia Lodge No. 5 for much nePded repair work on the first
Mas?nic T emple bui~t _in California. This temple is owned by Benicia Lodge
and 1s located at Benicia, one of the truly historical communities in California
and once the capital city of the state. It is also one of the three Masonic
Temples in California available for use by all lodges of our jurisdiction
without special dispensation from the Grand l\Iaster.
The_ pre~ent estimate of the amount necessa ry for repairs and suitable
restoration is $18,000.00. The resolution proposes that the Grand Lodge
advance an amount not to exceed $13,000.00 to Benicia Lodge. The loan

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

307

would be interest-free and would be repayable to the Grand Lodge at the rate
of $100.00 per month.
At the 197 1 Communication the need for restoration of this importan t
Masonic Temple was brought to the attention of the Grand Lodge. The proposal at that time was not approved by the Grand Lodge. However the disapproval was not based on lack of merit of the project, but rather on the
then suggested means of financing the work.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes there is no
question as to the necessity of preserving this building. Last year we recommended that the Grand Master and the officers of Benicia Lodge should
attempt jointly to develop a feasible plan for fina ncing the work. We believe
that the present resolution properly responds to that recommendation and we,
accordingly, recommend a "Yes" vote on Resolution No. 21.
It is not intended t hat th is action shoul d set a precedent for similar fu ture
proposals on financing. Each must be evaluated individually on its merit. In
this instance, the unique historical importance of t his project to Freemasonry
in California, plus the urgent need for commencement of the restoration work,
clearly leads to the conclusion uy the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes t hat now is the time for action on this proposal.
The Resolution calls for the advance of funds by Grand Lodge to be
interest-free. It is the belief of your Committee that a nominal interest
amount should be charged in order that there may be no question, bu t, tha t
the advance of funds, is in fact a bona fide loan.
In doing so we further suggest that the agreement which may be reached
between the Grand Lodge and Benicia Lodge N'o. 5 should be sufficiently
flexi ble so that Benicia Lodge will not be unduly burdened in discharging the
obligation to the Grand Lodge.
I move the adoption of R esolution No. 21 with the provision that a
nominal interest rate be applied to the loan, and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote. I am authorized to report
that the Committee on Finance concurs in that report.
NOTE: (By separate emergent a ction of Grand Lodge 5/ 6 approval was
given to an a pplicable interest rate of " not to exceed 3 per cent.")

The Committee on. Juris prudence indicated that no legislation was
required.
Adopted as amended.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General Purposes,
and on Public Schools.
The Committee on Public Schools at its meeting considered the reasons for
the change of date for Public Schools Week. Due to the advanced planning
of School Boards throughout the State and the problems of coordination and
communication, plus other school activities, the Committee on Public Schools
recommends a "No" vote on Resolution No. 22.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution has the laudable purpose of improving the opportunity for
Public Schools support. The school calendar for 1972-1973 has already been
decided in almost all school districts in California. The incoming Grand
Master, whoever he may be, has indicated a desire to declare the month of
April Public Schools Observance Month and to permit each school district to
select its own period of observance. San Francisco Unified School District has
changed its observance date to April 9th to 13th. There are vital differences
between rural and urban school districts in the dates preferred for Public
Schools Observance. Providing an entire month to choose dates from would
allow for these differences.
Your Committee wishes to emphasize that no single day, week, or month
observance has been, or will be, adequate for the support of Public Education.
Despite more than fifty years of Public Schools observances, Public Education
in California has been declining. Genuine support of the Public Schools is a
year round task. It requires attendance at School Board meetings, not as a
member of a Masonic Lodge but as a good citizen. It requires becoming informed as to the activities of the Public Schools, the use of school buildings
for community purposes, the need for volunteers to assist teachers in the
classrooms, and a willingness to take an active part in all these chores.

"CALIFORNIA FREEMASON" 1\t1AGAZINE

The per capita for the editing, printing and distribution of this fine
magazine has remained at 35¢ for the past six years. This per capita has
remained constant despite a deficit for the last two years.
The idea of increasing the per capita to cover this deficit was suggested to
and discussed by your Committee. Increasing the per capita to make this
project self-supporting has merit only because a balance may be achieved.
We know that our Grand Secretary's office has been investigating ways
and means to secure cost reductions. Notwithstanding this, we now suggest to
the incoming Grand Master that a more diligent study of all areas be pursued
this coming year in order to intelligently arrive at a proper basis for the per
capita assessment. Accordingly we recommend a continuance of the 35¢ per
capita for the year ending June 30, 1973.
COMMENTS RELATIVE TO PROPOSED BUDGET

In our report last year, we said, "you may rest assured that your Grand
Officers are at all times cognizant of the need to operate your Grand Lodge as
economically as is possible while promoting the many programs and activities
of this widespread ~fasonic jurisdiction." We believe that the Grand Lodge
Officers did, in fact, administer the financial affairs of Grand Lodge in a
creditable manner.
Similarly the Budget we are proposing to you for the year ending June 30,
1973, has been prepared in a most painstaking manner and we have every
confidence that our new administration, the committees, and other groups to
whom our finances are entrusted will use all due care to hold controllable
expenditures to a minimum consistent with the objectives of planned programs.
Notwithstanding increased salary and related costs, printing expense, etc.,
budgeted net e>..i>ense for the year ending next June 30th is close to $10,000
less than last year's actual expense.
Your Committee on Finance expresses appreciation to the Grand Lodge
Officers, Committee and Board Chairmen for their assistance and cooperation
in the preparation of the proposed budget.
